and he was victorious in every battle.
When the main army reached Xīnlín 新林,
he followed Wáng Mào 王茂 to Xīntíng 新亭,
and fought vigorously alongside Zhūquèháng 朱雀航,
capturing and killing many.
When Jiànkāng 建康 city was pacified,
he was made General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) and Commander of the Right Cavalcade (馬右夾轂主).
In the first year of Tiānjiān 天監 (502 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngfēng County 永豐縣侯,
with a fief of five hundred households.
He was appointed General of Elite Cavalry (驍騎將軍).
He was sent out as the Administrator of Xūyí 盱眙 (Xūyí Tàishǒu 盱眙太守).
In the second year (503 CE),
he was promoted to Acting Imperial Commissioner (假節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (督北徐州諸軍事), General Who Assists the State (輔國將軍), and Governor of Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (北徐州刺史),
stationed at Zhōnglí 鍾離.
When the Wèi 魏 invaders encroached upon the prefecture,
Yìzhī 義之 defeated them.
In the third year (504 CE),
he was advanced in rank to General Who Quells the Army (冠軍將軍),
and his fief was increased by two hundred households.
In the fourth year (505 CE),
a large-scale northern expedition was launched.
The Prince of Línchuān 臨川, Governor of Yángzhōu 揚州, led the various armies to encamp at Luòkǒu 洛口.
Yìzhī 義之, with the provincial troops, received orders
to be the vanguard.
He attacked the Wèi 魏 garrison at Liángchéng 梁城,
and captured it.
In the fifth year (506 CE),
Gāozǔ 高祖, finding the military campaign protracted,
issued an imperial decree recalling the armies.
The various armies dispersed and retreated.
Yuán Yīng 元英, the Prince of Zhōngshān 中山 of Wèi 魏, seized the opportunity to pursue them,
attacking and capturing Mǎtóu 馬頭.
The grain stores within the city
were all moved north by Wèi 魏.
All the strategists said:
"The Wèi 魏 are transporting grain back north,
so they will not advance south again."
Gāozǔ 高祖 said:
"Not so.
They will surely advance their troops;
this is not the truth."
He then sent skilled artisans to repair and fortify Zhōnglí 鍾離 city,
[一一] and ordered Yìzhī 義之 to prepare for defense.
That winter,
Yīng 英 indeed led his Prince of Ānlè 安樂 Yuán Dàomíng 元道明, General Who Pacifies the East (平東將軍) Yáng Dàyǎn 楊大眼, and a host of several hundred thousand men,
to invade Zhōnglí 鍾離.
Zhōnglí 鍾離 city was blocked to the north by the Huái Huái River.
The Wèi 魏 people built a pontoon bridge on the west bank of Shàoyáng Zhōu 邵陽洲,
crossing the Huái Huái River to open a path.
Yīng 英 occupied the east bank,
and Dàyǎn 大眼 occupied the west bank,
to attack the city.
At that time, the city only had three thousand troops.
Yìzhī 義之 commanded them,
resisting the attacks from all directions.
The Wèi 魏 army then used carts loaded with earth to fill the moat,
making their soldiers carry earth to follow,
while heavily armored cavalry pressed them from behind.
If anyone did not turn back in time,
they were crushed by the earth.
Soon, the moat was full.
Yīng 英 and Dàyǎn 大眼 personally supervised the battle,
attacking relentlessly day and night,
taking turns in shifts.
They fell and rose again,
none retreating.
They also deployed flying towers (飛樓) and battering rams (衝車) to strike,
wherever they hit, the city walls would collapse.
[一二] Yìzhī 義之 then used mud to repair the breaches.
Although the battering rams penetrated, they could not destroy the wall.
Yìzhī 義之 was skilled in archery.
Wherever the attack was most critical and dangerous,
he would gallop there to rescue.
Every time he drew his bow,
no one failed to fall when the arrow was released.
In one day, they fought dozens of engagements,
with tens of thousands killed and wounded before and after.
The Wèi 魏 dead piled up as high as the city walls.
In the fourth month of the sixth year (507 CE),
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Cáo Jǐngzōng 曹景宗 and Wéi Ruì 韋叡 to lead an army of two hundred thousand to relieve them.
Upon their arrival,
they fought with the Wèi 魏,
and utterly defeated them.
Yīng 英, Dàyǎn 大眼, and others all escaped and fled.
Yìzhī 義之 then led light cavalry in pursuit as far as Luòkǒu 洛口 before returning.
The number of beheaded and captured alive
was incalculable.
For his merit, he was advanced in rank to General of the Army Adviser (軍師將軍),
his fief was increased by two hundred households,

and he was promoted to Imperial Commissioner (持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Qīngzhōu 靑州 and Jìzhōu 冀州 (督青冀二州諸軍事), General Who Conquers the Barbarians (征虜將軍), and Governor of Qīngzhōu 靑州 and Jìzhōu 冀zhōu (青冀二州刺史).
Before he was formally appointed,

he was changed to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nányǎnzhōu 南兗州, Yǎnzhōu 兗州, Xúzhōu 徐州, Qīngzhōu 靑州, and Jìzhōu 冀zhōu (督南兗兗徐青冀五州諸軍事), General Who Assists the State (輔國將軍), and Governor of Nányǎnzhōu 南兗州 (南兗州刺史).
He was impeached by the authorities for allowing contraband goods to leave the province
and was dismissed.
That same year,
he was appointed 朱衣直閤 (zhūyī zhíhé, an official of the inner enclosure wearing red robes),
and made General of the Left Elite Cavalry (左驍騎將軍),
with his position as Inner Enclosure guard remaining as before.
He was promoted to Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (太子右衞率),
also holding the position of Colonel of Yue Cavalry (越騎校尉),
and Acting Imperial Commissioner (假節).
In the eighth year (509 CE),
he was sent out as Imperial Commissioner (持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xiāngzhōu 湘州 (督湘州諸軍事), General Who Conquers from Afar (征遠將軍), and Governor of Xiāngzhōu 湘zhōu (湘州刺史).
In the ninth year (510 CE),
he returned to court with his original rank,
and shortly after became the Grand Secretary (司馬) for the Prince of Línchuān 臨川, who was the Minister of Works (司空),
retaining his generalship as before.
In the tenth year (511 CE),
he was promoted to General of the Right Guard (右衞將軍).
In the thirteenth year (514 CE),
he was transferred to General of the Left Guard (左衞將軍).
That winter,
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Kāng Xuàn 康絢, Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (太子右衛率), to lead the armies in building the Jīngshān Jing Mountain Weir 荊山堰.
The following year (515 CE),
Wèi 魏 sent General Lǐ Tándìng 李曇定 with a large army to approach Jīngshān 荊山,
and spread rumors that they intended to destroy the weir.
An imperial decree granted Yìzhī 義之 a commissioner's staff,
and he was ordered to lead Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud (太僕卿) Yú Hóngwén 魚弘文, General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) Cáo Shìzōng 曹世宗, Xú Yuánhé 徐元和, and others to reinforce Xuàn 絢.
Before the army arrived,
Xuàn 絢 and his forces had already defeated the Wèi 魏 army.
Wèi 魏 again sent the great general Lǐ Píng 李平 to attack Xiáshí 峽石,
besieging General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) Zhào Zǔyuè 趙祖悅.
Yìzhī 義之 again led Zhūyī Zhíhé 朱衣直閤 Wáng Shénniàn 王神念 and others to relieve them.
At that time, the Wèi 魏 forces were strong,
and Shénniàn 神念 could not capture the pontoon bridge at Xiáshí 峽石,
so the relief forces could not advance in time,
and Xiáshí 峽石 subsequently fell.
Yìzhī 義之 returned with his army,
and was impeached by the authorities.
Gāozǔ 高祖, considering him a meritorious minister,
did not pursue the matter.
In the fifteenth year (516 CE),
he was again appointed Imperial Commissioner with Staff (使持節), Area Commander-in-Chief of Xiāngzhōu 湘州 (都督湘州諸軍事), General Who Commands with Trust (信威將軍), and Governor of Xiāngzhōu 湘zhōu (湘州刺史).
That same year,

he was reappointed Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs along the Huái Huái River in Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (都督北徐州緣淮諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the North (平北將軍), and Governor of Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (北徐州刺史).
Yìzhī 義之 was by nature generous and magnanimous,
and as a general, he was able to soothe and control his subordinates,
earning their utmost loyalty.
When he served in a provincial capacity,
the officials and people found peace under him.
Shortly after, he was granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments (鼓吹一部),
and was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Yíngdào County 營道縣侯,
with his number of households remaining as before.
In the third year of Pǔtōng 普通 (522 CE),
he was summoned to be General Protector of the Army (護軍將軍),
with the drum and wind instruments remaining as before.
In the tenth month of the fourth year (523 CE),
he passed away.
Gāozǔ 高祖 deeply mourned him,
and issued an edict saying:
"Chāng Yìzhī 昌義之, General Protector of the Army and Founding Marquis of Yíngdào County,
was resourceful and composed in strategy,
and his heart was generous and forbearing.
His sincerity was manifest at the beginning of the reign,
and his achievements were prominent in the border regions.
He was just about to be further used as a trusted aide,
entrusted with the imperial guard;
suddenly, he met his demise,
which saddens my heart.
He is hereby posthumously granted the titles of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (散騎常侍) and General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎將軍),
along with a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
A 'Secret Vessel from the Eastern Garden' (東園祕器) is granted,
and one set of court robes.
A funeral gift of twenty thousand coins,
two hundred bolts of cloth,
and two hundred catties of wax.
His posthumous name shall be 'Liè' 烈."
His son, Bǎoyè 寶業, succeeded him,
and his highest official post was General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) and Governor of Qiáozhōu 譙州 (譙州刺史).
Chén Lìbù Shàngshū Yáo Chá said: Zhāng Huìshào, Féng Dàogēn, Kāng Xuàn, Chāng Yìzhī,
initially rose from the ranks of the followers of the Emperor,
their achievements were therefore minor.
However, when the bandits set fire to the gates,
Huìshào distinguished himself through fierce fighting;
when Héféi and Shàoyáng were under siege,
Dàogēn and Yìzhī made significant contributions;
when the campaign of Fúshān began,
Kāng Xuàn took charge of the matter: they each had their own merits,
and it was fitting that they were promoted and honored.
Before this, the Zhenxing star guarded the Tiānjiāng river, and the weir was built;
when it retreated from its station, the weir broke.
This was not merely a matter of human affairs,
but also involved the Way of Heaven.
Jiàokān Jì
Lièzhuàn dì shí sān Zōng Jué Liú Tǎn Yuè Ài
Zōng Jué, courtesy name Míngyáng,
was from Nièyáng, Nányáng.
His family had long resided in Jiānglíng.
His grandfather, Bǐng,
was offered the position of Prince's Grand Tutor during the Sòng dynasty but declined,
holding a high reputation.
His father, Fán,
was a Xīzhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn.
Jué was diligent in his studies when young,
and had a firm and capable character.
At twenty,
he was recommended as Xiùcái in Yǐngzhōu,
and successively served as Línchuān Wáng Chángshì and Piàojì Xíngcānjūn.
When Qí Sītú Jìnglǐng Wáng gathered scholars at the Western Mansion,
and all viewed the paintings and calligraphy,
Jué was also among them.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
a peace agreement was made with Wèi.
Jué was commanded to receive the Wèi envoys along with Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng Rèn Fǎng,
both being selections of the time.
When Emperor Wǔ's legitimate grandson, Nánjùn Wáng, resided in Xīzhōu,
he appointed Jué to manage his correspondence.
Jué was known for his literary skills
and also admired for his integrity and uprightness,
which is why he was appointed.
Shortly thereafter, Wénhuì Tàizǐ died,
and the King became the Imperial Grandson.
Jué continued to manage his correspondence.
When the Grandson ascended the throne,
he often acted improperly.
Jué gradually distanced himself,
obtaining the position of Línglìng,
and later promoted to Shàngshū Dūguānláng.
At the end of the Lóngchāng era,
the Young Emperor was executed,
and many of his former favorites suffered misfortune.
Only Jué and Fù Zhāo escaped due to their integrity and uprightness.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he appointed Jué as Yǐngzhōu Zhìzhōng.
He was well-regarded and competent in his duties.
Due to his father's old age, he resigned and returned to his hometown.
When Nánkāng Wáng became Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
he appointed Jué as Biéjià.
When the Righteous Army rose,
he was promoted to Xīzhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn,
while retaining his position as Biéjià.
At that time, among the dignitaries in Xītǔ,
only Jué, Yuè Ài, and Liú Tǎn from the same commandery were trusted and recommended by the people of the province.
Therefore, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xiāo Yǐngzhòu greatly relied on them,
consulting them on every matter.
When Gāozǔ's army departed from Yōngzhōu,
Yǐngzhòu sent Jué from Yángkǒu
to personally report on military strategies
and to escort military supplies.
Gāozǔ treated him with great respect.
In the early days of Zhōngxīng,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
but resigned due to mourning for his father.
He was then appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Wèijūn Zhǎngshǐ.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
retaining his general title.
In the second year,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Yòuwèishul.
In the winter of that year,
he was promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
participating in the major selections.
In the third year,
he died
at the age of forty-nine.
His son, Yàoqīng, inherited his position.
Jué's cousin, Yuè,
had a good reputation and conduct,
and was praised by the people of the province,
surpassing Jué.
He successively served as Shàngshū Kùbùláng,
Yǐngzhōu Zhìzhōng,
and Běizhōngláng Lùshì Cānjūnshì.
Liú Tǎn, courtesy name Déduó,
was from Ānzhòng, Nányáng,
a seventh-generation descendant of Jìn Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Qiáo.
Tǎn was recognized by his cousin Qiú at a young age.
In the early Jiànchuán era of Qí,
he served as Nánjùn Wángguó Chángshì,
and was soon appointed Cánlíng Lìng,
then promoted to Nánzhōngláng Lùshì Cānjūn.
He was known for his capability and efficiency wherever he served.
When Nánkāng Wáng became Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Tǎn served as Xīzhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
concurrently holding the position of Zhǎnglìu.
When the Righteous Army rose,
he was promoted to Zīyì Cānjūn.
At that time, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Yáng Gōngzé, who was Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
led his army to Xiàkǒu.
The Western Court deliberated on who should govern the provincial affairs.
Tǎn said to the assembly:
"The disposition of the people in the Xiāng region
is easily disturbed and difficult to trust.
If only military men are used,
the common people will fear encroachment and exploitation;
if literati are sent,
their authority and strategy will not be asserted.
If you truly wish to pacify the provincial capital
and ensure sufficient food for both the army and civilians,
there is no one superior to this old minister.
In the campaign against the Xiānliú,
I secretly offered myself."
So they followed his suggestion.
He was then appointed Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ and Chángshā Tàishǒu,
acting as Xiāngzhōu Shì.
Tǎn had previously served in Xiāngzhōu
and had many old favors.
Many people welcomed him along the road.
Upon arrival, he selected capable officials,
assigned them to the ten commanderies,
mobilized all able-bodied men,
transported over three hundred thousand hú of grain,
delivering it to the Righteous Army,
thus providing ample provisions.
At that time, Dōnghūn sent Ānchéng Tàishǒu Liú Xīzǔ to defeat Fàn Sēngjiǎn, the Tàishǒu selected by Xītái, at Píngdū.
Xīzǔ then sent a proclamation to the Xiāng region,
whereupon Shǐxīng Nèishǐ Wáng Sēngcàn responded.
The people of Shàolíng drove out their Nèishǐ Chǔ Jiàn,
and Zhōu Huī of Yǒngyáng raised an army to attack Shǐ'ān Commandery,
both siding with Sēngcàn.
Shào Tánnòng and Dèng Dàojiè of Guìyáng sought revenge for private feuds,
and consequently formed a party and joined them.
Sēngcàn proclaimed himself Píngxī Jiāngjūn and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
appointing Zhōu Shū of Yǒngyáng as his chief strategist,
and headquartered his army in Jiànníng.
From then on, all the commanderies in the Xiāng region
rose up like swarms;
only the four counties of Línxiāng, Xiāngyīn, Líuyáng, and Luó remained intact.
The people of the province all wanted to flee by boat,
but Tǎn gathered all the boats and burned them.
He dispatched general Yǐn Fǎlüè to resist Sēngcàn,
and they were in a stalemate.
The former Xiāngzhōu Zhènjūn Zhōng Xuánshào secretly plotted to join Sēngcàn,
recruiting hundreds of gentry and commoners,
all signing their names and setting a date
to rebel against the provincial capital.
Tǎn heard of their plot,
but pretended not to know.
He prolonged a lawsuit until night,
thus the city gates were not closed,
which made them suspicious.
Xuánshào had not yet acted.
The next morning, he went to Tǎn to ask why.
Tǎn detained him and conversed with him for a long time,
secretly sending his personal soldiers to search his house for documents.
Xuánshào was still sitting and had not yet left,
when the soldiers returned, reporting that they had found all the documents and their contents.
Xuánshào immediately confessed,
and was executed on the spot.
His documents were burned,
and no questions were asked of his other confederates.
The people were ashamed and yet submitted,
and the province was thus pacified.
Fǎlüè and Sēngcàn were in a stalemate for several months.
When the city of Jiànkāng was pacified,
Gōngzé returned to the province,
and the bandits began to disperse.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
for his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Lìpǔ Xiànzǐ,
with three hundred households.
He was promoted to Píngxī Sīmǎ and Xīnxīng Tàishǒu.
In the third year of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Xīzhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ,
and died
at the age of sixty-two.
His son, Quán, inherited his position.
The next spring,
he dispatched the attendants Chén Jiànzūn (陳建孫) to send Jìlián's (季連) younger brother, the Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎) Zǐyuān (子淵), and Jìlián's (季連) two sons as envoys to Shǔ (蜀),
conveying the imperial decree to comfort and console them.
Jìlián (季連) received the order
and prepared for their return.
Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed Dèng Yuánqǐ (鄧元起), a general from Xītái (西臺), as the Governor of Yìzhōu (益州).
Yuánqǐ (元起)
was from Nánjùn (南郡).
When Jìlián (季連) was in Nánjùn (南郡),
he had always looked down on Yuánqǐ (元起).
A record-keeper named Zhū Dàochēn (朱道琛),
who had once served as a Dūlù (都錄) in Jìlián's (季連) administration,
was a lawless ruffian.
Having committed a crime,
Jìlián (季連) wanted to kill him,
but he escaped by fleeing.
At this time, he spoke to Yuánqǐ (元起), saying:
"Yìzhōu (益州) has been in chaos for a long time;
the public and private treasuries must have suffered great losses.
Liú Yìzhōu (劉益州) left completely empty-handed when he departed,
how could he possibly arrange for messengers to be sent far away again?
Dàochēn (道琛) requests to go first to inspect
and welcome you along the way;
otherwise,
provisions for a thousand li
will not be easy to obtain."
Yuánqǐ (元起) agreed to this.
Once Dàochēn (道琛) arrived,
his words were disrespectful,
and he also visited various officials and gentry in the prefecture and province,
seizing any objects he saw.
If he didn't get what he wanted,
he would say:
"It will eventually belong to others,
why be so reluctant to part with it?"
At this, the military and the government were greatly alarmed,
believing that when Yuánqǐ (元起) arrived, he would surely execute Jìlián (季連)
and bring disaster upon his allies,
and they all spoke of this to Jìlián (季連).
Jìlián (季連) also believed this to be true;
moreover, he regretted his past disrespect towards Yuánqǐ (元起),
and became increasingly resentful.
The Sīmǎ (司馬) Zhū Shìlüè (朱士略) persuaded Jìlián (季連)
to ask for Bāxī Jùn (巴西郡),
leaving his three sons as hostages,
and Jìlián (季連) agreed.
Soon after,
Jìlián (季連) summoned his assistants,
falsely claiming an order from Qí Xuāndé Huánghòu (齊宣德皇后),
gathered troops, rebelled again,
and captured and killed Zhū Dàochēn (朱道琛).
He sent a letter to Zhū Shìlüè (朱士略),
and also summoned Lǐ Yīng (李膺).
Yīng (膺) and Shìlüè (士略) both refused the summons.
When the envoy returned,
Yuánqǐ (元起) gathered his troops in Bāxī (巴西) to await him,
and Jìlián (季連) executed Shìlüè's (士略) three sons.
In the sixth month of the first year of Tiānjiān (天監) (502 CE),
Yuánqǐ (元起) arrived in Bāxī (巴西).
Jìlián (季連) sent his general Lǐ Fèngbó (李奉伯) and others to resist.
The armies engaged,
with gains and losses on both sides.
After a long time,
Fèngbó (奉伯) was defeated and retreated to Chéngdū (成都).
Jìlián (季連) herded the residents,
closed the city gates, and held firm.
Yuánqǐ (元起) gradually advanced and besieged him.
That winter,
Jiāng Xīzhī (江希之) and others, who were Jìlián's (季連) Chéngjú Cānjūn (城局參軍), plotted to surrender the city,
but it did not succeed,
and Jìlián (季連) executed them.
Shǔzhōng (蜀中) had been in turmoil for two years,
food in the city ran out,
a shēng (升) of rice cost three thousand (coins),
and there was nowhere to buy it.
Those who starved to death lay piled upon each other.
Those without relatives or friends
were even killed and eaten.
Jìlián (季連) ate porridge for months,
in dire hunger and with no plan.
In the first month of the second year (503 CE),
Gāozǔ (高祖) sent the Zhǔshū (主書) Zhào Jǐngyuè (趙景悅) to proclaim an imperial decree for Jìlián (季連) to surrender,
and Jìlián (季連) bared his upper body to beg for punishment.
Yuánqǐ (元起) moved Jìlián (季連) outside the city,
and soon after visited him,
treating him with courtesy.
Jìlián (季連) thanked him, saying:
"If I had known this earlier,
how could there have been the events of the other day?"
Yuánqǐ (元起) executed Lǐ Fèngbó (李奉伯) and all the other rebel leaders,
and sent Jìlián (季lián) back to the capital.
When Jìlián (季連) was about to depart,
no one saw him off,
except Gōng Qiè (龔愜).
Initially,
when Yuánqǐ (元起) was en route,
fearing the campaign would not succeed
and that he would have nothing to reward with,
he promised all who joined him
official appointments.
Thus, those who received the official documents of Biéjià (別駕) and Zhìzhōng (治中)
numbered nearly two thousand men.
After Jìlián (季連) arrived,
he went to the palace gate to express his apologies,
and Gāozǔ (高祖) granted him an audience.
Jìlián (季連) entered through the Dōngyèmén (東掖門),
bowing his head to the ground every few steps
until he reached Gāozǔ (高祖).
Gāozǔ (高祖) smiled and said to him:
"You wanted to emulate Liú Bèi (劉備), but you didn't even reach the level of Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述).
Did you have no '臥龍 (Wòlóng, Crouching Dragon)' minister?"
Jìlián (季連) bowed his head again to apologize.
He was pardoned and reduced to a commoner.
In the first month of the fourth year (505 CE),
while leaving through the Jiànyángmén (建陽門),
he was killed by Lìn Dàogōng (藺道恭) from Shǔ (蜀).
When Jìlián (季連) was in Shǔ (蜀),
he had killed Dàogōng's (道恭) father,
and Dàogōng (道恭) had fled.
Now, he took his revenge.
Chén Bózhī (陳伯之) was
from Suīlíng (睢陵), Jìyīn (濟陰).
As a child, he possessed great physical strength.
At thirteen or fourteen,
he liked to wear an otter fur hat
and carry a dagger.
He would watch for ripe rice in the neighboring fields
and steal and cut it.
Once, he was seen by a field owner,
who reprimanded him, saying:
"Chǔzǐ (楚子), don't move!"
Bózhī (伯之) said to the field owner:
"Your rice is fortunately abundant,
what's the harm in one load?"
The field owner was about to seize him,
but Bózhī (伯之) advanced with his staff-knife,
intending to stab him,
saying:
"Chǔzǐ (楚子) will definitely show you!"
The field owners all ran away,
and Bózhī (伯之) leisurely carried the rice home.
When he grew older,
he frequently committed robberies in Zhōnglí (鍾離).
Once, he used his face to spy on someone's boat,
and the boatman chopped at him,
cutting off his left ear.
Later, he followed Wáng Guǎngzhī (王廣之), a Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) from his hometown.
Guǎngzhī (廣之) admired his bravery,
and whenever he lay down at night,
he always brought Bózhī (伯之) with him on campaigns.
Qí Ānlù Wáng (齊安陸王) Zǐjìng (子敬) was in Nányánzhōu (南兗州),
and held a considerable armed force for self-defense.
Míngdì (明帝) dispatched Guǎngzhī (廣之) to suppress Zǐjìng (子敬).
When Guǎngzhī (廣之) reached Ōuyáng (歐陽),
he sent Bózhī (伯之) as a vanguard.
When the city gate opened,
he entered alone and decapitated Zǐjìng (子敬).
He also repeatedly achieved military successes,
and was successively promoted for his merits to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Piàojì Sīmǎ (驃騎司馬),
and enfeoffed as the Earl of Yúfù Xiàn (魚復縣),
with a stipend of five hundred households.
Initially,
Yuánchōng (元沖) raised an army.
He sought Zhāng Xiàojì (張孝季) of Xúnyáng (尋陽),
and Xiàojì (孝季) followed him.
After their defeat,
Bózhī (伯之) pursued Xiàojì (孝季) but did not catch him.
He captured Xiàojì's (孝季) mother, Lady Láng (郎氏),
and killed her by pouring hot wax on her.
He sent a messenger back to the capital to report to Hǔyá (虎牙) and his brothers.
Hǔyá (虎牙) and others fled to Xūyí (盱眙).
The people of Xūyí (盱眙), Xú Ān (徐安), Zhuāng Xīngshào (莊興紹), and Zhāng Xiǎnmíng (張顯明), ambushed them.
They could not resist
and were instead killed.
Gāozǔ (高祖) dispatched Wáng Mào (王茂) to attack Bózhī (伯之).
When Bózhī (伯之) heard that Mào (茂) was coming,
he said to Chǔ Quán (褚𥱰) and others:
"Since Wáng Guān (王觀) has not accepted the command,
and Zhèng Bólún (鄭伯倫) is unwilling to follow,
we should be trapped empty-handed.
Now, we should first pacify Yùzhāng (豫章),
open up the southern route,
mobilize more manpower,
and transport more provisions and grain.
Then, we can sweep northwards
to strike at their hungry and weary troops.
There will be no worry of failure."
So, he left the local man Táng Gàirén (唐蓋人) to guard the city,
and they all headed towards Yùzhāng (豫章).
The Grand Administrator, Zhèng Bólún (鄭伯倫), held his ground firmly,
and Bózhī (伯之) attacked but could not take it.
When Wáng Mào's (王茂) vanguard arrived,
Bózhī (伯之) arranged his troops to face the enemy.
He was defeated and fled,
escaping along a secret path to north of the Jiāng (江),
entering Wèi (魏) with his son Hǔyá (虎牙) and Chǔ Quán (褚𥱰).

Wèi (魏) appointed Bózhī (伯之) as Envoy with Credentials (使持節), Palace Attendant (散騎常侍), Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Huáinán (都督淮南諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the South (平南將軍), Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (光祿大夫), and Marquis of Qǔjiāng County (曲江縣侯).
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (天監) [505 CE],
an imperial edict commanded the Grand Commandant (太尉), Prince Hóng (宏) of Línchuān (臨川), to lead a large army to attack the north.
Hóng (宏) ordered his secretary Qīu Chí (丘遲) to write a private letter to Bózhī (伯之), saying: "General Chén (陳), are you well?
Most fortunately.
Your bravery surpasses all three armies,
and your talent is unique in the world.
You abandoned the small ambition of the sparrow,
and yearned for the wild goose to soar
high.
In the past, you adapted to opportunities,
met an enlightened lord,
achieved great deeds,
founded a state and inherited a family.
With crimson wheels and ornate hubs,
commanding banners across ten thousand li,
how magnificent that was!
How
is it that in one morning you became a fugitive captive,
trembling at the sound of a whistling arrow,
kneeling before a nomad's yurt?
How ignoble is that!
Examining your decision to leave or stay,
there was no other
reason,
but simply that you could not examine yourself internally
and were influenced by external rumors,
becoming lost and reckless,
leading to this.
The Sacred Court pardons crimes and evaluates merits,
overlooking flaws and employing talents,
gathering
loyal hearts from all under heaven,
and reassuring the wavering in all things.
This is known to you, General,
and requires no lengthy discourse from me.
Zhū Wěi (朱鮪) shed the blood of his kin,
Zhāng Xiù (張繡) raised a
weapon against his beloved son,
yet the Han (漢) lord did not doubt them,
and the Wei (魏) ruler treated them as before.
Moreover, General, you have not committed the crimes of those men of old,
and your achievements are significant in this age.
To know to turn back from a迷途 (lost path)
is what the ancient sages approved;
to return from not far off
is highly praised by old canons.
Our Emperor bends the law to extend grace,
letting even a swallowed boat escape.
General, your pines
and cypresses are not cut down,
your relatives live in peace;
your high platform has not collapsed,
your beloved concubine is still there.
Your lingering thoughts,
how can they not be mentioned!
Now, meritorious officials and famous generals,
arranged in an orderly line
like wild geese.
Wearing yellow and purple sashes,
they advise on strategies in the command tent;
riding light chariots and carrying credentials,
they undertake responsibilities on the frontier.
They have all sworn oaths by killing a horse,
to be passed down to their descendants.
General, are you alone
to shamelessly beg for your life,
and gallop about in a foreign land?
Is this not lamentable!
For with the strength of Mùróng Chāo (慕容超),
his body was sent to the eastern market;
with the might of Yáo Hóng (姚泓),
he was bound and presented at the western capital.
Therefore, it is known that where frost and dew are equally distributed,
no different species can grow;
in the old lands of Jī (姬)
and Hàn (漢),
no mixed breeds should be taken.
The northern barbarians have usurped the Central Plains,
for many years.
Their evil has accumulated and their misfortune is full,
it is time for them to be utterly destroyed.
Moreover, the false usurpers are foolish and cunning,
slaughtering
each other.
Their tribes are scattered,
and their chieftains are suspicious and disloyal.
They are about to be led by the neck to the barbarian mansion,
and have their heads displayed in the Straw Street.
Yet you, General, are like a fish swimming in a boiling cauldron,
and nesting atop a flying banner,
is this not bewildering!
In the late spring, the third month,
the grass in Jiāngnán (江南) grows long,
varied flowers blossom on trees,
flocks of birds fly about.
Seeing the banners and drums of your old country,
remembering your past in those days,
stroking the lute
and ascending the parapet,
would you not feel sorrow and regret?
Thus, Lián Gōng (廉公)'s longing for the Zhao (趙) general,
and Wú Zǐ (吳子)'s weeping by the Xīhé (西河),
are human emotions.
General, are you alone without feelings!
I hope
you will soon make a good plan,
and seek much fortune for yourself."
Bózhī (伯之) then, with 8,000 troops, returned to Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Hǔyá (虎牙) was killed by the Wèi (魏) people.
When Bózhī (伯之) arrived,

he was appointed Envoy with Credentials (使持節), Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Xīyù Prefecture (都督西豫州諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the North (平北將軍), Governor of Xīyù Prefecture (西豫州刺史),
Marquis of Yǒngxīn County (永新縣侯),
with a fief of one thousand households.
Before he took up the post,
he was again appointed Palace Attendant (通直散騎常侍), General of Agile Cavalry (驍騎將軍),
and then Grand Master of the Middle (太中大夫).
After a long time,
he died at home.
Some of his sons remained in Wèi (魏).
Chǔ Quán (褚𥱰) was in Wèi (魏),
and the Wèi (魏) people wanted to promote him.
At a Wèi (魏) imperial banquet,
Quán (𥱰) playfully composed a poem, saying:
"On my cap I wear a caged crown,
over my trousers I wear a crimson robe;
I do not know if this present is right,
I do not know if the past was not wrong."
The Wèi (魏) people were angered,
and exiled him to become the Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng (始平).
He hunted daily,
fell from his horse, and died.
The historian comments: "Liú Jìlián (劉季連) was a minor official of letters,
yet he could not preserve himself; this is indeed the result of accustomed chaos.
Chén Bózhī (陳伯之) was a small man who commanded the instruments of a gentleman,
and the bandits falsely accused and stripped him of them.
How could he last long?"
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 15: Wáng Zhān (王瞻), Wáng Zhì (王志), Wáng Jùn (王峻), Wáng Jiǎn (王暕) (son Xùn (訓)), Wáng Tài (王泰), Wáng Fèn (王份) (grandsons Xī (錫), Qiān (僉)), Zhāng Chōng (張充), Liǔ Yùn (柳惲), Cài Zūn (蔡撙), Jiāng Qiàn (江蒨).
Wáng Zhān (王瞻), courtesy name Sīfàn (思範),
was from Línyí (臨沂), Lángyé (琅邪), a grand-nephew of Sòng (宋) Grand Preceptor Hóng (弘).
His grandfather, Liǔ (柳),
was Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (光祿大夫) and Marquis of Dōngtíng (東亭).
His father, Yóu (猷),
was Minister of Justice (廷尉卿).
When Zhān (瞻) was a few years old,
he once received instruction from a teacher.
At that time, an entertainer passed by his gate,
and all his classmates went out to watch,
but Zhān (瞻) alone did not look,
continuing to recite as before.
His paternal cousin, Minister of the Secretariat (尚書僕射) Sēngdá (僧達), heard of this and was impressed,
saying to Zhān's (瞻) father:
"Our clan will not decline;
its future rests with this child."
At the age of twelve,
he mourned his father,
and was known for his filial piety.
When the mourning period ended, he inherited the title of Marquis of Dōngtíng (東亭).
Shì’s family resided generation after generation in Jìankāng’s Jìnzhōng Lǐ, Mǎfān Xiàng.
Since his father Sēngqián,
the family ethos was largely one of leniency and forgiveness;
Shì was especially generous and kind.
In all the offices he held,
he never impeached anyone for faults or transgressions.
A guest of his once stole the axle-pin from Shì’s carriage and sold it.
Shì knew but did not question him,
treating him as before.
For guests who frequented his home,
he would specifically cover up their faults and praise their good qualities.
His brothers, sons, and nephews were all earnest, modest, and amiable.
People of the time called the various princes of Mǎfān “the elders.”
In the fourth year of Pǔtōng,
Shì was reburied.
Gāozǔ bestowed a generous funeral stipend and gifts upon him,
and posthumously named him Ān.
He had five sons:
Jī, Xiū, Yīn, Cāo, and Sù,
all of whom were renowned.
Wáng Jùn, courtesy name Màoyuǎn,
was a native of Lángxié Línyí.
His great-grandfather, Jìnghóng,
was highly reputed in the Sòng dynasty,
holding positions up to Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
His grandfather, Zànzhī,
was Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
His father, Xiùzhī,
was Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
Jùn was handsome in appearance in his youth
and had refined manners.
He began his career as a Zhùzuò Zuǒláng,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngjūn Lúlíng Wáng Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
Shàolíng Wáng Wénxué,
and Tàifù Zhǔbù.
The prefect, Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng of Qí, greatly appreciated and valued him.
He was promoted to Sītú Zhǔbù,
but resigned due to his father’s mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ
and Jìan’ān Wáng Yǒu.
He was sent out as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Guìyáng Nèishǐ.
At that time, when the righteous army arose,
many commanderies in the upper reaches of the river were alarmed and disturbed.
Jùn closed the city gates and remained calm,
and the entire commandery was pacified,
for which the common people relied on him.
In the early Tiānjian era,
he was recalled and appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Gāozǔ was very pleased with his demeanor and conduct,
and he was appreciated and promoted alongside Xiè Lǎn of Chénjùn.
Soon after, he was promoted to Lìbù.
He was not considered competent in that office,
so he was transferred to Zhēnglǔ Ānchéng Wáng Chángshǐ.
He also served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ and Yóují Jiāngjūn.
He was sent out as Xuānchéng Tàishǒu.
His governance was pure and harmonious,
and the officials and people were at peace with him.
After serving for three years,
he was summoned and appointed Shìzhōng,
then promoted to Dùzhī Shàngshū.
He also concurrently held the original office of Qǐbù Shàngshū
and supervised the construction of the Tàijí Diàn.
After the project was completed,
he was sent out as Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Píngxī Chángshǐ, and Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn, Zhènxī Chángshǐ, and Shǔjùn Tàishǒu.
Upon his return, he served as Zuǒmín Shàngshū
and concurrently Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
where he gained an excellent reputation for his selections.
Jùn was by nature meticulous and elegant,
without any desire for competition or advancement.
He once made an agreement with Xiè Lǎn
that once they reached the office of Shìzhōng,
they would no longer seek further promotion.
Lǎn, after serving as Lìbù Shàngshū, was sent out as Wúxīng Jùn Tàishǒu.
He was impartial and unafraid of powerful oppressors,
which was also due to his indifferent attitude towards worldly affairs.
After Jùn became Shìzhōng,
although he did not withdraw,
he remained detached and self-possessed,
not pursuing any further engagements.
After a long time,
he submitted a memorial due to illness requesting to resign his post.
He was promoted to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
but did not accept the appointment.
In the second year of Pǔtōng,
he died
at the age of fifty-six,
and was posthumously named Huìzǐ.
His sons were Cóng
and Wán.
Cóng was a Guózǐ Shēng
and married the daughter of Shǐxīng Wáng, Fánchāng Xiànzhǔ.
He was not intelligent
and was ridiculed by the students,
which led to a divorce.
Jùn thanked the prince,
and the prince said:
“This was the emperor’s intention;
I truly did not wish for this to happen.”
Jùn replied:
“My great-grandfather was the maternal grandson of Xiè Rénzǔ;
we do not rely on Your Highness’s marriage connection for our family status.”
Wáng Jiǎn, courtesy name Sīhuì,
was a native of Lángxié Línyí.
His father, Jiǎn, was Qí Tàiwèi and Nánchāng Wénxiàn Gōng.
When Jiǎn was a few years old,
his spirit and bearing were sharp and outstanding,
possessing the demeanor of an adult.
At that time, Wénxiàn served as chancellor,
and guests filled his home.
Upon seeing Jiǎn, they remarked to each other:
“The Duke’s talent and reputation
are present here again.”
At twenty years of age,
he was selected to marry Princess Huáinán,
appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and then Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
He did not accept the appointment
and was instead appointed Jìn’ān Wáng Wénxué,
then promoted to Lúlíng Wáng Yǒu and Mìshū Chéng.
Emperor Míng issued an edict seeking extraordinary talents.
Shǐ’ān Wáng Yáoguāng submitted a memorial recommending Jiǎn and Dōnghǎi Wáng Sēngrú,
saying:
“I have heard that seeking worthy individuals is momentarily arduous,
but allows for eternal ease in governing with folded hands,
akin to cultivating sparse soil
or guiding a river.
I humbly observe that Your Majesty’s virtue is veiled by your imperial attire,
and your trust is complete in your seals.
White colts roam in empty valleys,
and egrets gather in the court.
Yet I fear that hidden dragons and diviners,
and treasured vessels among butchers and porters,
are being sought beyond the passes,
or found on the banks of the river.
This is not about making a single choice,
but rather seeking flavor from diverse sources.
And so, when the five notes weary the ear,
the nine artisans are consulted.
Deliberations sleep in the imperial ancestral temple,
while ears listen to the common people.
My position and responsibilities are weighty,
and my duty extends to the state and family.
I truly wish to ensure that reputation and reality do not diverge,
and that the path of opportunism is cut off.
Even powerful families of the highest rank
should be judged by their pure discourse;
talented young men of lower rank
should not be limited by their position or appearance.
I secretly observe Mìshū Chéng Wáng Jiǎn of Lángxié,
aged twenty-one,
whose family has shone brilliantly for seven generations,
the foremost scholarly clan within the seas.
His spirit is pure and his essence vibrant,
truly embodying moderation and harmony.
His discussions are as clear as Shūbǎo’s rational discourse,
and his joy in moral teachings rivals Yànfǔ’s.
Therefore, he already shines among his predecessors
and leads the younger generation.
His dwelling is free from worldly dust,
and his family possesses imperial gifts of books.
His prose and poetry are fresh and pure,
his essays profound and distant.
Though his chamber is close, his person is expansive;
though things are distant, the Dao is near.
He cultivates his virtue in retirement,
leaving official positions vacant.
Yet in the imperial court,
tens of thousands look up to him.
How can he be merely like Xún Lìng, who can be imagined,
or Lǐ Gōng, who is not forgotten?
He is truly a secret treasure of the eastern order,
a magnificent vessel of the state.”
He was appointed Piàojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Zhāng Chōng, courtesy name Yánfú,
was a native of Wújùn.
His father, Xù,
was a Tèjìn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū in the Qí dynasty,
and had a good reputation in previous generations.
When Chōng was young,
he did not uphold moral conduct,
and enjoyed idle roaming.
Xù once took leave to return to Wú.
As he first entered the western suburb (guō),
he chanced upon Chōng going out hunting,
an eagle on his left arm,
and a dog on a leash in his right hand.
When he met Xù's boat arriving,
he immediately released the leash and removed his falconer's glove,
bowing by the water's edge.
Xù said,
"Engaged in two activities at once,
is it not tiring?"
Chōng knelt and replied,
"I have heard that one stands firm at thirty (sānshí ér lì).
Now I am twenty-nine.
Please allow me until next year to respectfully change my ways."
Xù said,
"To be able to correct one's faults (guò ér néng gǎi),
Yán Shìzǐ (Yán Huí) had this quality."
By the next year,
he indeed cultivated himself and changed his conduct.
He had not studied for a full year,
yet had extensively read much,
especially excelling in Lǎo (Lǎozi) and Yì (Yìjīng),
and was skilled in pure conversation (qīngyán).
He and his paternal uncle Jì both enjoyed high renown.
He began his official career as an Xíng Cānjūn for the Fǔjūn,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén, Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng, and Wǔlíng Wáng Yǒu.
At that time, Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn held significant power in the court,
and Emperor Wǔ made all his decisions based on Wáng Jiǎn's advice.
Emperor Wǔ once wanted to appoint Chōng's father Xù as Shàngshū Púshè.
He consulted Jiǎn,
who replied,
"Zhāng Xù has had a clear reputation since he was young,
and is indeed an excellent choice;
however, people from the East (dōngshì) have rarely taken a firm stand (bǐ wú suǒ zhí),
and Xù's sons are mostly of loose conduct.
I believe this should be carefully considered."
The Emperor then stopped the plan.
Previously, Chōng's brothers were all rather wild (qīngxiá),
and Chōng himself did not pay attention to minor conduct (xìxíng) when he was young,
which is why Jiǎn spoke as he did.
Chōng heard this and was displeased,
so he wrote a letter to Jiǎn, saying: "Zhāng Chōng, a man from the state of Wú, respectfully sends this letter to His Excellency, Lord Wáng of Lángxié: Recently, the journey has been long,
and the continuous rain has kept things hidden.
The cool and hot seasons are not yet balanced;
I trust you are well
and taking care.
Fortunately, during my leisure from fishing
and free time from gathering herbs,
I occasionally amuse myself with scrolls,
leisurely exploring ancient histories.
Across myriad ages,
the paths of action and inaction are manifold;
in the hustle and bustle of a hundred years,
the ways of rising and falling are not uniform.
[一０] Thus, round for movement and square for stillness,
is the difference of instruments;
diamond hard and water soft,
is the distinction of natures.
One who is skilled
at managing nature
does not go against the essence of metal and water;
one who is skilled at making instruments
does not alter the function of round and square.
This is why Běihǎi (Kǒng Róng) held his hairpin high (guà zān dài zhī gāo),
and Hénán (Zhōng Yáo) received
the honor of imperial edicts.
[一一] Throughout my life, I have had few companions;
I have not allowed desires for profit to disturb my mind.
For thirty-six years,
I have managed to live in humble tranquility.
My resolute will
stands towering like a frosty
cliff;
my steadfast feelings
stretch like peaks across the coastline.
Hanging my cap in the celestial pavilion (piāo yīng tiān gé)
means I have renounced the splendor of the court;
adorning the Cloud Terrace with official cords (zhuì zǔ yún tái)
means I ultimately feel shame at the brilliance of high officials.
This is why
I have retired to the riverside (jiāng gāo)
and feigned madness by the hills (lǒng pàn),
truly because my disposition is lofty and reserved,
and my feelings are unyielding and detached.
I abide by my own unique sentiments,
not accepted by ordinary people;
my solitary brilliance on a spiritual
precipice
often faces twists and turns in this world.
Thus, Jūnshān (Shào Jiē), who went straight up,
was pressured in his time;
Shúyáng (Xu Shúyáng), who soared far,
was admired a thousand years later.
This is why I [Chōng] choose to live among
fish and birds,
spending my days beneath the pines.
Half an acre of land
is enough to pay taxes;
five acres of homestead
planted with mulberry and hemp.
I sing and chant by the rivers and lakes,
savoring verses
by the Mǐnchí,
indulging in the fisherman's pastime,
and resting in a chosen dwelling.
That is all.
What have I, Chōng, to regret?
As for towering cliffs that shade the sun,
and the vast sea that meets the sky;
precipitous rocks crumbling for fathoms,
dividing dangers and dropping for measures.
Cassia and orchids exquisitely bloom,
mingled in the mountain's depths;
pines and cypresses densely
shade,
intertwining along the winding streams.
Yuánqīng (Rì Yuánqīng) did not return from here,
and Bóxiū (Liú Bóxiū) also departed forever from this place.
If one were to cast a fishing rod by the islet,
and wash one's feet in the clear waters;
alone roaming
through mist and clouds,
reposing loftily among the wind and moon.
Distant zither and wine,
who comes from afar to the mountain peak;
brilliant literary conversations,
in vain, cease in one's mind.
Unconsciously, a thousand miles stretch,
the road blocked by rivers
and streams.
Whenever the west wind blows,
how can one not gaze back?
Taking advantage of this period of illness,
I briefly express my feelings;
holding these few words,
I lightly trespass upon your esteemed attention.
Your Excellency, your years are not yet advanced,
yet you excel in learning and serve in office;
you assist the common people with your Dao,
your achievements are as vast as the sea.
When in court, you harmonize with Chángqiàn's (Wèi Chángqiàn's) sincerity;
when debating, you uphold
Zhòngzǐ's (Bāo Zhòngzǐ's) integrity.
One can truly say you are a great virtue of the age,
a lone pine that stands out.
My own conduct is not yet fully understood,
and this journey is still obscure.
The talented men of Máolíng
look upon the noble retinues
with long-held aspirations;
the common folk of Bàshān
await the carriages and robes with sighs.
Could this not be regrettable?
If a swan were to pull a carriage,
and a crane were to soar empty,
then the riverbank would not refuse to wither,
and the mountain would be moistened by its influence.
Strange birds with exotic feathers
might be met by the cliffside;
tender mists and light smoke
suddenly gather at the forest's edge.
The Eastern Capital (Dōngdū) is not exceptional,
why should the Southern Mountains (Nánshān)
be considered precious?
I, Chōng, am one of the common people west of the Kūn (Kūn Wén),
one citizen on the periphery of Mount Dài (Dài Biǎo).
I raise silkworms for clothes,
and cultivate the land for food.
I cannot serve princes and kings,
nor seek confidants,
nor visit contemporaries,
nor display my persuasive
speeches.
Like tumbleweeds, I drift among butchers and markets,
and my joy is exceedingly great.
Your Excellency met with favor early on,
and later encountered great courtesy.
The attention from the highest positions
overflowed in your early days;
the words from your hometown
were mistakenly prolonged on occasion.
However, the whole world calls me, Chōng, mad.
What can I, Chōng, possibly tell all of you gentlemen about this?
Thus, I reveal what I have heard and seen,
Zǎo's nature was humble and retiring,
not seeking fame or advancement.
He was skilled at writing essays and poems,
especially fond of ancient styles.
Unless it was for public banquets,
he never wantonly engaged in writing.
Even if he had a small piece,
he would discard the original as soon as it was finished.
In the eleventh year,

he was appointed as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of Yōng, Liáng, and Qín three prefectures, and Jìnglín and Suí two commanderies, General of Awe-Inspiring Might (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn), Superintendent of the Barbarians of Níng (Níngmán Xiàowèi), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yōng Prefecture.
In the twelfth year,

he was recalled to be Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the five prefectures of Nányǎn, Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, and Jì, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎn Prefecture.
His military title remained as before.
He frequently served in several garrisons,
and the people and officials praised him.
He promoted good people and humbled himself before others,
always as if he was not good enough.
He was recalled to be Grand Mentor (Zhānshì) to the Crown Prince.
In the third year of Pǔtōng (普通),
he was promoted to General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn),
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the sixth year,
he served as General of the Military Adviser (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn),
and with Hóu Zhèngdé (侯正德), the Marquis of Xīfēng (西豐), campaigned northwards to Wōyáng (渦陽).
He then withdrew the troops.
He was impeached by the appropriate officials (yǒusī),
dismissed from office and stripped of his rank and fief.
In the seventh year,
he was reinstated as Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng).
In the eighth year,
his rank and fief were restored.
Soon after, he was appointed General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn),
and concurrently commanded the Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
In the first year of Dàtōng (大通),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Protector-General of the Army (Zhōnghùjūn).
At that time, Wōyáng (渦陽) had just surrendered.
So, Zǎo was appointed Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Expedition (Běitǎo Dūdū), and Grand General of the Pacification of the North (Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn),
garrisoned at Wōyáng (渦陽).
In the second year,
he was appointed General of the Central Command (Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn), [一０]Grand Master of Remonstrance with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
had his own staff appointed,
and was given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng (中大通),
he was promoted to Protector-General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn),
while his position as General of the Central Command (Zhōngquán) remained as before.
In the third year,
he was appointed General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn), [一一]Grand Mentor (Zhānshì) to the Crown Prince,
and sent out to serve as Administrator (Yǐn) of Dānyáng (丹陽).
Gāozǔ (高祖) often sighed and said:
“If all my sons and nephews were like Jiāyè (迦葉),
what worries would I have?”
Jiāyè (迦葉)
was Zǎo's (藻) informal name.
He was recalled to serve as General of Pacifying the Left (Ānzuǒ Jiāngjūn) and Left Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè),
with the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Zǎo (藻) firmly declined,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
In the fifth year of Dàtóng (大同),

he was promoted to General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn), Open the Residence with the Three Dukes' Privileges (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
his title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) remaining as before.
Zǎo's (藻) nature was tranquil and calm.
He lived alone in a room,
his bed had knee marks,
and the imperial clan and high officials
all took him as a model.
He always felt that his rank and emolument were excessive,
and constantly thought of retiring.
His gate and courtyard were quiet and solitary,
and visitors were rare.
Tàizōng (太宗) especially respected and loved him.
Since suffering family misfortune,
he wore coarse cloth and sat on rush mats,
did not eat fresh fowl,
and unless in a public court,
did not listen to music.
Gāozǔ (高祖) always praised him for this.
He was sent out to serve as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nánxú (南徐) Prefecture.
When Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion broke out,
Zǎo (藻) sent his eldest son Yù (彧) to lead troops in support.
When the city gates were opened,
he was given the additional titles of Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
Jǐng (景) sent his Commissioner of Ceremonial (Yítóng) Xiāo Yōng (蕭邕) to replace him,
who occupied Jīngkǒu (京口).
Zǎo (藻) then fell ill with a qi disorder,
and did not treat himself.
Someone advised him to flee north of the river,
but Zǎo (藻) said:
“I am a pillar of the state,
my position and responsibility are particularly high.
Since I cannot eliminate the rebel,
I should die with the imperial court.
How can I abandon myself to another kind,
wishing to preserve the rest of my life?”
Thereupon, he did not eat for several days.
In the third year of Tàiqīng (太清),
he died,
at the age of sixty-seven.
Yǒngyáng (永陽) Successor Prince Bóyóu (伯游), courtesy name Shìrén (士仁),
was the son of Gāozǔ's (高祖) second elder brother Fū (敷).
Fū (敷), courtesy name Zhòngdá (仲達),

first served in Qí (齊) as Campaigning Army Administrative Officer (Xíngcānjūn) to the Rear Army Conqueror-General (Hòujūn Zhēnglǔ). [一二]He was transferred to Crown Prince's Household Administrator (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
then Palace Attendant (Xǐmǎ),
and promoted to Assistant Administrator (Chéng) of Dānyáng (丹陽) Commandery.
He was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant (Zhōngshèrén) to the Crown Prince,
and then appointed General of Establishing Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Suí Commandery.
He rallied and comforted those near and far,
and the common people were at peace because of him,
believing that no previous administration had equaled his.
He was promoted to General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn),
and recalled to serve as Consultant (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Lúlíng (廬陵).
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ),
he died.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
ennobled as Prince of Yǒngyáng (永陽) Commandery,
and given the posthumous name Zhāo (昭).
Bóyóu (伯游) had a beautiful demeanor and spirit,
and was skilled at discussing profound theories.
In the fourth month of the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),
an imperial edict stated:
“My nephew Bóyóu (伯游),
though his knowledge is not yet extensive,
his intentions are roughly acceptable.
The remote region of Zhèdōng (浙東)
requires administration and governance.

He is to be Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the five commanderies of Kuàijī (會稽), Dōngyáng (東陽), Xīn'ān (新安), Yǒngjiā (永嘉), and Línhǎi (臨海), General Assisting the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Kuàijī (會稽).”
In the second year,
he inherited the title of Prince of Yǒngyáng (永陽) Commandery.
In the fifth year,
he died,
at the age of twenty-three.
His posthumous name was Gōng (恭).
Héngyáng (衡陽) Successor Prince Yuánjiǎn (元簡), courtesy name Xīyuǎn (熙遠),
was the son of Gāozǔ's (高祖) fourth younger brother Chàng (暢).
Chàng (暢) served in Qí (齊) up to Grand Minister of Sacrifices (Tàicháng),
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiānglíng (江陵) County,
and then died.
In the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),

he was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), and Open the Residence with the Three Dukes' Privileges (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Héngyáng (衡陽) Commandery.
His posthumous name was Xuān (宣).
Yuánjiǎn (元簡) inherited the title in the third year.
He was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
and promoted to Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Kuàijī (會稽).
In the thirteenth year,
he was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng),

and sent out to serve as Envoy with Credentials (Chíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the three prefectures of Guǎng (廣), Jiāo (交), and Yuè (越), Central Commander of Pacifying the Yue (Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guǎng (廣) Prefecture.
He returned to serve as Central Palace Attendant (Zhōngshùzǐ) to the Crown Prince,

and was promoted to Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the three prefectures of Yǐng (郢), Sī (司), and Huò (霍), General of Trusty Martiality (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐng (郢) Prefecture.
In the first month of the eighteenth year,
he died in the prefecture.
His posthumous name was Xiào (孝).
His son Jùn (俊) succeeded.
Guìyáng (桂陽) Successor Prince Xiàng (象), courtesy name Shìyì (世翼),
was the ninth son of Prince Xuānwǔ (宣武) of Chángshā (長沙).
Initially,
his uncle Róng (融) served in Qí (齊) up to Palace Attendant (Xǐmǎ) to the Crown Prince.
During the Yuányuán (永元) period,
during the misfortune of Xuānwǔ (宣武),
Róng (融) was killed.
When Gāozǔ (高zǔ) pacified Jīngyì (京邑),
he was posthumously granted the title of Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng).
In the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),
he was given the additional titles of Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand General of the Pacifying Army (Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed as Prince of Guìyáng (桂陽) Commandery.
His posthumous name was Jiǎn (簡).
He had no sons,
so an imperial edict designated Xiàng (象) as his successor,
to inherit his rank and title.
Xiāo Xiàng's countenance and bearing were composed and elegant,
and he was skilled in social interactions.
He was known for his filial piety towards his birth mother.
He began his career as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Not long after arriving at his post,
Princess Jiǎn Wángfēi passed away,
and he resigned his office.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was again appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Xiāo Xiàng had grown up in the deep palace,
and this was his first direct involvement in common administration.
His conduct was without fault,
and the imperial court praised him.
He was dispatched as Chíjié, Dū Sīhuò Yǐng Sān Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, he was transferred to Xiānghéng Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Qīngchē Jiāngjūn, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xiāngzhōu had previously suffered greatly from tiger attacks,
but during Xiāo Xiàng's tenure,
these ceased,
and the elders all attributed it to the influence of his virtuous governance.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Soon after, in his original capacity, he temporarily oversaw the military affairs of Shítóu Shù,
then was transferred to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng, concurrently leading the army (jiān lǐngjūn),
and again, in his original capacity, concurrently served as Zōngzhèng Qīng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìzhōng and Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
Before he could take up the post,
he was reassigned as Chíjié, Dū Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was relieved of duty due to illness.
Soon after, he was appointed Tàicháng Qīng,
given the additional title of Shìzhōng,
and then promoted to Mìshū Jiān, concurrently Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
In the second year of Dàtóng (536 CE),
he died,
and was posthumously granted the title Dūn.
His son, Xiāo Zào, inherited.
The imperial historian says: The successive princes of Chángshā,
all inherited their territories,
and brilliantly governed their feudal states.
Guìyáng Wáng Xiāo Xiàng was known for his filial piety,
and when he governed Xiāngzhōu,
ferocious tigers ceased their violence,
which was indeed due to his benevolent virtue.
How could the excellent governance of old surpass this?
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 18: Xiāo Jǐng (Younger brothers: Xiāo Chāng, Xiāo Áng, Xiāo Yù)
Xiāo Jǐng, courtesy name Zǐzhāo,
was a cousin of Gāozǔ.
His father, Xiāo Chóngzhī, courtesy name Màojìng,
was the son of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū Xiāo Dàocì.
Xiāo Dàocì had three sons: The eldest, Xiāo Shàngzhī,
courtesy name Màoxiān;
the second, Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì;
the third, Xiāo Chóngzhī.
Initially,
the Zuǒ Guānglù resided in his hometown,
exclusively practicing propriety and humility,
and was highly esteemed by the multitude.
His career included serving as a Cānjūn for Sòng Tàiwèi, Jiāngxià Wáng,
and he ended as Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
At the end of Qí,
he was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
Xiāo Shàngzhī was honest and possessed virtuous character,
serving as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn for Sītú, Jiàn'ān Wáng.
The entire administration referred to him as an elder.
Lángyá Wáng Sēngqián particularly esteemed him,
and often sought his counsel on many matters.
He was promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
and died in office.
In the early Tiānjiān era (502 CE),
he was posthumously granted the title Wénxuān Hóu.
Xiāo Shàngzhī's son, Xiāo Língjūn,
served as Guǎngdé Lìng in Qí.
When Gāozǔ's righteous army arrived,
he temporarily managed the affairs of Kuàijī Jùn,
and died shortly thereafter.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Dōngchāng Xiàn Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
His son, Xiāo Jiǎn, inherited.
Xiāo Chóngzhī distinguished himself through his competence and ability,
and his governance leaned towards severity.
He rose to the rank of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
In the Yǒngmíng era (483-493 CE),
when Táng Yǐn of Qiántáng rebelled,
his separate forces breached Dōngyáng,
and Xiāo Chóngzhī was killed.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he was posthumously granted the title Zhōngjiǎn Hóu.
Xiāo Jǐng, at eight years old, followed his father to the prefecture.
He was known for his extreme grief during mourning.
As he grew up, he was fond of learning,
and possessed eloquence and decisive judgment.
In the Jiànwǔ era (494-498 CE) of Qí,
he was appointed Zuǒ Chángshì for Jìn'ān Wángguó,
then promoted to Yǒngníng Lìng,
and his administration was considered the best among all cities.
Fàn Shù, the Tàishǒu of Yǒngjiā, who had previously governed the prefecture,
was renowned for his integrity and fairness.
He greatly admired Xiāo Jǐng's governance,
and thus posted a notice at the prefecture gate saying:
"For any unresolved or difficult matters in other counties,
you may consult the Yǒngníng Lìng for a decision."
Soon after,
he left office due to illness.
One thousand people from Yǒngjiā, including Hú Zhòngxuān, went to the imperial court,
to petition for Xiāo Jǐng to be appointed to the prefecture,
but it was not granted.
He returned to serve as Piàojì Xíng Cānjūn.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán (500 CE),
due to the meritorious service of Chángshā Xuānwǔ Wáng Xiāo Yì,
he was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
That winter,
Xuānwǔ Wáng was killed,
and Xiāo Jǐng also fled for safety.
When Gāozǔ's righteous army arrived,
Xiāo Jǐng was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Acting Military Affairs of Nányǎnzhōu.
At that time, the empire was not yet settled.
The "Cángchǔ" (barbarian/southern people) north of the Yangtze River each occupied fortified settlements.
Xiāo Jǐng demonstrated his authority and trustworthiness,
and the chieftains came forward, binding themselves, to plead guilty.
Within ten days, the entire region was pacified.
In the second year of Zhōngxīng (502 CE),
he was promoted to Dū Nányǎnzhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Jiān Nányǎnzhōu.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Wúpíng Xiàn Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
He continued to serve as Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Nánběi Yǎnqīng Jì Sì Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù,
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
An imperial edict granted Xiāo Jǐng's mother, Lady Máo, the title Guótàifūrén,
with ceremonies equivalent to a Wángguó Tàifēi,
and she was granted a golden seal and purple ribbon.
When Xiāo Jǐng governed the prefecture,
he was pure, diligent, and authoritative.
He had a clear understanding of official duties,
so paperwork was never delayed.
Subordinates dared not deceive him,
and officials and common people feared and respected him as a god.
It happened to be a year of famine,
so he calculated provisions per person and provided relief,
distributing porridge along the roads.
The deceased were provided with coffins and burial equipment,
and the people greatly relied on him.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (505 CE),
the imperial army launched a northern expedition.
Xiāo Jǐng led his troops out of Huáiyáng,
and advanced to slaughter Sùyù.
He entered mourning for his mother,
but an imperial edict ordered him to temporarily resume his duties.
In the fifth year (506 CE),
the army returned,
and he was appointed Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ,
then promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wèiwèi Qīng.
In the seventh year (508 CE),
he was promoted to Zuǒ Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
concurrently Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
The Lǐngjūn was in charge of all critical military affairs,
and oversaw the officials in the bureau.
Previously, many were arrogant and extravagant,
but Xiāo Jǐng's strictness in office
made the official departments solemn.
The Zhìjú Jiān were all favored intimates,
and many were quite resentful of his orders.
For this reason, he could not remain in the central government for long.
Soon after, he was dispatched as Shǐ Chíjié, Dū Yōngliáng Nánběi Qín Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu Zhī Suí Jùn Zhū Jūnfù, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the third month of the eighth year (509 CE),
Yuán Zhì, the Wèi Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, led an army of seventy thousand to invade Chán'gōu,
pressing the various Mán tribes.
All the Mán crossed the Hànshuǐ to surrender.
Debaters suggested that since the Mán had repeatedly been a border problem,
this was an opportunity to eliminate them.
Xiāo Jǐng said:
"Those who are in dire straits and come to us
should not be executed; it would be inauspicious.
Furthermore, when the Wèi people invade,
they always face resistance.
If we execute all the Mán,
then the Wèi army will have no obstacles,
which is not a wise strategy."
So, he opened Fánchéng to accept their surrender.
He then ordered his Sīmǎ Zhū Sīyuǎn, Níngmán Chángshǐ Cáo Yìzōng, and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Mèng Huìjùn to attack Yuán Zhì at Chán'gōu,
where they utterly defeated him,
capturing Yuán Zhì's Chángshǐ Dù Jǐng alive.
Over ten thousand heads were cut off,
and the floating corpses covered the Hànshuǐ.
Xiāo Jǐng sent Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Cuī Huì to lead soldiers to collect and bury them.
Stop.
My residence at Qīngmíng mén,
there is no room for co-existence.
The reason for this
also has its grounds.
Previously, the western side was given to Xuānwǔ Sì,
and having lost the west wing,
it is no longer
spacious.
I also thought of this as merely an inn,
why should it need to be grand?
I often regret that people of the time call it my residence.
From ancient times to the present,
the rich and powerful have followed in succession,
with high gates
and grand mansions,
connected courtyards and deep chambers.
When they are dead,
whose rooms are they truly?
But I cannot help but build a small mound-like hill,
gathering stones and moving fruit trees,
mixing them with flowers,
to
enjoy leisure and rest,
and to entrust my spirit.
I built it casually,
not aiming for grandeur,
but where the merits are,
I preferred it to be small.
Therefore, the interior is cramped,
without additional
rooms.
Recently, I have been building two residences for my sons and grandsons on the east side,
relying on the funds for the return journey of the ten who went south.
The required expenses for these
are still considerable.
Since the funds did not arrive as expected,
and it was
unacceptable to stop midway,
the garden in the suburbs
could not be maintained.
It was sold to Wéi Àn,
from which I obtained a hundred catties of gold,
to complete the two residences,
which consumed half of it.
How did the garden's
value
reach such an amount?
Because I started it years ago,
and it had largely taken shape.
The peach and plum trees were lush,
the paulownia and bamboo provided shade,
the paths and lanes were interconnected,
and the canals and ditches were
linked.
With elegant buildings and lofty pavilions,
it had considerable beauty for gazing afar;
solitary peaks and dense thickets,
not without an intricate charm.
The waterways were rich in water oats and hornwort,
and the ponds were especially abundant in water caltrops and
lotuses.
Although it was said to be outside human habitation,
it was close to the city walls.
Wéi Shēng desired it,
and it indeed possessed elegant charm.
Recounting this matter
is not due to a stingy heart,
but rather where the flow of writing
led.
I recall Xiè Língyùn's poem "Mountain Dwelling" which says:
"In the midst of heaven and earth,
it now belongs to a rustic fellow."
This garden of mine has been mine for twenty years,
now it belongs to heaven
and earth.
What difference is there between things and me,
when compared?
What I have left here,
I now divide for you,
to build a small farmhouse.
Since relatives and dependents are many,
it is reasonable that this is needed.
Moreover, the teachings of Buddhism
consider wealth as external life;
Confucian classics also state,
"What gathers people is wealth."
How could your common feelings
forget this?
I hear
that the land you bought in Gūshú
is very saline and barren,
how can you be at peace there?
The reason for this is
not due to competition among things.
Although the matter is different from "sleeping on a mound,"
it can somewhat
resemble it.
Confucius said:
"Managing a household well
can be transferred to official duties."
Since you have already begun it,
you should ensure its completion.
To fail in both advancing and retreating
would only bring more ridicule.
If
there is any harvest,
you can distribute it among the family, inside and out, young and old.
It should be appropriately allocated,
which is not for me to know.
Also, the daughters should receive their share.
Since you are the
eldest,
this responsibility falls to you.
Being the eldest for anyone
is indeed not easy.
You must ensure harmony within and without,
so that no one has cause for complaint,
prioritizing others before yourself.
Only then can you be esteemed.
The Old Master said:
"Put yourself last, and you will be first."
If you can do this,
you will attract even greater benefits.
You should strive hard,
see worthy people and emulate them,
and not neglect your days by idleness.
Not
only are you wasting days,
you are wasting yourself.
How great are the good or bad of one's reputation
and person!
Should you not be careful?
What I am now instructing
briefly states this intention:
that since I became
a household head,
I have not pursued assets.
Now that a villa has been established,
it deviates from my old ways.
To recount its beginning and end
leaves no shame in my heart.
Moreover, my years are decaying and old,
my mental and physical strength are gradually
exhausted.
I can barely manage to fulfill my official duties,
and almost fail to perform them.
Any remaining leisure
is barely enough for me to rest.
Perhaps in the winter sun,
or the summer shade,
during good seasons and beautiful scenery,
in the gaps between official documents,
leaning on my staff and wearing sandals,
strolling freely in my humble dwelling,
watching fish by the pond,
listening to birds in the woods,
with a cup of浊jiǔ,
playing a tune on the qín,
seeking a few moments of
temporary joy.
I hope to live out my days in this manner,
and should not again be burdened by trivial family affairs.
Since your contacts are established,
and this letter is issued,
all necessary provisions
will be supplied as
specified elsewhere.
From now on,
I will no longer speak of land matters,
nor should you speak of them to me again.
Even if there were a flood like Yáo's or a drought like Tāng's,
how would I know what to do;
if
your granaries are full and your chests overflowing,
that is your good fortune.
Such matters
do not require me to be informed.
The *Book of Rites* says:
"Filial piety means
skillfully continuing the aspirations of others,
and skillfully
carrying on their undertakings."
Now I hope that you will fully carry out this aspiration of mine,
then I will have no regrets.
Urging his second son, Fěi, upon his death,
deeply grieved,
not wishing to long neglect the affairs of the state,
he then composed "An Explanation to a Guest."
Its words are: In the second month, Dīngchǒu day, of spring in the fifth year of Pǔtōng,
the news of the death of my second son, Fěi, the Internal Historian of Jìn'ān, arrived,
and the whole family was grief-stricken,
our spirits as if fallen.

Shān Bīn 山賓 was of a sincere and honest nature.
His family often lacked resources,
so he sold the ox he rode.
After selling it and receiving the money,
he then said to the buyer:
"This ox once suffered from hoof-rot,
and although it has been cured for a long time,
I fear it might relapse later.
I cannot but tell you this."
The buyer immediately pursued him to reclaim the money.
Ruǎn Xiàoxù 阮孝緒, a recluse, heard of this
and sighed, saying:
"These words are enough to make people return to simplicity and sincerity,
and to stir up the generous and stop the vulgar!"
Five years later,
he was again appointed Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士,
while Chángshì 常侍 and Zhōngzhèng 中正 remained as before.
That year, he was granted the Jiǎjié 假節 with his original official post,
and provisionally oversaw the affairs of Běiyǎnzhōu 北兗州.
In Dàtōng 元年 (527 CE),
he died,
at the age of eighty-five.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Shìzhōng 侍中 and Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn 信威將軍.
His posthumous title was Zhìzǐ 質子.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ 昭明太子 held a mourning ceremony for him,
bestowing a funeral gift of one hundred thousand coins,
and one hundred bolts of cloth,
and also sent his Shèrén 舍人, Wáng Yǒng 王顒, to supervise the funeral arrangements.
He also sent a letter to the former Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ 司徒左長史, Yīn Yún 殷芸, which read:
"News from Běiyǎnzhōu indicates that
the esteemed Chángshì 常侍 has finally passed away.
Hearing this, I am deeply saddened.
This worthy scholar's learning was comprehensive and profound,
his aspirations and conduct adhered to ancient principles,
and he was warm, kind, simple, and harmonious,
cultured, elegant, and profoundly steadfast.
Since he began teaching the classics,
two cycles (twenty-four years) have passed.
His refusal to flatter superiors,
and his loyal remonstrances delivered face-to-face,
were not for outward show,
but came from his heart,
and indeed accumulated over time.
He took on the heavy responsibility of a provincial governor,
and was about to return home as expected,
but alas, he departed forever,
becoming a memory of days gone by.
Recalling our conversations,
they all turn into sources of sorrow.
Alas, what can be done now!
Having served together in the past,
it is only natural to feel profound grief."
Shān Bīn 山賓 repeatedly held positions in educational institutions,
and was very beneficial in his teaching and guidance.
However, his nature was rather open and free,
and in his interactions with students,
he was often familiar and close,
so everyone loved him.
His published works included the Jílǐ Yízhù 吉禮儀注 in two hundred twenty-four volumes,
Lǐyí 禮儀 in twenty volumes,
and Xiàojīng Sānglǐ Fúyì 孝經喪禮服義 in fifteen volumes.
His son, Zhèn 震,
whose courtesy name was Xīngdào 興道,
also carried on his father's profession.
He successively held posts as Tàixué Bóshì 太學博士,
Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人,
Shàngshū Cíbù Láng 尚書祠部郎,
and Yúyáo Lìng 餘姚令.
Yīn Jūn 殷鈞, whose courtesy name was Jìhé 季和,
was from Chénjùn Chángpíng 陳郡長平.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Jìn Tàicháng Róng 晉太常融.
His father, Ruì 叡,
was talented and eloquent,
well-known during the Qí 齊 dynasty,
and successively held the post of Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng 司徒從事中郎.
Ruì's 叡 wife was the daughter of Wáng Huàn 王奐.
Wáng Huàn 王奐, serving as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 雍州刺史 and Zhèn běi Jiāngjūn 鎮北將軍,
then petitioned the court
to appoint Ruì 叡 as Zhèn běi Zhǎngshǐ 鎮北長史 and Hénán Tàishǒu 河南太守.
When Wáng Huàn 王奐 was executed,
Ruì 叡 was also killed.
Jūn 鈞 was nine years old at the time
and was known for his filial piety.
As he grew up,
he was calm and quiet, with few companions,
and loved learning and reflective thinking.
He excelled at Lìshū 隸書 (clerical script),
serving as a model for the time.
Fàn Yún 范雲 from Nánxiāng 南鄉
and Rèn Fǎng 任昉 from Yuè'ān 樂安 both praised him.
Gāozǔ 高祖 and Ruì 叡 had been old acquaintances since youth,
and Gāozǔ 高祖 gave his daughter in marriage to Jūn 鈞,
who was Yǒngxīng Gōngzhǔ 永興公主.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān 天監 (502 CE),
he was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉,
starting his career as Mìshū Láng 祕書郎,
then Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人,
Sītú Zhǔbù 司徒主簿,
and Mìshū Chéng 祕書丞.
While in office, Jūn 鈞
requested to revise and collate the four divisions of books in the Mìgé 祕閣,
and create a new catalogue.
He also received an imperial edict to inspect the calligraphic works and ancient artifacts in the Xīshěng 西省,
and classify them into different categories.
He was promoted to Piàojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng 驃騎從事中郎,
Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎,
Tàizǐ Jiālìng 太子家令,
managing the records of the Eastern Palace.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng 給事黃門侍郎,
Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
Shàngshū Lìbù Láng 尚書吏部郎,
Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ 司徒左長史,
and Shìzhōng 侍中.
When scholars were established in the Eastern Palace,
Jūn 鈞 was again appointed to that position.
He was dismissed due to official business.
He was again made Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
concurrently holding the posts of Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士 and Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn 左驍騎將軍,
with his role as Bóshì 博士 remaining unchanged.
He was sent out as Míngwēi Jiāngjūn 明威將軍 and Línchuān Nèishǐ 臨川內史.
Jūn's body was frail and frequently ill.
He stayed behind closed doors to govern,
yet the common people were transformed by his virtue,
and all bandits fled beyond the borders.
Once, he captured a bandit leader,
but did not subject him to torture or interrogation,
only gently rebuking him.
The bandit leader knocked his head to the ground, begging to reform,
and Jūn immediately ordered him released.
Afterward, he became a good person.
The commandery previously suffered much from mountain malaria,
which would invariably recur with the summer heat.
But ever since Jūn took office,
there was no more malaria in the commandery.
When his mother died, he left his post,
mourning beyond the rites.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ worried about him,
and personally wrote a letter of admonition and instruction, saying:
"I know that among your many virtues,
your excessive grief is a fault.
Moreover, what you consume is barely more than a single grain,
which greatly distresses me.
You are a solitary person,
and the continuity of your family rests upon you.
To destroy oneself and extinguish one's nature
is not permitted by the sagely teachings.
You should slightly moderate your self-denial,
and humbly adhere to the established rites.
For gruel, porridge, fruits, and vegetables,
make a little more effort.
Since your worries are profound,
I will instruct Míu Dàozhēn to fully explain the specifics in person."
Jūn replied:
"I have received your imperial handwritten decree,
and Míu Dàozhēn has conveyed your instructions.
As I prostrate myself and read, I am choked with emotion;
my heart and liver are as if spilled on the ground.
I am a humble person without much emotion,
and my actions often fall short of the rites.
However, I was born with a weak constitution,
and as the years passed,
sins and transgressions accumulated,
further compounded by chronic illness.
Recently, I have been frail,
keeping vigil day and night,
my eyes blurring with confusion,
my heart lost in sorrow and joy.
I only seek to relieve this dangerous suffering,
unable to restrain myself with distant principles.
The nourishment of ginger and cinnamon
is indeed mentioned in ancient texts.
Not avoiding meat and fine grains,
I am also blessed by your present kindness.
Who am I,
to receive such concern and pity?
I will respectfully follow the sagely words,
and contemplate how to recover.
If I should fail to extend my life,
it will truly be due to fate."
After the mourning period concluded,
he was promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū.
Still suffering from chronic illness,
he was unable to accept the appointment,
so he was instead given the title Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently served as Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
attending the Eastern Palace.
Soon after, he was reappointed as Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Zhāomíng Tàizǐ passed away,
his officials were dismissed.
He was then appointed Yòuyóujī,
and made Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
with his Chángshì title remaining.
