In the fourth year of Zhōngdàtōng (532 CE),
he died
at the age of forty-nine.
His posthumous title was Zhēnzǐ.
He had two sons: Gòu
and Wò.
Lù Xiāng, courtesy name Shīqīng,
was a native of Wú Commandery.
His father, Xián,
served as Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng for Qí Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng.
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
Yáoguāng rebelled, occupying the Eastern Palace.
Someone advised Xián to leave him.
Xián said:
"I am his official;
how can I escape death?"
When the imperial army attacked and captured the city,
Xián was seized.
As he was about to be executed,
his second son, Jiàng, asked to die in his place,
but was not permitted.
He then shielded his father with his body,
and both were killed by the executioner.
Xiāng was deeply pained by the tragic deaths of his father and brother,
and his mourning exceeded the rites.
Even after the mourning period ended, he still seemed to be grieving.
In the third year of Tiānjiān (504 CE),
Dūguān Shàngshū Fàn Xiù submitted a memorial recommending Xiāng.
He was appointed Xuèzuò Zuǒláng,
and then appointed Yǒngníng Lìng.
After his term of office,
he was successively promoted to Sīkōng Línchuān Wáng Fǎcáo,
Wàibīng,
and Qīngchē Lúlín Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ heard of Xiāng's conduct and studies,
and memorialized Gāozǔ to invite him for companionship.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and then promoted to Zhōngshèrén,
concurrently overseeing the records.
He was sent out to serve as Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng.
As Xiāng's father had died in this office,
he firmly declined the post.
Gāozǔ did not permit it,
but allowed him to exchange residences with the Fǔsīmǎ.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ respected elders,
and Xiāng's mother was nearly eighty.
Along with Xiāo Chēn, Fù Zhāo, and Lù Gǎo, he would regularly send greetings and inquiries each month,
additionally bestowing rare delicacies and clothing.
Xiāng's mother once suddenly suffered heart pain.
The medical prescription required three sheng of millet gruel.
It was winter at the time,
and evening was approaching.
They searched everywhere but found none.
Suddenly, an old man came to the gate selling gruel,
the quantity exactly matching the prescription.
Just as they were about to pay,
he vanished without a trace. People at the time believed this was due to Xiāng's filial piety.
He was successively promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì,
Tàizǐ Jiālìng,
and again oversaw the records.
When his mother died, he left his post.
Xiāng was already fifty years old,
and his grief and debilitation exceeded the rites.
The Prince worried about him,
sending envoys daily to admonish and instruct him.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and again oversaw the records.
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng (531 CE),
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ passed away,
and his officials were dismissed.
His consort, Cài Shì, moved to reside in Jīnhuá Gōng,
and Xiāng was made Zhōngsàn Dàfū, concurrently Bùbīng Xiàowèi, Jīnhuá Gōng Jiālìng, and was put in charge of Jīnhuá Gōng affairs.
In the seventh year,
he was sent out to be the Interior Historian of Póyáng.
Prior to this,
a local man named Xiānyú Chēn practiced Dàofǎ by consuming substances,
and once entered the mountains to gather herbs.
He picked up a five-colored banner and a ceremonial staff,
and also found a stone seal in the ground,
which secretly puzzled him.
Chēn had previously separated his living quarters from his wife.
Looking towards where Chēn resided,
there was often an unusual aura,
which made her increasingly believe he was divine.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he then gathered his followers,
killed Wáng Jūn, the Magistrate of Guǎngjìn,
proclaimed the first year of Shàngyuàn,
and appointed officials.
His partisans continued to delude each other,
accumulating a crowd of over ten thousand people.
When they were about to attack the commandery,
Xiāng had already led the local people and officials to repair the city walls and moats,
preparing defenses.
When the bandits arrived,
he repeatedly fought and defeated them,
capturing Chēn alive.
The remaining crowd fled and dispersed.
At that time, the governors and magistrates of neighboring commanderies like Yùzhāng and Ānchéng
investigated the partisans,
and took the opportunity to demand bribes.
None of them found the truth,
and some good people suffered misfortune and their whole families were separated.
Only in Xiāng's commandery were the innocent and guilty distinguished without excess.
The people composed a song saying:
"After Xiānyú was pacified, good and evil were divided,
the people did not die unjustly,
thanks to Lord Lù."
There were also two families, Péng and Lǐ,
who had previously had a quarrel,
and then falsely accused each other.
Xiāng brought them into his inner chamber,
and did not reprimand them,
but only used gentle words to explain and mediate.
The two men were grateful,
and deeply blamed and regretted themselves.
He then prepared wine and food for them,
allowing them to enjoy themselves to the fullest.
After the wine,
they rode home together in the same carriage,
and became close friends.
The people again sang:
"Lord Lù's administration,
no one bears resentment,
when the fight is over,
enemies share a carriage."
He governed for six years,
and the commandery was greatly pacified.
Four hundred and twenty people, including the commoner Lǐ Xiàn, went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial,
describing Xiāng's virtuous influence,
and requesting to erect a stele in the commandery.
An imperial edict permitted it.
They also petitioned to keep Xiāng,
but Xiāng steadfastly requested to return.
He was summoned to be the Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
then promoted to Secretarial Court Director,
concurrently serving as the Grand Moderator of Yángzhōu.
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to Minister of the State Treasury,
retaining his concurrent post as Grand Moderator.
In the second year,
Hóu Jǐng raised troops and besieged the imperial palace.
Xiāng was in charge of the Ministry of the Imperial Attendants.
In the third month of the third year,
the city fell.
Xiāng fled back to Wú.
The bandits soon invaded the eastern border,
overwhelming Wújùn.
Jǐng's general Sòng Zǐxiān advanced to attack Qiántáng.
At that time, Lù Àn of Hǎiyán raised an army of righteousness,
with several thousand followers.
He launched a night attack on the commandery,
killed the false Grand Administrator Sū Dān Yú,
and nominated Xiāng to act as the commandery administrator.
At that time, Xiāo Níng, Marquis of Wénchéng and Grand Administrator of Huáinán, fled from the bandits into Wú.
Xiāng sent for Níng to be the leader of the alliance,
and dispatched Àn and his elder brother's son Yìnggōng to lead the troops to resist Zǐxiān.
Zǐxiān, hearing that an army had risen,
then retreated.
He fought with Àn and others at Sōngjiāng.
Àn was defeated and fled.
The Wúxià army, hearing of this,
also dispersed.
Xiāng hid in a tomb,
and died of grief and indignation overnight,
at the age of seventy.
Xiāng suffered a family misfortune in his youth,
and for the rest of his life ate vegetables and wore coarse cloth,
did not listen to music,
and did not speak of killing for about fifty years.
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Emperor Shìzǔ posthumously appointed him Grand Attendant and General of Yúnhuī.
For his meritorious service in raising the righteous army,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Yúgān County,
with five hundred households.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel for Chén, said: Lù Chuí was extensively learned in literature and principles,
Dào Qià was steadfast and vigorous, dedicating himself to public service,
Míng Shānbīn was refined, sincere, and pragmatic,
Yīn Jūn was quiet, simple, peaceful, and harmonious,
Lù Xiāng was pure, profound, and filial.
Although their appointments and treatment differed,
they were all ranked among the famous ministers.
Collated Notes
Biographies Twenty-two: Péi Suì (his elder brother's sons Zhīgāo, Zhīpíng, Zhīhéng), Xiàhóu Dǎn (his younger brother Kuí, Yú Hóng appended), Wéi Fàng.
Péi Suì, courtesy name Yuānmíng,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
He was a descendant of Chuò, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu in the Wèi dynasty.
His grandfather, Shòusūn, lived temporarily in Shòuyáng and served as the Army Commander for Emperor Wǔ of Sòng.
His father, Zhòngmù, was a Galloping Cavalry General.
Suì could compose essays at the age of ten
and was skilled in the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū.
In the early Jiànwǔ era of Qí,
Inspector Xiāo Yáochāng appointed him as his Household Registrar.
There was an Eight Dukes Mountain Temple in Shòuyáng;
Yáochāng had a stele erected for it
and commissioned Suì to write the inscription,
which was highly praised.
He was recommended as an outstanding talent,
achieved a high rank in the policy examination,
and served as an Imperial Attendant.
When Emperor Dōnghūn ascended the throne,
Xiāo Yáoguāng, Prince of Shǐ'ān, was appointed General of the Pacified Army and Inspector of Yángzhōu.
He appointed Suì as a Staff Officer.
Later, when Yáoguāng was defeated,
Suì returned to Shòuyáng.
At that time, Inspector Péi Shúyè surrendered Shòuyáng to Wèi,
and the powerful families of Yùzhōu were all driven out and plundered.
Suì then followed the crowd north.
The Wèi sovereign, Emperor Xuānwǔ, highly esteemed him,
and appointed him as a Subordinate of the Minister of Works,
Director of the Central Secretariat,
and Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
Wèi dispatched Wáng Sù to govern Shòuyáng.
Suì firmly requested to accompany Sù,
secretly planning to return south.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he escaped and returned to court,
and was appointed Military Advisor to the Rear Army.
Suì requested to prove himself on the border,
and was appointed General of the Stabilizing State and Grand Administrator of Lújiāng.
At that time, Wèi general Lǚ Pó led five thousand troops to suddenly attack the commandery.
Suì led his subordinates to resist and defeat them,
and was promoted to General of the Right Army.
In the fifth year,
he campaigned in Shàoyángzhōu.
The Wèi people built a long bridge to cross the Huái River.
Suì built fortifications to press against the bridge,
winning every battle.
Thereupon, he secretly built submerged assault ships.
Just then, there was heavy rain,
and the Huái River suddenly overflowed.
Suì rode the ships directly to the side of the bridge.
The Wèi troops were shocked and dispersed.
Suì took advantage of the victory to pursue,
and greatly defeated them.
He then captured Yángshí City,
beheading its lord Yuán Kāng.
He also captured Huòqiū City,
beheading its lord Níng Yǒngrén.
He pacified Xiǎoxiàn
and attacked Héféi.
For his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Yílíng County,
with three hundred households.
He was promoted to Chief Clerk of the Champion General and Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
Lǐ Xìng
admired the establishment of meritorious fame.
Every time he read books and saw loyal ministers and valiant warriors,
he never failed to lay aside his scroll and sigh, saying:
"Throughout my life,
I must not be unworthy of the ancients."
He was widely read and knowledgeable,
and possessed literary talent.
He once offered sacrifices at Kǒng Wénjǔ's tomb,
and also erected a stele for him,
composing a very beautiful inscription.
During the Tàiqīng reign,
Hóu Jǐng launched an internal invasion.
Lǐ Xìng gathered several hundred retainers
and lightly equipped, hastened to Nányān Zhōu,
following his elder brother Huìlǐ to provide aid.
He personally faced arrows and stones,
leading the soldiers.
When the city fell,
he again followed Huìlǐ back to Guǎnglíng,
then entered Qí as a hostage
to beg for troops.
After two days of travel,
it happened that Hóu Jǐng had sent Dǒng Shàoxiān to occupy Guǎnglíng,
who then pursued Huìlǐ,
and thus Lǐ Xìng was captured by him.
Shàoxiān guarded him very strictly,
preventing him from seeing his brothers.
So he falsely requested to return to the capital first
to bid farewell to his mother.
He told his elder sister, the princess Āngù Gōngzhǔ:
"Since matters have come to this,
how can the whole family suffer death?
If elder brother arrives,
I wish you would speak to him for me.
Encourage him to make good plans to exert himself,
and not to think of this as a burden.
The family and state are in dire peril;
though I die, there is no regret.
I also wish to achieve something in the future,
but I do not know what Heaven's will is."
Upon reaching the capital,
considering that Yuán Zhēn, a surrendered man from Wèi, was upright and loyal
and could be entrusted with his family,
he presented him with a jade-handled fan.
Zhēn found this strange
and refused to accept it.
Lǐ Xìng said:
"You will remember this later,
please do not decline."
At that time, Zǔ Hào raised an army.
Lǐ Xìng fled to Chánglú,
and gathered over a thousand soldiers.
Among his retinue, there were those who sided with the bandits,
and they seized an opportunity to abduct Huìlǐ.
His troops then dispersed in panic,
and he was killed by Hóu Jǐng
at the age of twenty-one.
Yuán Zhēn then understood his previous words
and went to collect and bury him.
Lúlíng Wēi Wáng Xù, courtesy name Shìxīn,
was the fifth son of Gāozǔ.
In the eighth year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as King of Lúlíng Commandery,
with an income of two thousand households.
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Light Chariot General and Administrator of Nánpéngchéng and Lángyá.
In the thirteenth year,
he was transferred to be Administrator of Kuàijī.
In the sixteenth year,
he became Overseer of All Military Affairs of Jiāngzhōu, General of Agile Cavalry, and Regional Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he was summoned to be General Who Manifests Valour,
and concurrently supervised military affairs at Shítóu Garrison.
Xù was brave and decisive in his youth,
with extraordinary physical strength.
He was skilled in horse archery and hunting,
hitting the target with every shot.
Gāozǔ often sighed, saying:
"He is my Rènchéng!"
He once competed in horse archery before Gāozǔ with Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé, Hú Guìtōng, Zhào Bózhāo, and others.
Xù excelled among all of them,
and Gāozǔ was greatly pleased.
In the third year,

he was appointed Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Yǒng, Liáng, Qín, and Shā, West Central Inspector-General, and Regional Inspector of Yǒngzhōu.
In the seventh year,
he was given the additional title of General Who Manifests Valour.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,

he was again appointed Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Yǒng, Liáng, Qín, and Shā, General Who Pacifies the North, Commandant for Pacifying the Man, and Regional Inspector of Yǒngzhōu,
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
Xù accumulated many horses and weapons,
and maintained brave and powerful men.
His gold and silk filled his inner chambers,
and his granaries were fully stocked.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he was appointed Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of Jiāngzhōu, General Who Pacifies the South, and Regional Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the third year,
he was summoned to be Protector-General, and concurrently supervised military affairs at Shítóu Garrison.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Cavalry General and Minister without Portfolio.

He then departed to be Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Nine Prefectures of Jīng, Yǐng, Sī, Yǒng, Nánqín, Běiqín, Liáng, Bā, and Huá, and Regional Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtóng,
he died in the prefecture
at the age of forty-four.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Minister of Works, Palace Attendant, and Grand Cavalry General,
a set of drums and pipes,
and given the posthumous name Wēi.
His eldest son was Ānsì.
Shàolíng Xié Wáng Lún, courtesy name Shìdiào,
was the sixth son of Gāozǔ.
He was intelligent in his youth,
widely learned and skilled in composition,
especially proficient in writing letters.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as King of Shàolíng Commandery,
with an income of two thousand households.
He went out to serve as General Who Pacifies the Distant, and Administrator of the two commanderies of Lángyá and Péngchéng,
then promoted to Light Chariot General and Administrator of Kuàijī.
In the eighteenth year,
he was summoned to be General Who Manifests Awe.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he concurrently supervised military affairs at Shítóu Garrison,
and soon after became Regional Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the fifth year,
as West Central Inspector-General, he provisionally governed Nányān Zhōu.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he was restored to his title,
and soon after, given the additional title of General Who Manifests Awe,
and assigned assistant officials.
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he became Governor of Dānyáng.
In the fourth year,
he became Palace Attendant, General Who Manifests Favor, and Regional Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Because he exploited the common people,
the Vice Director of the Privy Treasury, Hé Zhìtōng, reported the matter.
Lún learned of this
and ordered his guest, Dài Zǐgāo, to stab him to death in the capital's lane.
Zhìtōng's son complained at the imperial court.
Gāozǔ ordered Lún's residence to be surrounded
and Zǐgāo to be arrested.
Lún hid him,
and he was never produced.
For this, Lún was dismissed and reduced to commoner status.
After a short while,
he was restored to his title.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he became Palace Attendant and General of Agile Cavalry.
In the seventh year,

he went out to serve as Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Yǐng, Dìng, Huò, and Sī, General Who Pacifies the West, and Regional Inspector of Yǐngzhōu,
In the first year of Zhōngdàtóng,
he went out to serve as General Who Guards the East and Regional Inspector of Nánsúzhōu.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Guard) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Bureau-Founding Commissioner with Rights and Privileges Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers).
When Hóu Jǐng instigated a rebellion,
he was additionally appointed Zhēngtǎo Dàdūdū (Grand Commander of the Punitive Expedition)
and led his troops to suppress Jǐng.
As he was about to depart,
Gāozǔ cautioned him, saying:
“Hóu Jǐng is a mere upstart,
quite skilled in military formations.
He cannot be annihilated in a single battle;
you must plan to subdue him over months and years.”
Lún reached Zhōnglí,
but Jǐng had already crossed Cǎishí.
Lún then traveled day and night,
sending his mobile forces to respond.
〔一三〕As they crossed the Yangtze River, a strong wind arose in mid-stream,
and one or two tenths of the men and horses drowned.
He then led Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Distant) Xīfēng Gōng Dàchūn, Xīngàn Gōng Dàchéng, and others,
〔一四〕with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
departing from Jīngkǒu.
General Bó chāo said:
“If we follow the main road through Huángchéng,
we will certainly encounter the rebels.
It would be better to take a direct route straight to Zhōngshān,
catching them by surprise.”
Lún agreed.
When the combined forces arrived suddenly,
the rebel band was greatly alarmed
and divided into three columns to attack Lún.
Lún fought them
and utterly defeated them,
beheading over a thousand.
The next day,
the rebels attacked again.
The stalemate lasted until late evening,
when the rebels gradually retreated.
Nán'ān Hóu Jùn (Marquis Jùn of Nán'ān) chased them with dozens of cavalry.
The rebels turned to resist Jùn,
and Jùn’s troops fell into disarray.
The rebels then pressed the main army,
which subsequently disintegrated.
Lún reached Zhōngshān
with barely a thousand men.
The rebels surrounded them,
and they were defeated again,
so he fled back to Jīngkǒu.
In the spring of the third year,
Lún again entered to provide aid with Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Dōngyáng Prefecture) Dàlián and others,
arriving at Piàojìzhōu.
He was promoted to Sīkōng (Minister of Works).
When Táichéng fell,
he fled to Yǔxué.
In the first year of Dàbǎo,
Lún arrived at Yǐngzhōu.
The Cìshǐ (Governor) Nánpíng Wáng Kè (Prince Kè of Nánpíng) yielded the prefecture to Lún,
but Lún refused it.
Kè then proposed Lún be appointed Jiǎ Huángyuè (Acting Imperial Axe) and Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of All Military Affairs, Internal and External).
Lún then established his officials
and renamed the administrative hall Zhèngyáng Diàn (Hall of the Correct Yang).
There were frequent omens of disaster,
which Lún greatly disliked.
At that time, Yuándì had long besieged Hédōng Wáng Yù (Prince Yù of Hédōng) in Chángshā,
cutting off internal and external communications.
Lún, hearing of his plight,
wanted to go rescue him,
but due to insufficient military provisions,
he stopped.
He then wrote to Shìzǔ, saying: "I humbly reflect that the sagely virtue of the former dynasty
governed the world with filial piety.
The nine degrees of kin were harmonious and affectionate,
and the four corners of the realm held no grievances.
This was truly the nation's governance,
and indeed also the family's tradition.
Only I and you
have jointly upheld the divine instruction;
we should adhere to this teaching
and together maintain it unchanged.
Moreover, this path is beautiful
and values harmony above all.
How much more so when the timing and geographical advantage
are less important than human concord.
How can
limbs and supports
slaughter each other?
Recently, I heard that Yù was self-willed and ignored instruction,
and as a junior, trespassed against a senior.
Within Xiāng and Xiá,
this eventually led to conflict.
As for Fāng and others, they
met with mutinous soldiers
and perished in battle,
dying in Wú.
Their fate in this regard was not unjust.
Hearing this news, I cried out in sorrow and pain,
only increasing my heartbreak and indignation.
My thoughts are tinged with mourning;
how can I express them?
My residence in the prefecture is remotely separated;
though I know the situation,
I do not understand the reasons.
When I reached this border region,
I made thorough inquiries.
Everyone said that Yù's responses and treatment were often inconsistent,
and his military provisions
were obstructed.
His younger brother's teachings also did not correct him,
thus an army was raised to attack.
Yù did not understand the greater principles;
he acted on his own will.
Though he was in dire straits,
how could he know our secret thoughts?
He was unable to politely
contend,
and instead brought an army.
Strife arose within the family,
turning close relatives into enemies.
To reach this point in one day,
how can one not sigh?
Since there are letters and inquiries,
spreading like clouds and rain,
there are rumors
in between,
making it impossible to fully investigate the details.
Currently, the nation is in peril and shame,
with deep wounds and profound pain.
Humans are not birds or beasts;
they know their ruler and father.
At present, the great enemy is still strong,
and the heavenly vengeance has not been avenged.
We, your
brothers,
are three outside.
If we do not assist in this crisis,
what use are we as ministers and sons?
We should only lay bare our hearts and taste gall,
weep blood and sleep on spears,
swear to the vast sky,
and rely on the spirits of the ancestral
sacrifices,
planning day and night,
together contemplating restoration.
As for other minor grievances,
perhaps they should be treated with leniency.
Truly, if a son's resentment is momentary,
what will be done about the nation's unavenged grievance?
It is proper to weigh the heavy and the light,
to prioritize the great over the small,
to discard unbeneficial emotions,
and to cut off lower-level mourning.
Broad-mindedness should guide us,
and sagacious understanding should strive for this.
Now that Zhōngshān has been lost,
and a nephew is again executed,
is this not like trying to stop boiling water by pouring in hot water,
or curing cold by swallowing ice?
If Yù's unrighteousness is such that
near and far equally resent him,
and his younger brother again follows his bad example,
then it is not his
sole fault.
Hopefully, you will be lenient with the general opinion
and endure until affairs are settled.
If external invaders are not yet eliminated,
and family disasters continue to arise,
then comparing the present with the past,
none have failed to perish.
The principle of warfare
lies in achieving victory;
as for battles between kin,
the more one wins, the more cruel it becomes.
Victory is not merit,
and defeat brings loss.
It exhausts soldiers and harms
righteousness,
resulting in many losses.
The reason Hóu Jǐng's army has not yet ventured beyond the river
is precisely because the frontier defenses are solid
and the imperial kinsmen are strong and numerous.
If we slaughter each other,
this is
to wage war on behalf of Jǐng.
Jǐng would then not need to expend military strength,
but would achieve success sitting idle.
When the ugly rebels hear of this,
what could please them more?
Furthermore, Zhuāng Tiě, a petty upstart, caused rebellion,
and has long held Guānníng and Huái'ān,
the two marquises,
as his pretext.
Dāngyáng is preoccupied with matters and constrained,
greatly neglecting its defensive border.
Upon hearing of punitive expeditions,
it again causes troops to be divided.
This is to slice
He was sent out as a Chief Bearer of the Imperial Ensign and Grand Supervisor of all military affairs along the Huái River, Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Běiyǎnzhōu.
At that time, there was a demonic rebel Buddhist monk Sēngqiáng who proclaimed himself emperor.
The local magnate Cài Bólóng raised an army in support of him.
Sēngqiáng had considerable knowledge of magical arts,
and they incited and deluded each other.
Their forces reached thirty thousand.
They attacked and captured Běixúzhōu.
Jìyīn Tàishǒu Yáng Qǐwén abandoned the city and fled.
Zhōnglí Tàishǒu Shān Xībǎo was killed.
Qìngzhī was sent to suppress them.
The imperial carriage proceeded to Báixià to see him off.
Gāozǔ said to Qìngzhī:
"The soldiers of Jiāng and Huái are strong;
their vanguard is difficult to withstand.
You should use strategy to control them,
and not engage in a decisive battle."
Qìngzhī accepted the order and departed.
Less than a full day had passed,
when he beheaded Bólóng and Sēngqiáng,
and sent their heads as a report.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he was appointed Grand Supervisor of the military affairs of the four prefectures of Nán Sī, Běi Sī, Xī Yù, and Yù, and Governor of Nán Sī and Běi Sī prefectures.
All other titles remained as before.
When Qìngzhī arrived at his post,
he then besieged Xuánhù.
He defeated Wèi Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Lóu Qǐ and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Shì Yúnbǎo at Zhēnshuǐ.
He also defeated Xíngtái Sūn Téng, Dàdūdū Hóu Jìn, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yáo Xióng, and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Gōng at Chǔchéng.
He disbanded the garrison troops at Yìyáng,
ceased water and land transport,
and the various prefectures along the rivers and lakes were all able to rest.
He opened six thousand qǐng of farmland.
Two years later,
the granaries were full.
Gāozǔ always praised and rewarded him.
He also memorialized to abolish Nánsīzhōu,
restore Ānlù Jùn,
and establish Shàngmíng Jùn.
In the second year of Dàtóng,
Wèi dispatched general Hóu Jǐng leading seventy thousand men to invade Chǔzhōu.
Cìshǐ Huán Hé was captured.
Jǐng then advanced his army to the Huái River,
and sent a letter to Qìngzhī asking him to surrender.
An imperial edict ordered Xiāngtán Hóu Tuì, Yòuwèi Xiàhóu Kuí, and others to go to their aid.
When the army reached Líjiāng,
Qìngzhī had already defeated Jǐng.
At that time, there was a severe cold and snow.
Jǐng abandoned his baggage and fled.
Qìngzhī collected it and returned.
He was promoted to the title of Rénwēi Jiāngjūn.
In that year,
Yùzhōu suffered from famine.
Qìngzhī opened the granaries to provide relief,
saving many lives.
Eight hundred people, including Lǐ Shēng from the prefecture, presented a memorial requesting a stele to be erected to praise his virtue.
An imperial edict granted it.
In the tenth month of the fifth year,
he died,
at the age of fifty-six.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
with a set of drum and wind instruments.
His posthumous title was Wǔ.
An imperial edict ordered Yìxīng Jùn to dispatch five hundred able-bodied men to attend the funeral.
Qìngzhī was reverent and cautious by nature.
He did not wear fine silks,
did not enjoy music,
was not skilled in archery,
and was not good with horses,
but he was good at comforting his soldiers
and could obtain their utmost loyalty.
His eldest son, Zhāo, inherited his titles.
His fifth son, Xīn,
had the courtesy name Jūnzhāng.
At seven, he could ride and shoot.
At twelve, he followed his father to Luòyáng,
but fell ill on the way
and returned to the capital.
He went to Hónglú Qīng Zhū Yì,
who inquired about the situation in the north.
Xīn gathered earth and drew on the ground,
pointing and explaining clearly.
Zhū Yì was very impressed by him.
In the fourth year of Dàtóng,
he became Shàolíng Wáng Chángshì, Wéndé Zhǔshuài, and Yòuwèi Zhàngzhǔ.
An imperial edict ordered him to assist in the defense of Yìyáng.
Wèi Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yáo Xióng was
a fierce general in the north,
and his nephew Bǎolè
was particularly brave and daring.
When Qìngzhī besieged Xuánhù,
Xióng came to his aid.
Bǎolè asked for a single horse to challenge him to battle.
Xīn spurred his horse directly towards Bǎolè.
Yáo Xióng immediately dispersed and fled.
He then captured Zhēnchéng.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Wēiyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Master of Xiǎoxiànchéng,
but was dismissed for an official matter.
In the tenth year,
the demonic rebel Wáng Qínzōng rose up in Bāshān Jùn.
Xīn was made Xuānměng Jiāngjūn
and given a temporary imperial seal to suppress him.
After Qínzōng was pacified,
he was appointed Yīnlíng Shùzhǔ and Běiqiáo Tàishǒu,
but did not take up the post due to illness.
He was then appointed Piàojì Wàibīng,
and soon became Línchuān Tàishǒu.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
Hóu Jǐng besieged Lìyáng.
An imperial edict summoned Xīn back.
Xīn reported:
"Cǎishí urgently needs a strong garrison.
Wáng Zhì's naval forces are weak and light;
I fear they will not suffice."
Thereupon, Xīn was appointed Yúnqí Jiāngjūn,
replacing Zhì.
Before he could reach Zhǔ,
Jǐng had already crossed the river.
He was then ordered to lead his subordinates to patrol outside the city,
and was not allowed to enter and guard it.
He wanted to flee to Jīngkǒu,
but was captured by Jǐng.
Jǐng saw Xīn's earnestness,
and so he kept him and drank heavily with him,
saying:
"I have obtained you here;
no one else can do anything."
He ordered Xīn to gather his troops
and intended to use him.
Xīn vowed not to comply.
Jǐng had his Yítóng Fàn Táobàng strictly guard him.
Xīn then persuaded Táobàng to lead his subordinates to surrender,
and to attack and kill Wáng Wěi and Sòng Zǐxiān as proof.
Táobàng agreed,
and they made an alliance.
A letter was shot into the city,
and Xīn was sent to rappel down at night and enter.
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased,
and issued an edict to immediately accept the surrender.
Tàizōng hesitated for several days and did not make a decision.
The external matter was exposed.
Xīn did not know this,
and still descended according to the appointed time.
Jǐng intercepted and captured him,
then forced Xīn to shoot another letter into the city,
saying
"Táobàng will lightly lead a few dozen men in first."
Jǐng wanted to follow him with armored troops.
Xīn, however, refused to write the letter,
determined to die.
He was then killed by Jǐng
at the age of thirty-three.
Lán Qīn, courtesy name Xiūmíng,
was a person from Zhōngchāng Wèi.
during the Tiānjiān period,
reached the official position of Yúnní Jiāngjūn due to military achievements,
and Governor of Jìzhōu.
Qīn was resolute and decisive in his youth,
and his swiftness surpassed others.
He followed his father in the northern campaigns
and was appointed Zhíhé of the Eastern Palace.
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he attacked Wèi Xiāochéng
and captured it.
He then defeated Péngchéng Biéjiāng Jiāo Zhòng,
advanced to attack Nǐshān Chéng,
and defeated their Dàdūdū Liú Shǔ's forces of two hundred thousand.
He advanced to attack Lóngchéng
and captured over a thousand horses.
He also defeated their Dàjiàng Chái Jí, as well as Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu Gāo Xuān, Biéjiāng Fàn Sīniàn, Zhèng Chéngzōng, and others.
He then attacked Juégù, Zhāng Lóng, and Zǐchéng.
Before they were captured,
Wèi Péngchéng Shǒujiàng Yáng Mù dispatched his son Yáng Xiàoyōng to lead light troops to reinforce.
Qīn intercepted and repelled him.
He also defeated Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ Liú Hǎiyóu,
then returned and captured Juégù,
taking its households.
Yáng Mù again dispatched Dūdū Fàn Sīniàn and Biéjiāng Cáo Lóngyá with tens of thousands of troops to reinforce.
Qīn engaged them in battle
and beheaded Cáo Lóngyá on the battlefield,
sending his head to the capital.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Hóu Jǐng's forces arrived,
he entered and guarded the Dōngyèmén Gate.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
When the palace city fell,
Wǎn fled,
and traveled externally to Jiānglíng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng, acting as regent,
appointed him Shìzhōng, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, Xiàngguó Chángshǐ,
with Shìzhōng as before.
He was then dispatched as Chíjié, Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, Xiāngdōng Nèishǐ.
In the second year of Chéngshèng,
he was recalled to serve as Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
and soon after, was additionally appointed Shìzhōng.
The following year,
Jiānglíng fell,
and all court officials were taken captive and brought into the passes.
Wǎn was excused due to illness,
and later died in Jiānglíng,
at the age of sixty-three.
His second son, Jiāo,
whose courtesy name was Shàoyóu,
was quite learned in literature,
and was selected to marry Ānyáng Gōngzhǔ, the eleventh daughter of Tàizōng.
he reached the office of Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
Mìshūchéng,
and was in charge of the records of the Eastern Palace.
Yáo Chá, the Chén Lìbù Shàngshū, said: In the chaos of Tàiqīng,
relatives were estranged and disloyal.
Zuǎn could not reconcile the regional princes
and achieve a harmonious and benevolent administration.
Instead, harboring private grudges,
he created discord in Xiāoxiāng,
which eventually brought calamity upon himself,
not due to loyalty and integrity.
Following this, the fall of Jiānglíng
was indeed rooted in these events.
Considering Zuǎn's character,
he ultimately became a cause of the turmoil in Liáng.
What a pity!
Textual Criticism Notes
Biographies, Volume 29: Xiāo Zǐkè (Disciple Fàn, Zǐxiǎn, Zǐyún)
Xiāo Zǐkè, courtesy name Jǐngchōng,
was a native of Lánlíng,
and the second son of Qí Yùzhāng Wénxiàn Wáng Yí.
During Yǒngmíng,
as a prince, he was enfeoffed as Nánkāng Xiàn Hóu.
At the age of twelve,
he composed a rhyme-prose with his elder cousin, Sītú Jìnglíng Wáng Gāo Sōng,
and Wèijūn Wáng Jiǎn saw it and marveled at him.
Initially, he served as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Huáilíng Tàishǒu.
During Jiànwǔ,
he was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wújùn Tàishǒu.
When Dàsīmǎ Wáng Jìngzé raised troops in Huìjī to rebel,
using the name of supporting Zǐkè,
Míngdì summoned Zǐkè's brothers and over seventy of his close relatives into the Western Bureau,
intending to harm them that night.
It happened that Zǐkè had abandoned his commandery and rushed back,
arriving that very day,
so Míngdì stopped.
He appointed Zǐkè as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Dōnghūn ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Mìshūjiān,
also serving as Yòujūn Jiāngjūn,
and soon after became Shìzhōng.
In the second year of Zhōngxīng,
he was promoted to Fǔguó Zīyì Cānjūn.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
his rank was demoted to Zǐ,
and he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
also serving as Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Due to illness, he did not accept the appointment,
and was transferred to Guānglù Dàfū.
Soon after, he became Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn 蕭子顯 once wrote an autobiography.
Its summary says:
"I, as the Imperial Tutor of Shàolíng Wáng 邵陵王,
was honored to return to the capital.
Recalling those before me from afar,
there were Táng 唐 and Sòng 宋 of Chǔ 楚,
and Yán 嚴 and Zōu 鄒 of Liáng 梁.
Reflecting on my life,
I was quite fond of literary embellishment.
Although I achieved no fame,
my heart's desire was fulfilled.
Whenever I ascended a height and gazed to the horizon,
or watched things float away by the water,
or felt the wind stir on a spring morning,
or saw the moon bright on an autumn night,
or the early geese first appeared,
or flowers bloomed and leaves fell—
whenever there was an occasion, I responded,
and could never stop myself.
In previous generations, Jiǎ, Fù, Cuī, Mǎ, Hándān, Miào, Lù 賈、傅、崔、馬、邯鄲、繆、路 and their like,
all became prominent through their writing.
Therefore, I frequently presented eulogies,
comparing myself to the ancients.
In the sixteenth year of Tiānjiān 天監,
I first attended the Ninth Day imperial banquet.
Amongst the dense crowd,
I alone received an imperial edict that said: 'The clouds and scenery today are exceedingly beautiful;
how can you not compose a poem?'
After the poem was completed,
another imperial edict descended, saying: 'He can be called a talented scholar.'
I retired and said to others: 'Such a glance of favor
came unexpectedly.
How then can I compare myself to Jiǎ Yì 賈誼?
It is not easy to bear.'
Whenever I composed something,
I particularly lacked laborious thought;
I waited for it to come naturally,
not forcing it with effort.
The poems and rhymed prose I wrote in my youth,
especially the preface to Hóngxù 鴻序—
its style encompassed many forms,
and its literary quality was comprehensive in many ways.
It was quite widely circulated by those who appreciated literature,
thus my reputation spread easily."
Among Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's 蕭子顯 works were the Hòuhàn Shū 後漢書 in one hundred volumes,
the Qí Shū 齊書 in sixty volumes,
the Pǔtōng Běifá Jì 普通北伐記 in five volumes,
the Guìjiǎn Chuán 貴儉傳 in thirty volumes,
and a collection of his writings in twenty volumes.
His two sons, Xù 序 and Kǎi 愷,
both became famous in their youth.
Xù 序,
during the Tàiqīng 太清 period, successively held offices such as Táizǐ Jiālìng 太子家令
and Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
and was also in charge of official documents.
During the rebellion,
he died within the city.
Kǎi 愷,
initially a student of the Guózǐ 國子,
ranked highly in the policy examination.
The province also recommended him as Xiùcái 秀才.
He began his career as Mìshū Láng 祕書郎,
and was promoted to Táizǐ Zhōngshèrén 太子中舍人,
Wángfǔ Zhǔbù 王府主簿,
and Táizǐ Xǐmǎ 太子洗馬.
He resigned from office due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was reinstated as Táizǐ Xǐmǎ 太子洗馬,
then promoted to Zhōngshèrén 中舍人,
and was also in charge of official documents.
He was successively promoted to Xuānchéng Wáng Wénxué 宣城王文學,
Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎,
and Táizǐ Jiālìng 太子家令,
again in charge of official documents.
Kǎi's 愷 talent, learning, and reputation
were at the time compared to his father's.
Tàizōng 太宗, while in the Eastern Palace,
early on invited and befriended him.
At that time, Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子 Xiè Gǔ 謝嘏 was dispatched to govern Jiàn'ān 建安.
A farewell banquet was held in Xuānyóu Táng 宣猷堂,
and talented scholars of the time were invited to compose poems,
all using fifteen difficult rhymes.
Kǎi's 愷 poem was finished first,
and its words were also beautiful.
Tàizōng 太宗 sent a message to Xiāngdōng Wáng 湘東王, saying:
"Wáng Yún 王筠 is originally an old master,
but among the younger generation, Xiāo Kǎi 蕭愷 is notable;
he is indeed a talented scholar."
Before this, Gù Yěwáng 顧野王, a Tàixué Bóshì 太學博士, had been ordered to compile the Yùpiān 玉篇.
Tàizōng 太宗 felt that its detailedness and brevity were not entirely appropriate,
and since Kǎi 愷 was learned
and particularly skilled in philology,
he was instructed to revise it with other scholars.
He was promoted to Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
but before he could be formally installed,
he was transferred to Lìbù Láng 吏部郎.
In the second year of Tàiqīng 太清,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞.
Soon after,
Hóu Jǐng 侯景 instigated a rebellion.
Kǎi 愷 was promoted to Shìzhōng 侍中 within the city,
but died in office shortly thereafter,
at the age of forty-four.
His collected works were all lost.
Zǐyún 子雲, courtesy name Jǐngqiáo 景喬,
was the ninth younger brother of Zǐkè 子恪.
At the age of twelve,
in the fourth year of Qiánwǔ 建武 of Qí 齊,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīnpǔ Xiàn 新浦縣.
He drafted his own petition for the appointment,
which already possessed literary elegance.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān 天監,
his peerage was reduced to a Viscount.
When he grew older, he was diligent in his studies.
Since there was no complete book on the Jìn 晉 dynasty,
he dedicated himself to compiling one in his youth.
By the age of twenty-six,
the book was completed.
He presented it to the throne,
and an imperial edict ordered it to be deposited in the Imperial Library.
Zǐyún 子雲 was by nature calm and quiet,
and did not enjoy seeking official advancement.
At the age of thirty,
he finally began his career as Mìshū Láng 祕書郎.
He was promoted to Táizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人.
He compiled and presented the Dōnggōng Xīnjì 東宮新記,
and was awarded silk by imperial decree.
He was successively promoted to Běizhōngláng Wàibīng Cānjūn 北中郎外兵參軍,
Jìn'ān Wáng Wénxué 晉安王文學,
Sītú Zhǔbù 司徒主簿,
and Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng 丹陽尹丞.
At that time, Xiāngdōng Wáng 湘東王 was the capital's governor,
and deeply appreciated and favored him,
treating him as a friend of humble origins.
He was promoted to Běizhōngláng Lúlíng Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn 北中郎廬陵王諮議參軍,
concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞.
In the first year of Dàtōng 大通,
he was appointed Huángmén Láng 黃門郎,
then shortly promoted to Qīngchē Jiāngjūn 輕車將軍,
concurrently Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ 司徒左長史.
In the second year,
he entered the court as Lìbù 吏部.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Chángjiān Shìzhōng 長兼侍中.
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng 中大通,
he was transferred to Tàifǔ Qīng 太府卿.
In the third year,
he was dispatched as Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn, Línchuān Nèishǐ 貞威將軍、臨川內史.
In the commandery, he was praised for his harmonious governance,
and the people and officials were pleased with him.
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍,
then shortly thereafter reinstated as Shìzhōng 侍中.
In the second year of Dàtóng 大同,
he was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì 員外散騎常侍 and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ 國子祭酒,
concurrently holding the position of Nánxú Zhōu Dàzhōngzhèng 南徐州大中正.
Soon after,
he was again made Shìzhōng 侍中.
His positions as Jìjiǔ 祭酒 and Zhōngzhèng 中正 remained as before.
He was appointed as Clerk to the Ministry of Ceremonies, and subsequently, Secretary of the Ministry of Carts.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng (501 CE),
Gāozǔ entered Shítou.
At that time, Yuán Áng, the Administrator of Wúxìng, held the commandery and resisted the righteous army.
So, Gāozǔ ordered Jiāng Gé to draft a decree for Áng.
He completed it while seated,
and its language and meaning were elegant and refined.
Gāozǔ greatly admired and praised it,
and consequently ordered him to manage the secretarial affairs together with Xú Miǎn.
When the Prince of Jiàn'ān was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
he submitted a memorial requesting Jiāng Gé to be his secretary.
Thus, Jiāng Gé was appointed Aide to the General of the North and Chief Clerk,
concurrently holding the position of Magistrate of Zhōnglú.
He and his younger brother, Jiāng Guān, had lived together since childhood,
unable to bear separation.
Jiāng Gé earnestly pleaded for Guān to accompany him.
So, Guān was appointed Provisional Aide to the General of the North,
and concurrently Chief Clerk.
At that time, Shěn Yuē of Wúxìng and Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān both highly appreciated each other.
Fǎng wrote to Jiāng Gé, saying:
"This selection of outstanding talents for the Yōngzhōu court,
for the positions of literary staff,
encompasses both you and your younger brother.
It can be said to be like driving two dragons on a long road,
or galloping a fine steed for a thousand *lǐ*."
While en route in Jiāngxià,
Guān fell ill and died.
Jiāng Gé was in Yōng at the time,
treated with great courtesy by the Prince of the Prefecture,
as if he were a commoner.
When the Prince was recalled to serve as Prefect of Dānyáng,
he appointed Jiāng Gé as Chief Clerk,
concurrently heading the Five Bureaus,
and then promoted him to Palace Attendant,
and Magistrate of Jiànkāng.
He was frequently transferred to be Magistrate of Mòlíng and Jiànkāng.
His governance was clear and severe,
and powerful families feared him.
He was appointed as a Gentleman-in-Waiting of the Central Secretariat,
Assistant Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and Minister of Agriculture.
He was then reassigned out as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Jìn'ān, with the title of Commander of the Cloud Brigade, Administrator of Xúnyáng, and acting Administrator of Jiāngzhōu Prefecture.
He was transferred to be Chief Clerk to the Prince of Lúlíng, with the title of General of Awesome Benevolence.
His positions as Administrator and acting official remained as before.
His strict integrity made him feared by all cities.
At that time, the young Prince, while acting as governor, often inclined his favors towards his personal retainers.
Jiāng Gé, upholding his uprightness,
refused to sit with these retainers.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nánpíng, and Imperial Censor,
impeaching powerful and influential figures,
without any hesitation.
He was appointed Minister of the Imperial Treasury,
then reassigned out as General of Awesome Power, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nánkāng, with the title of General of the Northern Central Guard, and Administrator of Guǎnglǐng.
He was then reassigned as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Yùzhāng, with the title of General of the Garrison of the North.
His positions as General and Administrator remained as before.
At that time, Yuán Fǎsēng, the Wei Inspector of Xúzhōu, surrendered and defected.
Jiāng Gé was commanded to accompany the Prince of the Prefecture to garrison Péngchéng.
When the city was lost,
Jiāng Gé, being habitually uncomfortable on horseback,
returned by boat.
Passing through Xiàpī,
he was captured by the Wei people.
Yuán Yánmíng, the Wei Inspector of Xúzhōu, having heard of Jiāng Gé's talent and reputation,
received him with great generosity.
Jiāng Gé claimed to suffer from a foot ailment and did not prostrate himself.
Yánmíng intended to harm him,
but seeing Jiāng Gé's stern and upright demeanor,
he instead respected him greatly.
At that time, Zǔ Jī was also captured.
Yánmíng ordered Jī to compose inscriptions for an *yīqì* (a self-emptying vessel) and a clepsydra.
Jiāng Gé cursed Jī, saying:
"You have received great favor from the state,
yet you have not repaid it.
Now you are writing inscriptions for barbarians,
betraying the imperial court."
Hearing this, Yánmíng
then ordered Jiāng Gé to compose an inscription for the Zhàngbā Temple stele and a text for sacrificing to Péng Zǔ.
Jiāng Gé declined, saying that he had been imprisoned for so long
that he had lost all capacity for thought.
Yánmíng pressed him even more harshly,
threatening to whip him.
Jiāng Gé, with a stern expression, said:
"I, Jiāng Gé, am sixty years old.
Unable to die for my lord,
I would consider it fortunate to die today.
I vow never to write for another."
Yánmíng, knowing he could not be coerced,
stopped.
He was given three *shēng* of hulled grain daily,
barely enough to sustain his life.
When the Wei Emperor requested Yuán Luè, the Prince of Zhōngshān, to return to the North,
Jiāng Gé and Zǔ Jī were released and allowed to return to court.
An imperial edict stated:
"Jiāng Gé, formerly General of Awesome Power, Chief Clerk of the Garrison of the North, and Administrator of Guǎnglǐng,
is intelligent and resourceful,
with a reputation both in and out of office.
In court, he is righteous;
in danger, he is unyielding.
As a chief assistant to the government,
he truly meets with unanimous approval.
He is appointed Chief Clerk to the Prince of Línchuān, the Grand Commandant."
At that time, Gāozǔ was deeply devoted to Buddhism,
and many court officials requested to receive the precepts.
Jiāng Gé deeply believed in cause and effect,
but Gāozǔ did not know this,
thinking that Jiāng Gé did not follow Buddhism.
So, he bestowed upon Jiāng Gé a poem of five hundred characters titled "Awakening to Understanding,"
saying:
"One should diligently strive forward,
and strengthen oneself in virtuous cultivation;
How can one be so obstinate,
like those certain to die in prison?
This I tell Jiāng Gé,
and also all noble gentlemen."
He also sent a personal decree saying:
"The retribution of the world
cannot be disbelieved.
How can you be as stubborn as you were when facing Yuán Yánmíng?"
Jiāng Gé then memorialized to request receiving the Bodhisattva precepts.
He was again appointed Minister of the Imperial Treasury, Chief Clerk, and Commandant.
At that time, the Prince of Wǔlíng was in the Eastern Province,
and was rather arrogant and unrestrained.
The Emperor summoned Jiāng Gé and personally decreed:
"The Prince of Wǔlíng is young,
and Zāng Dùn is weak by nature,
unable to correct him.
I wish to appoint you to replace him as acting governor.
No one but you will do,
and you must not refuse."

So, he was appointed General Who Crushes the Attack, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Wǔlíng, with the title of General of the Eastern Central Guard, Vice-Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery, and acting governor of the prefecture.
Jiāng Gé's protégés and former subordinates,
many of whose families were in the Eastern Province,
hearing that Jiāng Gé was about to arrive,
all brought gifts and waited along the road to greet him.
Jiāng Gé said:
"I generally do not accept gifts.
It is not right for me to accept baskets from former acquaintances alone."
Upon arriving at his post,
he relied only on his official salary,
and his meals never had more than one dish.
The commandery was vast and prosperous,
with hundreds of lawsuits daily.
Jiāng Gé judged and analyzed them,
never having any doubts or delays.
Merits were certainly rewarded,
and transgressions were certainly punished.
The people were at peace, and officials feared him,
causing all cities to tremble.
Wáng Qiān of Lángyá, as Magistrate of Shānyīn,
was notoriously corrupt.
Hearing of Jiāng Gé, he voluntarily resigned.
The Prince of the Prefecture feared him,
and thus held him in elegant respect.
Whenever he attended banquets,
their discussions always revolved around poetry and classics.
The Prince consequently became engrossed in learning and fond of literature.
Diǎnqiān Shěn Chìwén presented the poems composed by the Prince to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ said to the Grand Astrologer Xú Miǎn:
"Jiāng Gé is indeed capable of fulfilling his duties."
He was then appointed Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
When he was about to return,
the people all felt reluctant to part with him,
but he accepted none of their farewell gifts.
The farewell boats were arranged as before,
but Jiāng Gé did not accept any of them.
He only took the single boat provided by the court.
The hull of the boat was uneven,
making it impossible to sleep comfortably.
Someone said to Jiāng Gé:
"Since the boat is unbalanced,
crossing the river will be very dangerous.
You should move heavy objects
to weigh down the light side of the hull."
As Jiāng Gé had no belongings,
he collected over ten pieces of stone from the bank of Xīlíng to balance it.
Such was his incorruptibility and poverty.
Soon after, he became Supervisor of Wújùn.
At that time, the region suffered from famine and desolation,
and bandits roamed openly.
When Jiāng Gé arrived at the commandery,
he only had twenty officially provided guards for himself.
The common people feared that he would not be able to quell the bandits;
they even feared the roaming military officials even more.
The common people were even more afraid of the patrolling military officials.
Jiāng Gé then extensively extended grace and comfort,
and clearly enforced regulations.
The bandits ceased their activities,
and the people and officials were at peace.
Initially,
Jǐng plotted rebellion.
The Prefect of Hézhōu, King Póyáng Fàn, and the Prefect of Sīzhōu, Yáng Yārén, both repeatedly submitted memorials reporting this.
Cái, however, believing Jǐng to be isolated and relying on them for survival,
thought he surely wouldn't do such a thing.
So he told the envoy,
"King Póyáng truly will not allow the state to have even one guest!"
He then suppressed the reports and did not submit them.
Therefore, the imperial court made no preparations.
When the invaders arrived,
all the civil and military officials in the city blamed him.
The Crown Prince also composed "An Ode to the Besieged City,"
the last stanza of which reads:
"Those with high caps and thick shoes,
who feast sumptuously and ride in comfort,
ascend to the crimson ground of the purple heavens,
and push open the golden doors of the jade palace.
They present strategies and offer advice,
proclaim the fortunes and might of governance and punishment.
Because of them, the four borders are filled with ramparts,
and all nations are still unsettled.
We ask, which are the jackals and wolves?
We inquire, who are these vipers and lizards?"
This was meant to refer to Cái.
Cái, feeling ashamed and indignant,
fell ill and died,
at the age of sixty-seven.
An imperial edict stated:
"The late Grand Warden of the Palace Guard, Cái,
possessed a broad and penetrating intellect,
and ample talent and strength.
He advised from within the帷幄 (wéiwò, staff tent)
for many years.
He was still assisting in the affairs of the court
and diligently fulfilling his appointed duties.
His sudden demise before his time
fills us with both sorrow and compassion.
He is hereby posthumously granted the titles of Attendant Censor and Right Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs,
and given one set of imperial ceremonial implements.
All necessities for his funeral
shall be provided as required."
It was not customary for the title of Shàngshū (尚書) to be given posthumously.
When Cái died,
Gāozǔ regretted it deeply,
and was about to discuss the matter of posthumous grants.
Among his attendants, some who were close to Cái
then memorialized, saying:
"Although Cái held many nominal positions,
what he truly wished for in life
was to hold the position of an enforcer of the law."
Gāozǔ, honoring his long-held aspiration,
made this special posthumous grant.
Cái held positions of power for over thirty years.
He was skilled at discerning the subtle intentions of the ruler,
and adept at flattery to cater to the emperor's will,
thus he was especially favored and trusted.
His official career ranged from Gentleman-in-Waiting to Attendant Censor,
four offices all adorned with mink tails.
From Commander of the Right Guard to Grand Warden of the Palace Guard,
four positions all allowed him to drive with official escorts.
This was unprecedented in recent times.
Cái and his sons owned a series of residences from Cháogōu to Qīngxī,
complete with terraces, ponds, and amusements.
Whenever he had leisure, he would visit them with guests.
Gifts from all directions,
wealth and goods, piled up.
He was naturally parsimonious,
never dispensing charity.
His valuable delicacies would rot,
and every month he would discard over ten cartloads,
without even sharing them with his sons in their separate quarters.
The "Lectures on the Rites and Changes," "Ceremonial Regulations," and "Collected Works" he compiled, totaling over a hundred chapters,
were mostly lost during the chaos.
His eldest son, Sù,
served as Doctor of the National Academy;
his second son, Rùn,
was a Sītú Yuán (司徒掾, Assistant in the Ministry of Works).
Both met their end in the rebellion.
Hè Chēn, courtesy name Guóbǎo,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His paternal uncle, Yáng,
was a Commandant of Infantry,
and considered a great Confucian scholar of his generation.
When Chēn was young,
Yáng taught him the classics,
and he grasped their meaning upon first hearing.
Yáng was astonished,
often saying:
"This child will achieve nobility through his understanding of the classics."
After Yáng's death,
Chēn's family was poor.
He often traveled to Zhūjì
to sell grain to support himself.
In his free time, he would study,
especially excelling in the Sānlǐ (三禮, Three Rites).
Initially,
Yáng gathered students in his hometown to teach.
Now, they also relied on Chēn.
During the Pǔtōng (普通) era,
the Prefect, King Línchuān, appointed him as Libationer and Aide-de-camp.
When Chēn first arrived in the capital,
Gāozǔ, hearing of his scholarship,
summoned him to the Wéndédéng (文德殿, Hall of Literary Virtue).
He was pleased after conversing with him,
and said to the Right Executive Assistant Xú Miǎn:
"Chēn truly possesses a generational legacy."
He was then appointed Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Royal Domain,
and soon concurrently served as Doctor of the Imperial University.
He gradually rose to the positions of Military Advisor to the Central Guard and Executive Secretary of the Department of State Affairs,
participating in ceremonial matters.
He was successively promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance,
while retaining his position as Executive Secretary.
He also served as Registrar to King Póyáng of the Western Expedition,
and concurrently as Assistant Executive of the Left in the Department of State Affairs,
becoming full-time after a year.
An edict commanded Chēn to compile a new method for posthumous titles,
which is still in use today.
At that time, the Crown Prince debated
that at the end of the Dàgōng (大功, Major Mourning) period, one could crown a son or marry off a daughter.
Chēn refuted this, saying: "The imperial directive states that
at the end of Dàgōng, one may crown a son and marry off a daughter,
but not crown oneself or marry oneself.
Judging by the ancient texts,
I am still somewhat perplexed.
The rites of marriage and capping
were originally performed by the father.
A person without a father
may cap themselves.
Therefore, when Dàgōng and Xiǎogōng (小功, Minor Mourning) are mentioned,
they are always presented as 'capping a son and marrying off a daughter' in the text,
not implying that one
may only do so for a son
but not for oneself.
At the end of the Xiǎogōng period,
one may indeed marry oneself,
yet it also states
'capping a son and marrying a wife,'
the meaning of which becomes even clearer.
Therefore, by first listing
the two mourning periods,
and consistently specifying 'capping a son and marrying off a daughter'
at the end of the sentence,
the meaning of marrying oneself becomes apparent.
Since it is clear that one can marry oneself at the end of Xiǎogōng,
it follows that one can cap oneself at the end of Dàgōng.
This
is a condensed statement that reveals the underlying principle.
If it is argued that because one observes Dàgōng for a father,
and a son observes Xiǎogōng,
and Xiǎogōng is a lighter mourning,
one may therefore cap a son and marry a daughter for him,
while Dàgōng is a heavier mourning,
thus
one may not marry or cap oneself—
then at the end of Xiǎogōng,
unless it explicitly states that the mourning for father and son is different,
it should not again mention
'capping a son and marrying a daughter.'
If it is argued that the text for Xiǎogōng
states that one may marry oneself,
but the text for Dàgōng does not state that one may cap oneself,
hence it is understood that one in Dàgōng
may not perform auspicious rites for oneself,
but only cap a son or marry off a daughter for him—
I believe that
not performing auspicious rites while in mourning
is fundamentally because auspicious and inauspicious events cannot intermingle.
Although a son at the end of Xiǎogōng
may perform capping and marriage,
he still requires his father to cap
and marry him.
If a father at the end of Dàgōng may cap his son and marry off his daughter,
this implies no obstruction in the rites for auspicious and inauspicious events;
if there is no obstruction,
how could he not cap
or marry himself?
If capping and marrying oneself would be obstructed,
how then could capping a son and marrying off a daughter be permissible?
Now, to permit capping a son but forbid capping oneself,
this is what perplexes
Chēn.
Furthermore, the imperial directive reasons:
'If one in Xiǎogōng for a junior prematurely deceased child cannot marry a wife,
then one in Dàgōng with reduced mourning cannot cap a son or marry off a daughter either.'
Upon careful consideration of this directive,
if it means that one in
Dàgōng with reduced mourning cannot cap a son or marry off a daughter,
then one in Xiǎogōng with reduced mourning also cannot cap oneself or marry oneself.
This would mean that all those in Dàgōng or Xiǎogōng with reduced mourning cannot perform capping
or marriage.
The ancient texts should then say 'if in reduced mourning, then not permissible,'
how could it only refer to a junior prematurely deceased child?
Now, it does not speak of reduced mourning generally,
but specifically cites a junior prematurely deceased child,
which indeed has its own meaning.
For
After being married off,
or having remarried,
the person who was married off
has a Dàgōng (大功) relationship with their natal sisters.
If it is a Dàfū (大夫) serving as a Shì (士) father,
and the reduction in mourning (jiàng 降) is due to status (zūn 尊),
then it becomes Xiǎogōng (小功).
For capping and marriage,
the principle is no different.
The reason for this is that
when married out, there is one who receives me,
and when married in (as a daughter-in-law, ‘out after’), there is one who transmits the trọng (重) [lineage/inheritance].
It is intended to make light of
this and favor that;
though this mourning服 (fú) is reduced,
that mourning服 is elevated.
In the past, those who were Qīqīn (期親),
even if the mourning was reduced twice, still followed the rites of Xiǎogōng (小功),
and could be capped or married.
As for
Qī (期) reduced to Dàgōng (大功),
and Dàgōng (大功) reduced to Xiǎogōng (小功),
it is only one grade,
a reduction and lessening with order.
As for mourning for marriage and capping,
therefore there is no difference.
Only for the mourning of Xiàshāng (下殤)
is it specifically
stated that they do not marry.
This is because of their young age;
the grief of untimely death is deep.
Since there is no receiving the thick (mourning) from another surname,
and it is also different from transmitting the trọng (重) to that clan,
it is feared that due to their young age,
the mourning might be light,
abruptly becoming a major reduction.
Therefore, it is specifically stated that they do not marry,
to show the favor of the original importance.
Therefore, in all cases of reduced mourning,
capping and marriage are not distinguished;
only for Xiàshāng (下殤)
is it
stated that they do not marry.
If the principle is like this,
then it cannot be said that all reduced mourning for Dàgōng (大功)
cannot be capped or married.
Moreover, the record says,
"Xiàshāng (下殤) is Xiǎogōng (小功)."
To speak of Xiàshāng (下殤)
means it cannot apply to Zhōngshāng (中殤) or Shàngshāng (上殤);
to speak of Xiǎogōng (小功) means it cannot include Dàgōng (大功).
If in fact, all reduced mourning for Dàgōng (大功) and Xiǎogōng (小gōng) cannot be capped or married,
and the two types of Shàng (上) and Zhōng (中) Shāng (殤) also
cannot be capped or married,
then the record could not simply say,
"Xiàshāng (下殤) Xiǎogōng (小gōng) then cannot."
This might not be the meaning of the text.
This is also what Chēn (琛) doubted.
So, Chēn’s (琛) proposal was followed.
He was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍).
Previously, the Nán Zuò (南坐) in the Shàngshū (尚書) did not wear marten fur (diāo 貂);
marten fur began with Chēn (琛).
Shortly after,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞),
participating in ritual matters as before.
Chēn’s (琛) family wealth was abundant;
he bought a lord's residence as his home.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities (Yǒusī 有司)
and was dismissed from office for this offense.
Soon after, he again became Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞),
then promoted to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎),
concurrently Guózi Bóshì (國子博士).
Before being installed,
he was changed to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍),
leading Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞),
and also participating in ritual matters.
Throughout his various positions,
Chēn (琛)
initiated and established many of the rituals for suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples.
Whenever he met Gāozǔ (高祖),
their conversations often lasted for a long time.
Therefore, in the palace (shěng zhōng 省中), a saying emerged:
"Hè Yǎ (賀雅) goes up to the hall and doesn't come down."
Chēn’s (琛) demeanor was elegant and refined,
hence people of the time called him that.
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
participating in ritual matters as before.
At this time,
those whom Gāozǔ (高祖) had appointed to office
were all cunning and sycophantic,
deeply harming the governance of the time.
Chēn (琛) then submitted a memorial detailing various matters, stating:
"I have received the grace of being promoted,
yet I have not been able to perform a single duty;
holding the responsibility of offering advice,
I have also not been able to recommend a single word.
I humbly hear
that 'a benevolent father does not love a useless
son,
and an enlightened ruler does not keep a useless minister.'
This is why I sigh
in the middle of the night, even abandoning my meal.
I now presume to speak on current affairs,
listing them below.
This is not
to offer counsel,
nor to present advice.
I keep my thoughts sealed within my chest,
not speaking to my wife or children.
My words are without embellishment;
if edited, they are burned.
If they are fortunate enough to be heard,
I ask that they be carefully considered.
If they do not align [with your wishes],
then I acknowledge my foolishness.
The first matter states: Now, the northern borders are subservient,
weapons are laid down and peace prevails.
This is precisely the time for production, accumulation, education, and training.
However, the population of the empire is declining,
which is indeed
the urgent task of today.
Although all areas are suffering from devastation and displacement,
it is even worse outside the passes.
Commanderies (jùn 郡) cannot endure the overall control of the provinces (zhōu 州),
and districts (xiàn 縣) cannot endure the levies and reductions of the commanderies.
They harass each other,
unable
to manage their administration,
focusing only on responding to requisitions and collections.
The common people cannot bear their lot and
move away,
some relying on influential families,
others gathering in fortified settlements.
They flee out of necessity,
not by choice.
The state's taxes and levies outside the passes are rather light;
yet, annual rents and taxes
often lead to arrears and accumulation.
Meanwhile, the people lose
their peaceful homes.
Is this not the fault of the governors and magistrates?
The eastern border's population is sparse,
all due to the frequent imperial envoys.
A dog does not bark at night,
thus the people can live in peace.
Now,
in large states and large districts,
those bearing imperial decrees by boat
are not just a few dozen;
even remote villages
and distant towns
are all reached.
Every time an envoy arrives,
they cause
disturbance;
moreover, this accumulated harassment
deeply harms the people.
Incompetent district magistrates
merely stand by and let them exploit;
while cunning and vicious senior officials
take advantage of this to become
corrupt and cruel.
Even if there are honest and fair ones,
the commandery still restricts them.
Therefore, district magistrates holding their seals
rarely have their performance evaluated;
ordinary people abandon their occupations,
and many become vagrants.
Although imperial edicts for the restoration
of occupations are issued annually,
and graces of tax remission are frequently bestowed,
they ultimately cannot return to their homes.
The second matter states: The compassionate heart of the sagely ruler,
and the concern for those in peril,
are known far and wide.
Even tiny creatures that fly and crawl
are saved,
let alone the countless
common people.
Yet, the provinces and commanderies have no will to care for the people.
Thus, the whole world looks up eagerly,
relying solely on one person,
truly embodying the saying:
'Love them like parents,
look up to them like the sun
and moon,
revere them like ghosts and spirits,
fear them like thunder.'
If there is pain that needs relief and medicine,
how can it not be treated?
Today, the reason why all local officials (zǎishǒu 宰守) throughout the empire are inclined towards
greed and cruelty,
and few are incorruptible,
is truly due to the extravagant customs,
which make them so.
The abuses of extravagance and excess
are numerous;
I will briefly mention two points,
speaking of their worst.
Xiǎn was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and was known as a child prodigy by his contemporaries.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was recommended as a Xiùcái.
He was appointed as the Aide to the Commander of the Central Army, Prince Línchuān, upon shedding his civilian clothes.
Shortly after, he was appointed as the Fa Cáo.
Xiǎn loved learning
and was broadly knowledgeable and well-versed.
Rèn Fǎng once obtained a damaged scroll with missing sections,
on which the characters were fragmented.
He showed it to various people,
but none could identify it.
Xiǎn said it was a lost chapter deleted from the ancient Shàngshū.
Fǎng checked the Zhōu Shū,
and it was indeed as he had said.
Fǎng greatly admired and marvelled at him.
When he was in mourning for his mother,
after the period of mourning ended,
Shàngshū Lìng Shěn Yuē ordered his carriage to visit him.
At the meeting, he quizzed Xiǎn on ten topics from the Classics and Histories,
and Xiǎn answered nine of them.
Yuē said:
"This old man is dim-witted and forgetful,
and cannot be questioned;
nevertheless,
I will try a few things,
but not all ten."
Xiǎn asked him five questions,
and Yuē answered two.
Lù Chuí heard of this and sighed, saying:
"Master Liú can be called an extraordinary person.
Even if Píngyuán of our family visited Zhāng Zhuàngwǔ,
or Wáng Càn met Bójiē,
they would certainly not have such an exchange."
Such was the praise and admiration he received from eminent figures.
When Yuē became the Taìzǐ Shǎofù,
he appointed him as Wǔguān Yuàn,
and shortly after, he concurrently served as Tíngwèi Zhèng.
Wǔbīng Shàngshū Fù Zhāo, who was in charge of literary works,
was compiling the national history
and appointed Xiǎn as his assistant.
In the ninth year,
the Wǔ Dū Xuǎn system of the Shàngshū was reformed for the first time.
Xiǎn concurrently served as Lìbù Láng in his original post.
He was also appointed as the Waìbīng Cānjūn for Sīkōng, Prince Línchuān,
and later promoted to Shàngshū Yícáo Láng.
He once composed a poem for the imperial court.
Shěn Yuē saw it and praised its beauty.
At that time, Yuē's suburban residence had just been completed,
so he commissioned a calligrapher to inscribe it on the wall.
He was dispatched as Jìshì Cānjūn for Prince Línchuān.
After the pacification of Jiànkāng,
he re-entered service as Shàngshū Yícáo Shìláng,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was dispatched as the Magistrate of Mòlíng,
and then appointed Jìshì for Piàojì, Prince Póyáng,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He was successively promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi and Zhōngshū Shìláng,
with his Shèrén position remaining unchanged.
Xiǎn, along with Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng, Liú Zhīlín of Nányáng, and Gù Xié of Wújùn,
held positions together within the forbidden palace.
They taught and befriended each other,
and contemporary people all admired them.
Xiǎn was broadly learned and had a strong memory,
surpassing Péi and Gù.
At that time, Wei people presented ancient artifacts
with embossed characters,
which no one could identify.
Xiǎn examined the text and read it
without any difficulty or hesitation.
He verified the year and month,
and not a single character was wrong.
Gāozǔ greatly commended him.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng
and appointed Guózǐ Bóshì.
He was dispatched as Zhǎngshǐ for Xuānyuǎn, Prince Yuèyáng,
managing the affairs of the prefecture and state.
Before he took up the post,
he was promoted to Zhǎngshǐ of Yúnhuī, Prince Shàolíng, and Prefect of Xúnyáng.
In the ninth year of Dàtóng,
the Prince moved his garrison to Yǐngzhōu,
and he was appointed Píngxī Zīyì Cānjūn,
and granted the title Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn.
He died that year
at the age of sixty-three.
His friend Liú Zhīlín petitioned the Crown Prince, saying:
"Zhīlín has heard
that if Yí and Shú, and Liǔ Huì,
had not encountered one word from Zhòngní,
then the starving man of Xīshān,
and the dismissed scholar of Dōngguó,
how could their names have spread to later generations?
Indeed!
One born with a seven-foot stature
eventually becomes earth for a single coffin.
The matter of immortality
is entrusted to epitaphs.
One who possesses pearls and embraces jade,
yet whose name is not proclaimed until death,
is truly worthy of a long sigh,
and who surpasses this?
I secretly grieve for my friend Liú Xiǎn of Pèiguó,
who treasured literary arts,
diligently researched profound subjects,
was exceptionally intelligent,
and stood out from the crowd.
Having died in Yǐngdū,
his soul returns to the capital.
The day for selecting his tomb site is set,
and a tombstone must be carved.
Zhīlín has already briefly compiled his deeds and actions,
and now humbly presents them.
I earnestly wish for Your Benevolent Grace
to bestow your sagely prose,
to bring glory to his dry bones,
and comfort his departed soul.
Presumptuously bringing this to your esteemed ears,
I tremble beyond measure."
The Crown Prince then granted a memorial inscription which read:
"Fánruò drew forth its essence,
Kōngsāng gave forth its sound.
Their distinct qualities were prized,
their music and renown spread.
Who could compare to him?
A handsome and eminent scholar.
His rites were established in youth,
his achievements shone in maturity.
He fully absorbed the classics and histories,
diligently studied profound principles.
He never forgot what he saw once,
remembering it after a single glance.
Like consulting Jiǎ Kuí,
or asking Bóshǐ.
His talent emerged like an awl through a sack,
his learning complete, he entered officialdom.
Having assisted in judging cases,
he then grasped the fragrant orchid.
He struggled in the Phoenix Pond,
he gave way to others at the Imperial Academy.
He participated in inner court affairs,
and assisted regional lords externally.
The slanting light has already departed,
it sinks into the western flow;
all rivers reach the sea,
then return to follow the eastern current.
The bustling soul returns,
the drifting boat is empty.
White horses face the suburbs,
red streamers turn away from Gǒng.
Dust of the wilds rises and falls,
mountain clouds are light and heavy.
Lǚ covers the book mound,
Yáng returns to the dark tomb.
Heed their example,
the road ends at the earthen mound.
Tender vines are just spreading,
clustered branches daily entwine.
Willows sprout in spring,
birds shiver and gather their down.
The vast sky is always dark,
a cold spring uniquely bubbles forth.
He is buried beside his old tomb,
his fragrance endures and follows. "

Chí,
Zhēn.
Zhēn became famous early.
Liú Zhīlín, courtesy name Sīzhēn,
was a native of Nièyáng, Nányáng.
His father, Qiú,
was the Guózǐ Bóshì of Qí,
posthumously honored as Wénfàn Xiānshēng.
