Xiāo Jǐ
zi Déxuán, was the son of Qí Qǔjiāng Gōng Yáoxīn.
At the age of ten,
he was able to compose literature.
He was orphaned early,
and had nine younger brothers,
all of whom were young children.
Jǐ's profound affection and harmony
were known throughout the court and the countryside.
He was of a gentle and mild nature,
without contention with others,
and was pure, poor, and self-reliant.
He loved learning
and was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts.
Yáng Gōngzé, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu,
was a former subordinate of Qǔjiāng.
Whenever he saw Jǐ,
he would say to others:
"This son of Kāng Gōng
can be said to be Huán Língbǎo reborn."
〔一二〕When Gōngzé died,
Jǐ wrote an elegy for him.
He was then fifteen years old.
Shěn Yuē saw it and was amazed,
saying to his uncle Cài Zǔn:
"Yesterday I saw the elegy for Yáng Píngnán by your excellent nephew.
It is no less than the works of Xīyì,
and it verifies the blessings of Kāng Gōng's accumulated virtues."
He began his career as a Zuǒ Láng in the Bureau of Authorship,
then became Lúlíng Wáng Wénxué,
Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and was in charge of records.
He was promoted to Shùzǐ,
Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng.
In his later years,
he devoted himself exclusively to Buddhism.
He served as the Administrator of Xīn'ān,
a commandery abundant in mountains and waters,
which was particularly to his liking.
He traveled according to his nature,
and thus wrote an account of it.
He died in office.
His son Wéi,
zi Yuánzhuān,
〔一三〕also had literary talent.
He rose to the positions of Tàizǐ Shèrén
and Yǒngkāng Lìng.
The court historian remarked: "The likes of Wáng Guī
all achieved fame and reputation.
Having met with favorable times,
their talents and abilities were each displayed,
which is excellent.
Xiāo Qià's compositions at Dāngtú
showed him to be a magnificent wordsmith.
Liú Xiàoyí and his brothers
all became prominent through their writings.
Gentlemen know that the Liáng dynasty had indeed produced talented individuals."
Textual Notes
Biographies 36: Zāng Dùn (younger brother Jué), Fù Qí
Zāng Dùn,
zi Xuānqīng, was a native of Jǔ, Dōngguǎn.
His great-grandfather Táo was
Sòng Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
His grandfather Tánzhī was
Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū.
His father Wèizhēn
was widely read in literature and history,
and possessed talent and ability. In his youth, he was recognized by his maternal cousin Zhōu Yǒng of Rúnán.
At the end of the Sòng dynasty,
he began his career as a Lǐngjūn Zhǔbù.
The person he served was
Qí Wǔdì.
Upon entering Qí,
he successively held the positions of Tàiwèi Jìjiǔ,
Shàngshū Zhǔkè Láng,
Jìshì for the two princely establishments of Jiàn'ān and Lúlíng,
Qiánjūn Gōngcáo Shǐ,
Tōngzhí Láng,
Zhōngzhèng of Nánxúzhōu,
and Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng.
When Gāozǔ pacified Jīngyì
and established his hegemon's residence,
Dùn was appointed Piàojì Xíngyù Cānjūn.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he was appointed Hòujūn Zīyì Zhōngláng and Nánxúzhōu Biéjià.
He entered the court as Huángmén Láng
and was promoted to Yòujūn Ānchéng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ and Shǎofù Qīng.
He was then sent out as Administrator of Xīn'ān,
where he earned a reputation for competence.
Returning to court, he served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
Sīnóng Qīng,
and Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ.
He observed mourning for his birth mother,
living in a hut by her tomb for three years.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Tíngwèi Qīng.
He was sent out again as Ānchéng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ and Jiāngxià Tàishǒu,
and died in office.
Dùn, as a child, studied the Five Classics under the recluse Zhūgě Qú of Lángxié,
mastering their chapters and sentences.
Qú always had dozens or hundreds of students,
but Dùn, among them,
never formed close associations or rivalries.
Qú found him extraordinary
and exclaimed:
"This student is a great talent,
fit to be a king's advisor!"
He first served as Fǔjūn Xíng Cānjūn,
then was promoted to Shàngshū Zhōngbīng Láng.
Dùn had a handsome demeanor
and good deportment.
Whenever he presented reports,
Gāozǔ was very pleased.
He was appointed concurrently Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén,
then Ányòu Lùshì Cānjūn,
while retaining his position as Shèrén.
Dùn was filial.
While on night duty with his father at the Tíngwèi,
his mother, Lady Liú, at home,
suddenly died during the night.
His left middle finger suddenly ached,
preventing him from sleeping.
At dawn,
a messenger from home indeed reported the terrible news;
such was his spiritual connection.
Before his mourning period for his mother was over,
his father also died.
Dùn observed mourning for five years,
not leaving his hut.
His body became emaciated and withered,
so much so that his family no longer recognized him.
A local, Wáng Duān, reported his situation,
and Gāozǔ praised him,
ordering repeated exhortations to make him desist.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng,
then transferred to Zhōngshū Láng,
again concurrently Zhōngshū Shèrén,
promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng,
and served as Dōngzhōngláng Wǔlíng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ,
managing affairs for the princely establishment, prefecture, and state,
and concurrently as Huìjī Jùn Chéng.
Upon his return, he was appointed Shǎofù Qīng,
concurrently Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
and then promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Dùn was upright and resolute by nature,
and served very competently in the Censorate.
In the second month of the fifth year of Zhōngdàtōng,
Gāozǔ visited Tóngtài Temple to lecture,
and held a grand assembly for the four monastic orders.
Tens of thousands of people were present.
A trained elephant, presented by Nányuè,
suddenly went wild among the crowd.
The imperial carriage, feather guards, and all those assembled were terrified and scattered.
Only Dùn and Sǎnqí Láng Péi Zhīlǐ remained composed and fearless.
Gāozǔ greatly praised them.
Soon, an edict was issued,
adding the title of Sǎnqí Chángshì.
Before he was invested,
another edict stated:
"To command the entire six armies,
one must not appoint those without talent.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng and newly appointed Sǎnqí Chángshì Dùn
possesses loyal and careful intentions,
and is discerning and cautious in his actions.
He is fair and impartial in office
and diligent and dedicated in his duties.
He will surely be able to manage these military affairs.
He may concurrently lead the armies (Lǐngjūn),
and retain his former position as Chángshì."
In the second year of Dàtóng,
he was promoted to Zhōng Lǐngjūn.
The Lǐngjūn oversaw the critical military affairs of the empire,
and the supervisory duties were many.
Dùn was quick-witted and capable,
with strong character,
skilled at handling complex matters,
and his official duties were well managed.
In the Tiānjiān era,
Xiāo Jǐng, Marquis of Wúpíng, held this position,
and gained a good reputation.
Now, Dùn succeeded him.
Jiāng Zǐyī 少年時便喜好學習，
有志向和操守，
因為家境貧寒，缺乏供養，
於是終身素食。
起初擔任王國侍郎，
奉朝請。
他請求允許到秘閣觀閱書籍，
Gāozǔ 答應了他，
並下敕令讓他在華林省值守。
他的姑夫、右衛將軍 Zhū Yì，
權勢顯赫，在朝中擔任要職，
休沐之日，
賓客雲集，
但 Jiāng Zǐyī 從未登門拜訪，
其高潔如此。
他逐漸升遷為尚書儀曹郎，
出任 Suíchāng 和 Qū'ē 兩縣的縣令，
都留下了良好的政績。
後被授予通直散騎侍郎之職。
又出任戎昭將軍、
南津校尉。
他的弟弟 Jiāng Zǐsì，
曾任金部郎，
Dàtóng 初年，
升遷為右丞。
兄弟二人的性情都剛烈。
Jiāng Zǐsì 自右丞之位上呈奏疏，
極力陳述政事的得失，
Gāozǔ 非常讚賞他，
下詔令尚書省詳細審議並施行。
左民郎 Shěn Jiǒng 和少府丞 Gù Yú 曾上奏事情不獲批准，
Gāozǔ 厲聲呵斥他們，
Jiāng Zǐsì 於是快步上前代替 Shěn Jiǒng 等人應對，
言辭非常激切，
Gāozǔ 怒而下令將他捆綁起來，
Jiāng Zǐsì 踞地不從，
Gāozǔ 的怒氣也因此消解，
於是釋放了他，
但仍免去了他的職務。
等到 Hóu Jǐng 造反，
攻陷 Lìyáng，
從 Héngjiāng 準備渡江時，
Jiāng Zǐyī 率領舟師一千餘人，
在下游準備阻擊他，
他的副將 Dǒng Táoshēng 家在長江以北，
於是與其黨羽四散逃走。
Jiāng Zǐyī 於是退回 Nánzhōu，
重新收攏餘眾，
徒步前往京師。
叛賊也隨後而至，
Jiāng Zǐyī 稟告 Tàizōng 說：
「叛賊的包圍尚未合攏，
仍然可以出擊蕩平，
如果營壘一旦堅固，
就無處施展武力了。」
他請求與他的弟弟 Jiāng Zǐsì、Jiāng Zǐwǔ 率領所屬的一百餘人，
打開 Chéngmíngmén 門去挑戰叛賊。
Tàizōng 答應了。
Jiāng Zǐyī 於是身先士卒，
拔出長戈獨自前進，
眾叛賊從兩側夾攻他，
跟隨的人沒有一個敢於繼上，
Jiāng Zǐsì、Jiāng Zǐwǔ 見事態危急，
互相拉著奔向叛賊，
都遇害了。
詔書說：
「故戎昭將軍、通直散騎侍郎、南津校尉 Jiāng Zǐyī，
前尚書右丞 Jiāng Zǐsì，
東宮直殿主帥 Jiāng Zǐwǔ，
他們的禍事和犧牲已經聽聞，
實在令人憐憫和悲傷，
為國犧牲的待遇應當加等，
這也是舊有的規章。
可追贈 Jiāng Zǐyī 為給事黃門侍郎，
Jiāng Zǐsì 為中書侍郎，
Jiāng Zǐwǔ 為散騎侍郎。」
Hóu Jǐng 平定後，
Shìzǔ 又追贈 Jiāng Zǐyī 為侍中，
諡號 Yìzǐ；
Jiāng Zǐsì 為黃門侍郎，
諡號 Yìzǐ；
Jiāng Zǐwǔ 為中書侍郎，
諡號 Lièzǐ。
Jiāng Zǐyī 續寫了《黃圖》以及 Bān Gù 的
「九品」之說，
並有辭賦文章數十篇，
流傳於世。
Zhāng Shèng 字 Sīshān，
是鎮北將軍 Zhāng Jì 的兒子。
他少年時方正雅致，
有志向和操守，
善於清言。
他的父親在 Qīngzhōu 任職時，
被當地百姓所殺害，
Zhāng Shèng 感於家禍，
終身素食布衣，
手不持刀刃。
被州府舉為秀才。
起初擔任秘書郎，
歷任太子舍人，
洗馬，
司徒左西掾，
中書郎。
出任永陽內史，
回京後被授予中軍宣城王司馬、散騎常侍之職。
又出任鎮南湘東王長史、尋陽太守。
Zhōngdàtóng 元年，
被徵召為太府卿，
不久升遷為吳興太守。
Tàiqīng 二年，
Hóu Jǐng 圍攻京城，
Zhāng Shèng 派遣弟弟 Zhāng Yī 率領郡兵數千人前往救援。
Tàiqīng 三年，
宮城陷落，
御史中丞 Shěn Jùn 避難東歸，
Zhāng Shèng 前往拜訪並對他說：
「叛賊猖獗，
國家危亡受辱，
正是我等臣子效命之時。
如今我想收集兵力，
據守在貴鄉。
如果天道無靈，
忠義之節無法伸展，
即使因此而死，
也實在沒有遺憾。」
Shěn Jùn 說：
「鄙郡雖小，
仗義抗逆，
誰敢不從呢！」
於是堅決勸 Zhāng Shèng 舉義。
於是 Zhāng Shèng 收集士卒，
修繕城壘。
當時 Shàolíng Wáng 東逃至 Qiántáng，
聞訊後，
派遣檄文授予 Zhāng Shèng 征東將軍之職，
加秩中二千石。
Zhāng Shèng 說：
「朝廷危急，
天子蒙難，
今日我怎能有心情，
再接受榮耀的封號呢！」
於是留下了檄文。
叛賊的行臺 Liú Shénmào 攻破 Yìxīng，
派遣使者勸說 Zhāng Shèng 說：
「如果早日投降歸附，
當仍以郡守之職安置你，
並再加爵賞。」
Zhāng Shèng 命人斬殺其使者，
隨後派遣軍主 Wáng Xióng 等人率兵在 Lí Dú 迎擊他們，
擊敗了 Liú Shénmào，
Liú Shénmào 敗退。
Hóu Jǐng 聽聞 Liú Shénmào 戰敗，
於是派遣他的中軍 Hóu Zǐjiàn 率領精兵兩萬人，
協助 Liú Shénmào 攻打 Zhāng Shèng，
Zhāng Shèng 派遣軍主 Fàn Zhìlǎng 出郡西迎戰，
被 Liú Shénmào 所敗，
退回郡中。
叛賊騎兵乘勝焚燒柵欄，
柵內眾軍士氣渙散。
Zhāng Shèng 於是脫下戎服，
坐在聽事廳中，
叛賊持刀逼近他，
他始終不屈服，
於是將 Zhāng Shèng 逮捕並送給 Hóu Jǐng，
Hóu Jǐng 在都市中將他處刑，
他的子弟一同遇害者有十餘人，
當時他六十二歲。
叛賊平定後，
Shìzǔ 追贈他為侍中、中衛將軍、開府儀同三司。
諡號為 Zhōngzhēnzǐ。
Shěn Jùn 字 Shūyuán，
是吳興武康人。
他的祖父 Shěn Xiàn，
是齊國的散騎常侍，
在《齊史》中有傳。
It happened that Gāozǔ wished to see the eldest sons of the various kings.
Shìzǔ sent Fāngděng and others to attend.
Fāngděng joyfully boarded the boat,
hoping to avoid sorrow and humiliation.
When they reached the Yáoshuǐ River,
they encountered Hóu Jǐng's rebellion.
Shìzǔ summoned them back.
Fāngděng reported,
"In ancient times, Shēn Shēng did not begrudge his death;
how could Fāngděng cling to his life?"
Shìzǔ read the letter with a sigh,
knowing there was no intention of returning.
So he allotted ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
and sent them to aid the capital.
Whenever the rebels attacked,
Fāngděng would invariably expose himself to arrows and stones.
When the palace city fell,
Fāngděng returned to Jīngzhōu,
gathered soldiers and horses,
and greatly earned the people's support.
Shìzǔ then began to praise his ability.
Fāngděng also advised building and repairing city walls and stockades,
to guard against unforeseen events.
Once completed,
watchtowers were visible to one another,
extending over seventy *lǐ* in circumference.
Shìzǔ viewed them with great pleasure,
and entered to tell Xú Fēi:
"If I had another son like this,
what more would I have to worry about?"
Xú Fēi did not reply,
but withdrew weeping.
Shìzǔ was enraged by this,
and therefore exposed her disgraceful conduct,
posting it on the grand pavilion.
When Fāngděng entered and saw it,
he felt even more imperiled.
At that time, the King of Hédōng was the *cìshǐ* of Xiāngzhōu,
and would not obey the orders of the *dūfǔ*.
Fāngděng then requested to go and conquer him.
Shìzǔ granted it,
appointing him *dūdū*,
and ordered him to lead twenty thousand elite troops on a southern expedition.
Before Fāngděng departed,
he said to his close associates:
"In this expedition of mine,
I am certainly destined to die;
if I die in a worthy cause,
why should I cling to life?"
When they reached Máxī,
the King of Hédōng led his army to meet them in battle.
Fāngděng attacked him,
his army was defeated,
and he drowned.
He was twenty-two years old at the time.
When Shìzǔ heard of it,
he did not grieve.
Later, reflecting on his talent,
he posthumously granted him the titles of *shìzhōng*, *zhōngjūn jiāngjūn*, and *Yángzhōu cìshǐ*.
His posthumous name was Zhōngzhuàng Shìzǐ.
And a ritual to summon his soul was performed to mourn him.
Fāngděng had annotated Fàn Yè's *Hòuhànshū*,
but did not complete it.
His compiled *Sānshíguó Chūnqiū* and *Jìngzhùzǐ*
circulated in the world.
Zhēnhuì Shìzǐ Fāngzhū, courtesy name Zhìxiāng,
was Shìzǔ's second son.
His mother was Lady Wáng.
As a child, he was intelligent, alert, and widely learned,
understanding Lǎo and Yì,
and skilled in abstruse discussions.
His demeanor was clear and outstanding,
and his arguments were sharp and incisive.
He was especially beloved by Shìzǔ,
and his mother, Lady Wáng, was also favored.
When Fāngděng was defeated and died,
Shìzǔ said to him:
"Unless something is removed,
how can something else rise?"
He then appointed him *zhōngfǔjūn* to serve as his deputy,
and also sent him out as *Yǐngzhōu cìshǐ*,
to garrison Jiāngxià,
with Bào Quán as the acting official,
to defend against the lower reaches.
At that time, Shìzǔ had sent Xú Wénshèng to supervise the various armies,
who was in a stalemate with Hóu Jǐng's general Rèn Yuē.
Fāngzhū, relying on Wénshèng being nearby,
did not attend to military affairs,
but spent his days with Bào Quán in drinking and gambling.
Hóu Jǐng, knowing this,
then dispatched his general Sòng Zǐxiān to lead several hundred light cavalry,
to attack him by a secret path.
It happened to be dark and stormy.
When Zǐxiān arrived,
the common people ran to report,
but Fāngzhū and Bào Quán still did not believe it,
saying:
"Xú Wénshèng's large army is downstream,
how could the barbarians come?"
He only then ordered the gates closed,
but the rebel cavalry had already entered.
The city thus fell,
and Zǐxiān captured Fāngzhū and returned.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn's army reached Càizhōu,
Jǐng then killed him.
Shìzǔ posthumously granted him the titles of *shìzhōng* and *dàjiāngjūn*.
His posthumous name was Zhēnhuì Shìzǐ.
The imperial historian comments: Among the sons of Tàizōng and Shìzǔ,
although they expanded their territories,
their era belonged to a time of chaos and upheaval.
Being captured by bandits,
many died unnatural deaths.
Alas!
It is lamentable.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Volume 39: Wáng Sēngbiàn
Wáng Sēngbiàn, courtesy name Jūncái,
was the son of Right Guard General Shénniàn.
He came to surrender with his father during the Tiānjiān era.
He began his career as Left Attendant of the King of Xiāngdōng's state.
When the king served as Administrator of Dānyáng,
he was transferred to be a Staff Officer in the administration.
When the king went out to govern Kuàijī,
he also served as Middle Military Staff Officer.
When the king served in Jīngzhōu,
he was still appointed Middle Military,
within the specified term.
At that time, Wǔníng Commandery rebelled.
The king ordered Sēngbiàn to suppress and pacify it.
He was promoted to Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Wǔníng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Guǎngpíng.
When his term expired,
he returned to serve as Registrar in the king's administration,
and Staff Officer as before.
When the king was summoned to be Protector-General,
Sēngbiàn also served as Chief Clerk of the administration.
When the king served in Jiāngzhōu,
he was still appointed Yúnqí Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ,
and garrisoned Péngchéng.
Soon after, he supervised Ānlù Commandery,
but returned not long after.
Soon he became Grand Administrator of Xīncài,
still holding the title of Sīmǎ,
and retaining his generalship as before.
When the king was appointed to Jīngzhōu,
he became Consulting Staff Officer in the Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn's administration,
granted a stipend for a thousand people,
and replaced Liǔ Zhònglǐ as Grand Administrator of Jìnglín,
his title changed to Xióngxìn Jiāngjūn.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
the king ordered Sēngbiàn to temporarily hold the *jié*,
and fully supervise a naval force of ten thousand,
also carrying provisions to go to aid.
He had just reached the capital,
when the palace city was overrun,
and the Son of Heaven was in distress.
Sēngbiàn, together with Liǔ Zhònglǐ and his brothers, and Zhào Bóhào and others,
first submitted to Jǐng,
and then entered the court.
Jǐng confiscated all their military supplies,
but treated them with great kindness and appeasement.
Not long after,
he sent Sēngbiàn back to Jìnglín.
Thereupon, traveling twice the usual speed,
he went west to join Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ, acting on imperial authority,
appointed Sēngbiàn as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Jīng and Xiāng were suspected of wavering,
and the army commander suffered a defeat,
Shìzǔ again ordered Sēngbiàn and Bào Quán to lead troops to suppress them.
He allocated soldiers and provisions
and set a date for them to depart.
At that time, Sēngbiàn's subordinates from Jìnglíng had not all arrived yet,
and he wished to wait for them to gather
before setting out.
He said to Bào Quán,
"You and I have both been commanded to campaign in the south,
but if the army's morale is like this,
what do you plan to do?"
Quán replied,
"Since we have received the imperial strategy
and are leading valiant and strong men,
this task is like melting snow with hot water;
why worry so much?"
Sēngbiàn said,
"That is not so.
What you say
is merely the usual talk of a literati.
Hédōng has few military talents,
but their weapons are strong,
preserving their strength to await the enemy.
Unless we have ten thousand elite soldiers,
it will not be enough to control them.
My Jìnglíng armored soldiers
have experienced many battles;
I have already sent for them,
and they should arrive soon.
Although there is a deadline,
it can still be reiterated.
I wish to go with you to speak of this to the emperor,
hoping for your assistance."
Quán replied,
"The success or failure of this undertaking
depends on this expedition.
As for the propriety of delay or speed,
we must ultimately obey the emperor."
Shìzǔ was by nature severe and suspicious.
When he vaguely heard their words,
he thought they were procrastinating and unwilling to go,
and gradually became angry.
When Sēngbiàn was about to enter,
he said to Quán,
"I will speak first,
you can act as my subordinate."
Quán again assented.
When they met Shìzǔ,
Shìzǔ greeted them and asked,
"Are you ready?
What day will you depart?"
Sēngbiàn answered fully as he had just said.
Shìzǔ was furious,
clutched his sword, and sternly said,
"Are you afraid to go?!"
Then he rose and went inside.
Quán was terrified and turned pale,
not daring to speak at all.
A moment later,
he sent dozens of attendants to arrest Sēngbiàn.
When Sēngbiàn arrived,
Shìzǔ said,
"You defy orders and refuse to go,
this is to conspire with the rebels.
Now there is only death."
Sēngbiàn replied,
"As Sēngbiàn has long enjoyed official emoluments,
my worry and responsibility are truly heavy.
To face execution today,
how could I harbor resentment?
I only regret not seeing my elderly mother."
Shìzǔ then struck him,
hitting his left thigh,
and blood flowed to the ground.
Sēngbiàn fainted,
and only revived after a long time.
He was immediately sent to the Grand Judge,
and his sons and nephews were also arrested
and all imprisoned.
At that time, the army of Yuèyáng Wáng attacked Jiānglíng.
The people were agitated,
and the defense preparations were uncertain.
Shìzǔ sent his attendants to the prison
to ask Sēngbiàn for advice.
Sēngbiàn fully articulated his strategy,
and was immediately pardoned and made Governor of the Inner City.
Soon after, Yuèyáng retreated in defeat.
Bào Quán was unable to overcome Chángshā,
so Shìzǔ ordered Sēngbiàn to replace him.
He enumerated Bào Quán's ten crimes,
and sent the palace attendant Luó Chónghuān to lead three hundred imperial guards
to depart with Sēngbiàn.
Upon arrival,
they sent a message to Quán saying,
"Palace attendant Luó has been ordered
to bring Wáng Jìnglíng."
Quán was greatly astonished,
and looked to his左右 (attendants) saying,
"If I can have Wáng Jìnglíng assist me in planning,
the rebels will not be difficult to pacify."
Soon after, Chónghuān entered first with the imperial decree,
and Sēngbiàn followed with the imperial guards.
Quán was just dusting his mat,
sitting and waiting for them.
When Sēngbiàn entered,
he sat with his back to Quán
and said,
"Lord Bào,
you are guilty.
The imperial decree orders me to arrest you;
do not treat this as a personal matter."
Then he told Chónghuān to read out the decree.
Quán immediately descended to the ground
and was arrested by the side of the couch.
Sēngbiàn then organized the generals and commanders,
and concentrated their efforts on the siege,
and thus pacified the land of Xiāng.
This month,
Qí (齊) general Guō Yuánjiàn (郭元建) attacked Qínzhōu (秦州) Inspector Yán Chāoyuǎn (嚴超遠) at Qínjùn (秦郡).
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) ordered Cè (崱) to go to his aid.
Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) also came from Ōuyáng (歐陽) to join them.
They fought a great battle with Yuánjiàn (元建) at Shìlín (士林).
Bàxiān (霸先) ordered his strong crossbowmen to shoot,
and Yuánjiàn's (元建) forces retreated.
Cè (崱) then unleashed his troops to attack,
and thoroughly defeated them.
Over ten thousand heads were severed,
and more than a thousand men were captured alive.
Yuánjiàn (元建) gathered his remaining forces and fled.
At this time, Shìzǔ (世祖) captured Wáng Lín (王琳) in Jiānglíng (江陵).
His chief clerk, Lù Nà (陸納) and others, then rebelled in Chángshā (長沙).
Shìzǔ (世祖) summoned Cè (崱) and Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) to suppress them.
In the second year of Chéngshèng (承聖) era,
they engaged Nà (納) and his forces in battle at Chēlún (車輪),
suffering a great defeat.
Two of their strongholds were captured.
Nà (納) and his forces fled to hold Chángshā (長沙),
and Cè (崱) and others besieged them.
Later, Nà (納) and his forces surrendered.
Cè (崱) then joined Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) in a western expedition against Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王) at Xiákǒu (硤口).
Upon arrival, they immediately defeated and pacified him.
Thereupon, he returned to his garrison,
contracted an illness, and died.
An imperial edict stated:
"Cè (崱),
a scion of an old Jīngzhào (京兆) family,
a descendant of Yuánkǎi (元凱),
whose family traditions include scholarship
and generations of loyalty and integrity.
Since his transfer to the river islets,
his governance was known for integrity and competence.
Promoted from humble beginnings,
he was truly known for his clear and quiet administration.
His sudden demise
fills Our heart with sorrow.
He is to be posthumously granted the title of Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn, 車騎將軍),
and given an additional musical ensemble.
His posthumous name shall be Wǔ (武)."
Cè (崱) had nine brothers.
His elder brothers Sōng (嵩), Cén (岑), (巘), Jí (岌), Ní (嶷), Yǎn (巘), Àn (岸), and younger brother Yòu'ān (幼安),
were all famous in their time.
Àn's (岸) courtesy name was Gōnghéng (公衡).
From a young age, he possessed military talent
and was fond of strategies of alliance and conflict.
During the Tàiqīng (太清) era,
he and Cè (崱) together pledged allegiance to Shìzǔ (世祖).
Shìzǔ (世祖) appointed him with the staff of authority (chíjié, 持節), General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn, 平北將軍), and Inspector of Běiliángzhōu (北梁州),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Jiānglíng (江陵) County,
with a thousand households.
Àn (岸) then requested to take Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and Shìzǔ (世祖) granted his request.
Àn (岸) then marched day and night,
first going to attack its city,
but failed.
When Yuèyáng (岳陽) arrived,
he fled to his elder brother Yǎn (巘) in Nányáng (南陽).
Yǎn (巘) was at that time the Administrator of Nányáng (南陽).
Yuèyáng (岳陽) soon dispatched forces to attack and capture their city.
Àn (岸) and Yǎn (巘) were both killed.
Yòu'ān (幼安) was by nature extremely filial,
generous,
heroic and brave beyond others.
During the Tàiqīng (太清) era,
he and his elder brother Cè (崱) together pledged allegiance to Shìzǔ (世祖).
Shìzǔ (世祖) appointed him General of Cloud-like Cavalry (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, 雲麾將軍) and Inspector of Xījīngzhōu (西荊州),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Huáróng (華容) County,
with a thousand households.
He was ordered to join General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn, 平南將軍) Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) in attacking Hédōng Wáng Yù (河東王譽) at Chángshā (長沙),
and pacified him.
He was also ordered to lead ten thousand elite armored troops
to assist Left Guardian General (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, 左衞將軍) Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛) in an eastern expedition against Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
Upon reaching Bèijī (貝磯),
they encountered Jǐng's (景) general Rèn Yuē (任約) who came to oppose them.
They then fought,
and utterly defeated him,
beheading his Equal in Rank (yítóng, 儀同) Chìluó Zǐtōng (叱羅子通), Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (湘州) Zhào Wēifāng (趙威方), and others,
and sending their heads to Jiānglíng (江陵).
They then advanced their army to Dàjǔkǒu (大舉口),
where they stood in confrontation with Jǐng (景).
He separately attacked Wǔchāng (武昌),
and captured it.
Jǐng (景) crossed the upper stream of Lúzhōu (蘆洲) to press Wénshèng (文盛) and others.
Yòu'ān (幼安) and the various armies attacked him.
Jǐng (景) was greatly defeated,
and all his boats and ships were captured.
It happened that Jǐng (景) secretly sent forces to raid and capture Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
taking Inspector Fāng Zhū (方諸) and others captive back with them.
People were greatly alarmed.
Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛) fled back from Hànkǒu (漢口).
The various armies were greatly defeated,
and Yòu'ān (幼安) then surrendered to Jǐng (景).
Jǐng (景) killed him,
because of his frequent reversals.
Kān (龕) was
the son of Cén (岑), Cè's (崱) second elder brother.
From a young age, he was brave and skilled in warfare.
Also during the Tàiqīng (太清) era, he and his paternal uncles together pledged allegiance to Shìzǔ (世祖).
Shìzǔ (世祖) appointed him with the staff of authority (chíjié, 持節), Loyal and Martial General (Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn, 忠武將軍), and Inspector of Yúnzhōu (鄖州),
Marquis of Zhōnglú (中廬) County,
with a thousand households.
He and his uncle Yòu'ān (幼安) together followed Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) to attack Hédōng Wáng (河東王),
and pacified him.
He then followed Sēngbiàn (僧辯) downstream,
and, following Xú Wénshèng's (徐文盛) army, arrived at Bālíng (巴陵).
Hearing that Hóu Jǐng (侯景) had raided and captured Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
and was moving west and about to arrive,
he and Sēngbiàn (僧辯) and others held Bālíng (巴陵) to await him.
When Jǐng (景) arrived,
he besieged it for several tens of days,
but failed to take it and fled.

He was promoted to Minister of the Grand Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng, 太府卿), General Who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn, 安北將軍), Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Dìngzhōu (Dū Dìngzhōu Zhūjūnshì, 督定州諸軍事), and Inspector of Dìngzhōu (定州),
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant in Ordinary Service (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, 通直散騎常侍),
with an increase of five hundred households.
He then followed Sēngbiàn (僧辯) in pursuit of Jǐng (景) to Jiāngxià (江夏),
and besieged its city.
Jǐng's (景) general Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) abandoned the city and fled.
Kān (龕) pursued him to Yángpǔ (楊浦),
and captured him alive.
In the third year of Dàbǎo (大寶) era,
the allied armies reached Gūshú (姑孰).
Jǐng's (景) general Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒) met them in battle.
Kān (龕) and Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先), Wáng Lín (王琳), and others led the elite troops to attack him,
and greatly defeated Zǐjiàn (子鑒).
They then reached Shítou (石頭).
Jǐng (景) personally led his faction to join battle.
Kān (龕) and the allied armies fought bravely,
and utterly defeated Jǐng (景).
Jǐng (景) then fled eastward.
His merits were considered the greatest,
and he was appointed General Who Pacifies the East (Píngdōng Jiāngjūn, 平東將軍) and Inspector of Dōngyángzhōu (東揚州),
with an additional enfeoffment of a thousand households.
In the second year of Chéngshèng (承聖) era,
he again joined Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) in suppressing Lù Nà (陸納) and others at Chángshā (長沙),
and they surrendered.
He was also summoned to suppress Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王) at Xīlíng (西陵),
and also pacified him.
Later, Jiānglíng (江陵) fell.
Qí (齊) appointed Zhēnyáng Hóu (貞陽侯) as successor to the Liáng (梁) lineage,
and appointed Kān (龕) as Inspector of Zhènzhōu (震州) and Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).

He was also appointed General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, 鎮南將軍), Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Nányùzhōu (Dū Nányùzhōu Zhūjūnshì, 都督南豫州諸軍事), Inspector of Nányùzhōu (南豫州), and Marquis of Lìyáng (溧陽) County,
and granted a musical ensemble;
he was also given the additional titles of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì, 散騎常侍) and Grand General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn, 鎮東大將軍).
It happened that Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) raided and captured the capital,
arresting Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) and killing him.
Kān (龕) was Sēngbiàn's (僧辯) son-in-law.
As Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興),
because Bàxiān (霸先) was not of noble birth,
and his troops were disorderly,
during the days he served in the military administration,
he never took Bàxiān (霸先) seriously.
And when he became the Administrator of his own commandery,
he always used the law to discipline Bàxiān's (霸先) clan,
showing no leniency.
Bàxiān (霸先) resented him deeply.
When Sēngbiàn (僧辯) was defeated,
Kān (龕) then held Wúxīng (吳興) to resist him.
He sent his military deputy Dù Tài (杜泰) to attack Chén Qiàn (陳蒨) at Chángchéng (長城),
but was in turn defeated by Qiàn (蒨).
Bàxiān (霸先) then sent general Zhōu Wényù (周文育) to attack Kān (龕).
Kān (龕) ordered his cousin Běisǒu (北叟) to go out and resist,
but he was again defeated by Wényù (文育).
He fled to Yìxīng (義興).
Bàxiān (霸先) personally led his forces to besiege him.
It happened that Qí (齊) general Liǔ Dámó (柳達摩) and others raided the capital.
Bàxiān (霸先) was afraid,
and so returned and made peace with the Qí (齊) people.
When Kān (龕) heard that the Qí (齊) army had returned,
he surrendered,
and was then killed.
Yīn Zǐchūn (陰子春), courtesy name Yòuwén (幼文),
was a native of Gūzāng (姑臧) in Wǔwēi (武威).
At the end of the Jìn (晉) Yìxī (義熙) era,
his great-grandfather Xí (襲),
followed Sòng Gāozǔ (宋高祖) in his southward migration,
and settled in Nánpíng (南平).
His father, Zhìbó (智伯),
was a neighbor of Gāozǔ (高祖)
and they were good friends in their youth.
He once entered Gāozǔ's (高祖) bedchamber
and saw a wondrous five-colored light.
He then grasped Gāozǔ's (高祖) hand and said:
"You will surely achieve great nobility later;
you will not be a mere subject.
The world is in turmoil,
and those who will bring peace to the common people,
will it be you?"
Gāozǔ (高祖) said:
"Fortunately, do not speak too much."
Thereupon, their friendship grew closer,
and whenever Gāozǔ (高祖) had needs,
it was as if he was visiting an external treasury.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he held office as Inspector of Liáng (梁) and Qín (秦) Prefectures.
Zǐchūn,
in the early Tiānjiān reign,
started his career as Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn,
and Xīyáng Tàishǒu.
In the Puǒtōng reign,
he was successively promoted to Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Nánliángzhōu Cìshǐ;
then again promoted to Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Liáng Qín Huá Sānzhōu Zhūjūnjì, and Liáng Qín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he suppressed the rebellious Man in Xiá zhōng,
and pacified them.
He was summoned to be Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and later promoted to Shìzhōng.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Shìzǔ ordered Zǐchūn to accompany Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēngbiàn in attacking Shàolíngwáng in Yǐngzhōu,
and pacified him.
He then, with Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Xú Wénshèng, marched east to attack Hóu Jǐng.
Upon reaching Bèijī,
they encountered Jǐng.
Zǐchūn fought bravely,
surpassing all other generals,
and repeatedly defeated Jǐng.
However, as Yǐngzhōu was captured,
the army was subsequently defeated and retreated.
In the second year of Dàbǎo,
he died in Jiānglíng.
His grandson, Hào,
was well-known in his youth.
He began his career as Fèngcháoqǐng,
and successively held the post of Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng.
Later, he entered Zhōu.
He compiled twenty juan of Qiónglín.
The court historian says: Hú Sēngyòu was renowned for his courage and competence;
he captured banners and defeated enemies numerous times.
When he sacrificed his life for his country,
dying for the king's cause,
even the loyal and valiant of ancient times
could not surpass him.
Xú Wénshèng initially established merits,
but failed to maintain his reputation until the end,
which was unrighteous.
Dù Zè understood the principles of change and adaptation,
and knew what was proper to support and what to oppose.
Furthermore, he frequently commanded armies,
repeatedly annihilated rebels and invaders.
His achievements and contributions were outstanding,
and he ultimately became a meritorious official of the restoration.
How righteous!
Collation Notes

Biography Forty-one: Xiàoxíng: Téng Tán’gōng (Xú Pǔjì, Wǎnlíng Nǚzǐ), Shěn Chóngsù, Xún Jiàng, Yǔ Qiánlóu, Jí Fēn, Zhēn Tián, Hán Huáimíng, Liú Tánjìng, Hé Jiǒng, Yǔ Shāmí, Jiāng Fú, Liú Jì, Chǔ Xiū, Xiè Lìn.
The Classic states:
"Filial piety
is the root of virtue."
This is the greatest among the people,
and what a state prioritizes!
Gāozǔ, in establishing his enterprise and founding his dynasty,
rectified himself and transformed customs.
The degenerate customs were reformed,
and the art of governance through filial piety was established.
Each time he issued decrees,
he extended distant commendations.
Yet, with harmony widespread in every household,
few sought peculiar or extraordinary reputations.
Concealed virtue became a trend,
and those who surpassed the multitude humbly took their place.
What was made manifest to sight and hearing
was indeed very little.
Now, these are compiled to record what might otherwise be lost.
Téng Tán’gōng was
a native of Nánchāng, Yùzhāng.
When he was five years old,
his mother, Yáng Shì, suffered from a fever
and longed for cold melon.
Such melons were not locally produced,
and Tán’gōng searched everywhere but could not find one.
He was filled with sorrow and grief.
Soon, he met a monk who asked him the reason.
Tán’gōng told him everything.
The monk said:
"I have two melons;
I will give you one."
Tán’gōng bowed in thanks,
then took the melon home
and offered it to his mother.
The whole household was astonished.
They searched for the monk,
but his whereabouts were unknown.
When his parents died,
Tán’gōng abstained from food and drink for ten days,
and was so overwhelmed with grief that he vomited blood,
fainting and then recovering.
In deep winter, he wore no padded clothes,
and ate only vegetables for the rest of his life.
Every anniversary of their death,
he was consumed by longing and grief,
lamenting day and night.
Outside his gate were two evergreen trees.
At times, a divine light would suddenly rise from the trees,
and soon Buddha images and attendant figures would appear,
radiant and conspicuous,
entering through the gate.
Tán’gōng's family, old and young,
all bowed in worship.
After a long while, it disappeared.
People, both lay and monastic, near and far, spread the story.
Tàishǒu Wáng Sēngqián invited Tán’gōng to be Gōngcáo,
but he firmly declined.
Wáng Jiǎn, who was then with Sēngqián in the prefecture,
referred to him as Téng Zēngzǐ.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
Lù Lián, on an imperial mission to inspect customs,
reported his deeds.
Tán’gōng had three sons,
all of whom had good conduct.
At that time, there was Xú Pǔjì,
a native of Línxiāng, Chángshā.
While mourning his parent and before burial,
a fire broke out at his neighbor's house,
and spread to his dwelling.
Pǔjì wailed and threw himself onto the coffin,
shielding it with his body from the fire.
Neighbors rushed to rescue him;
he was already unconscious from the burns,
and it took several days for him to recover.
In Wǎnlíng, Xuānchéng, there was a woman who slept in the same bed as her mother.
Her mother was attacked by a fierce tiger.
The daughter screamed and fought the tiger,
causing all its fur to fall out.
The tiger carried her for ten-some li,
then finally abandoned her.
The daughter carried her mother back;
she still had breath,
but died after some time.
Tàishǒu Xiāo Chēn offered condolences;
he reported her deeds,
and an imperial edict commended her family gate.
In the seventh year,
Ānchéng Tàifēi Chén shì passed away.
Ānchéng Wáng Xiù, the *cìshǐ* of Jiāngzhōu, and Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn, the *cìshǐ* of Jīngzhōu,
both submitted memorials requesting to be relieved of their duties due to their compassionate mother.
The imperial edict did not permit it.
They returned to their original posts.
However, as the Tàifēi passed away in the capital,
there was no one to preside over the funeral rites.
The *shèrén* Zhōu Shè debated, saying:
"Hè Yànxiān said, 'A son of a compassionate mother does not observe mourning for the compassionate mother's relatives.
A wife does not follow her husband to mourn for her compassionate mother-in-law.
This is because the *xiǎogōng* mourning attire has no precedent to follow.'
Yǔ Wèizhī said, 'Not only does a son not follow his mother to mourn her relatives,
a grandson also does not follow his father to mourn his compassionate mother.'
it is clear that there is no mourning attire for a compassionate grandmother.
Reflecting on the sorrow within the family,
it cannot be treated as ordinary.
According to the auspicious rites of a father,
all sons receive condolences.
Now, for the sons of the two princes,
on the day of assuming mourning attire,
they should wear plain clothes for one day
From this,
An imperial decree said:
"Since the two princes are far away,
their sons should preside over the sacrificial rites."
"The *Lǐ* says, 'A white hat and black sash are the crown of the sons and grandsons.'
Thus, the attire of the heir apparent should be different from the usual.
He may wear fine cloth clothing,
with a silk collar and sash,
and not listen to music for three years.
Furthermore, the *Lǐ* and *Chūnqiū* state
that a *shùmǔ* is not offered sacrifices for generations,
which probably refers to those without royal decree.
Since Wú Tàifēi was appointed by imperial decree,
and the rites of Ānchéng were used,
then she should be enshrined in the ancestral temple.
The destruction of the shrine should only occur when the kinship of five generations ends.
Although Chén Tàifēi's mandate was equally significant,
since the compassionate grandsons do not observe mourning,
there is no reason for her to be worshipped in the ancestral temple for generations.
The son performs the sacrifice, and the grandson stops it.
This conforms to the classical texts."
Gāozǔ thereupon ordered the ritual officials to deliberate on the mourning attire for the emperor's compassionate mother.
Yún debated:
"According to the five grades of mourning attire system of the Sòng dynasty,
an imperial prince observes mourning for his nursemaid.
According to the rites, a *shùmǔ* who has been compassionate to oneself
should observe the *xiǎogōng* mourning system.
According to the *Zēngzǐ Wèn*,
Zǐyóu said, 'To mourn a compassionate mother as one's own mother,
is this according to the rites?'
In ancient times, a nobleman had a tutor outside
and a compassionate mother inside.
They were appointed by the sovereign to educate the son.
What mourning attire is there?'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says, 'This refers to the son of a sovereign.'
If the son of a sovereign does not observe mourning,
then it is understandable that the son of a king does not observe mourning.
Also, the *Sāngfú Jīng* says, 'The son of a *jūnzǐ* for a *shùmǔ* who has been compassionate to oneself.'
The commentary says, 'A son of a *jūnzǐ*
is the son of a noble person.'
Zhèng Xuán cited the *Nèizé*,
stating that the three mothers only applied to high officials and grandees.
From this,
the mourning attire for a compassionate mother
does not extend upwards to the five ranks of heirs
nor downwards to the sons of the three types of officials.
If those who observe mourning are limited to high officials and grandees,
then considering that the sons of feudal lords do not even have this mourning,
how much more so should it be applied to imperial princes?
I suggest that according to the rites, this should be abolished
to correct the confusion of previous generations."
Gāozǔ thought otherwise.
He said:
"The *Lǐ* mentions 'compassionate mother'
in three categories: Firstly, a concubine's son who has no mother
is raised by a concubine who has no son.
They are designated mother and son,
and observe three years of mourning.
This is what the *Sāngfú Qīcuī* chapter refers to as 'a compassionate mother as one's own mother.'
is raised by a concubine.
She provides compassionate and utmost care.
Although the love is equal,
for the son of a principal wife,
the concubine has no claim to be a mother.
However, due to deep affection and significant service,
*xiǎogōng* mourning is observed.
The *Sāngfú Xiǎogōng* chapter does not directly state 'compassionate mother'
but says 'a *shùmǔ* who has been compassionate to oneself,'
clearly distinguishing it from the three-year compassionate mother.
The third is when the son is not motherless,
but a person of lower status is chosen to look after him,
equivalent to a teacher or guardian,
yet not without compassion.
Hence, she is also called a 'compassionate mother.'
Since a teacher or guardian has no mourning attire,
then this compassionate mother also has no mourning attire.
one is chosen to be the son's teacher;
the next is the compassionate mother;
the next is the nursemaid.'
This is a clear statement.
This statement about choosing 'various mothers'
means choosing persons to be these three mothers,
not choosing the mothers of one's brothers.
How do we know this?
If she were a brother's mother who already had a son,
then she would be a senior concubine.
The rites for a senior concubine
indeed have special additions.
How could a junior concubine who has given birth
then be relegated to a nursemaid?
This is not permissible.
Also, for a person with many brothers,
this might be acceptable in terms of righteousness.
But if it is a newborn son,
would all three mothers immediately be lacking?
From this,
it can be inferred that the 'various mothers' mentioned in the *Nèizé*
refer to the three mothers,
clearly not the mothers of one's brothers.
What Zǐyóu asked about
was precisely the compassionate mother who served as a teacher or guardian,
not the three-year or *xiǎogōng* compassionate mother.
Is this not proof that the compassionate mother who serves as a teacher or guardian has no mourning attire?
Zhèng Xuán did not distinguish the three types of compassionate mothers,
mixing them in his explanations,
citing the lack of mourning for one
to annotate 'compassionate to oneself.'
The errors of later generations
indeed stem from this.
The *Jīng* says 'son of a *jūnzǐ*.'
Although this originated from grandees,
it implies that if grandees are already like this,
then above this,
it should be even more so.
Thus, the commentary says, 'A son of a *jūnzǐ*
is the son of a noble person.'
The general term 'noble'
encompasses everything.
The *Jīng* and its commentary are interdependent
and illuminate each other.
Thus, the meaning of 'compassionate care'
extends to grandees and above.
The Sòng dynasty's regulation on this matter
was not contrary to the meaning of the rites.
Its abrupt abolition
is truly questionable."
Thereupon, Yún and others requested to revise and finalize according to the imperial decree: If the son of a principal wife
has his mother pass away and is raised by his father's concubine,
he shall observe five months of mourning.
This shall apply equally to both noble and humble,
and be made a permanent regulation.
Yún was successively promoted to *Wángfǔ Zīyì* and *Quánzhī Zuǒchéng Shì*,
and soon after was appointed *Shàngshū Zuǒchéng*.
He was sent out as *Shǐxīng Nèishǐ*
and died in office.
His son, Shòu,
inherited his father's profession
and was learned in the *Three Rites*.
During the Dàtóng era,
he held successive official positions as *Shàngshū Cíbù Láng*,
and was sent out as *Qǔ'ē Lìng*.
Biàn Huá, courtesy name Zhāojiū,
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Jìn Piàoqí Jiāngjūn, Zhōngzhēn Gōng Hú.
His father, Lúnzhī, was a *Gěishìzhōng*.
Huá was orphaned and poor in his youth but loved learning.
At the age of fourteen,
he was summoned and appointed a *Guózǐshēng*,
mastering the *Zhōu Yì*.
When he grew up,
he studied all five classics extensively,
and was a good friend and fellow student of Píngyuán Míng Shānbīn and Kuàijī Hè Yáng.
During the Jiànwǔ reign of Qí,
he began his career as the Administrator of the Legal Section of the Rear Army.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Principal Clerk of the General Who Conquers the Barbarians.
When Gāozǔ first came to power,
he sought out and promoted virtuous and outstanding talents,
and deeply admired his abilities.
When the Eastern Palace was established,
he was made a Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting.
At that time, the Academy of Scholars was set up in the Wéndé Diàn,
and highly talented and learned scholars were summoned to serve there as academicians,
tasked with collating and editing historical records.
An imperial edict granted Hàng full access.
At that time, Gāozǔ hosted a banquet at Huáguāng Diàn,
and ordered his officials to compose poems.
Hàng alone was instructed to compose a two-hundred-character poem,
to be completed within three kè.
Hàng composed and presented it immediately,
and its writing was exceptionally beautiful.
Soon after, as Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting, he was put in charge of the Eastern Palace's secretariat and the excellent policy documents of the Cabinet of Scattered Cavalry.
In the third year,
an imperial edict stated that officials of the Department of State Affairs who were upright and capable, or exceptionally talented, should be made Gentlemen.
Hàng was appointed Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng Cáo.
Hàng's paternal cousins, Gài and Qià,
both possessed talent and fame,
and at that time, they successively served as Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng.
The contemporary world regarded this as an honor.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor's Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Hàng was not boastful,
did not discuss the faults of others,
and was good friends with Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān and Fàn Yún of Nánxiāng.
In that year,
he was promoted to Assistant of Dānyáng Yǐn,
but due to illness, he could not perform his duties,
and was transferred to Consultative Aide to the General of the Northern Central Army.
In the fifth year,
he died in office,
at the age of thirty.
Gāozǔ deeply grieved and lamented his passing,
and issued an edict granting him twenty thousand coins
and thirty bolts of cloth.
He authored over a hundred poems and rhapsodies.
Qiū Chí, courtesy name Xīfàn,
was a native of Wúxīng Wūchéng.
His father, Língjū,
was talented and famous,
and served in Qí, reaching the office of Grand Master of the Central Court.
Chí was able to compose essays at the age of eight,
and Língjū often said that his spirit and bones resembled his own.
Xiè Chāozōng, Yellow Gate Gentleman, and Hé Diǎn, recluse, both saw him and were impressed.
When he grew up,
the prefecture appointed him as Administrator,
he was recommended as a Cultivated Talent,
and was appointed Erudite of the Imperial Academy.
He was promoted to Acting Administrator of the Grand Marshal,
but left office due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Administrator of the Western Central Army.
He was successively promoted to Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng,
but left office due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he again served as Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng,
and was promoted to Registrar Administrator of the Chariots and Cavalry.
When Gāozǔ pacified Jīngyì,
and the Duke's Residence was established,
he was brought in as Principal Clerk of the Hussar General.
He received great courtesy and respect.
The exhortations to advance King Liáng and the special rituals
were all written by Chí.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant, concurrently serving as Magistrate of Wúxīng District and Academician of the Wéndé Diàn.
At that time, Gāozǔ wrote a series of "linked pearls,"
and ordered dozens of officials to follow suit.
Chí's writing was the most beautiful.
In the third year of Tiānjiān,
he was sent out as the Administrator of Yǒngjiā,
but did not perform his duties well in the commandery
and was impeached by the relevant authorities.
Gāozǔ, loving his talent,
shelved the impeachment.
In the fourth year,
when Liánchuān Wáng Hóng, General of the Central Army, led a northern expedition,
Chí served as Consultative Aide,
and was in charge of the secretariat.
At that time, Chén Bózhī was in the north,
and came to resist with the Wèi army.
Chí persuaded him with a letter,
and Bózhī subsequently surrendered.
Upon his return, he was appointed Palace Attendant,
and was promoted to Senior Administrator to the Grand Minister of Education.
In the seventh year,
he died in office,
at the age of forty-five.
His collected poems and rhapsodies were circulated in the world.
Liú Bāo, courtesy name Xiàocháng,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His grandfather, Miǎn,
was the Minister of Works of Sòng.
His father, Xuān,
was the Prince's Attendant-in-Ordinary of Qí.
Bāo's father died when Bāo was four,
and when he was six or seven,
he often wept upon seeing his paternal uncles.
At that time, his paternal uncles Quān and Huì, among others, were all prominent and noble.
Bāo's mother thought he was afraid
and was angry with him.
Bāo replied:
"I was orphaned early and too young to understand.
I heard that my paternal uncles resembled my father greatly,
so my heart felt like weeping;
there was no other intention."
With that, he choked up and sighed,
and his mother also wept bitterly.
Initially,
Bāo's parents and two elder brothers had successively died,
and were all temporarily interred.
When Bāo was sixteen,
he began to move the burial site,
managing the reburial himself.
He did not rely on his paternal uncles,
and it was all completed within a short time.
Huì often sighed in admiration of him.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was capable of composing essays.
He began his career as Acting Administrator of the Legal Section of the Minister of Education,
but did not take the post.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
because he was the younger brother of the King of Línchuān's consort,
he was directly promoted from Principal Clerk of the General Who Conquers the Barbarians to Merit Officer of the King's Central Army.
He was successively promoted to Gentleman of the Treasury Bureau of the Department of State Affairs,
Assistant of Dānyáng Yǐn,
Assistant of the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
Gentleman of the Diànzhōng of the Department of State Affairs,
and Chief Administrator of Nánxú Prefecture.
He was dismissed due to official matters.
After a long time,
he became Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting,
in charge of the secretariat,
and lectured at Shòuguāng Diàn.
Since Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he promoted literary scholars who were junior to him.

Bāo, his paternal cousin Xiàochuò, his paternal younger brother Rú, Dào Gài of the same commandery, Gài's younger brother Qià, his paternal younger brother Hàng, Lù Chuí of Wújùn, and Zhāng Shuài were all recognized for their literary talent,
and frequently attended banquets.
Although their official advancements occurred at different times,
their rewards and gifts were not dissimilar.
In the tenth year of Tiānjiān,
he died,
at the age of thirty.
On his deathbed,
he called upon his friend Liú Zhīlìn of Nányáng to entrust him with his funeral arrangements,
emphasizing simplicity and frugality.
Bāo had a reputation for ability in office.
His character was gentle yet upright.
When interacting with people,
he would directly point out their faults,
but afterwards would praise their virtues.
He concealed nothing in his feelings,
and thus scholars and friends alike admired and lamented him.
Yuán Jùn, courtesy name Xiàogāo,
was a native of Chénjùn Yángxià,
and an eighth-generation descendant of Huàn, Superintendent of the Palace in Wèi.
Jùn was orphaned early,
and was earnestly devoted to learning.
His family was poor and had no books,
so he always borrowed them from others.
He would always transcribe them,
setting himself a daily quota of fifty sheets.
If the number of sheets was not reached,
he would not rest.
He was slow of speech,
but skilled in writing.
When the righteous army conquered Jīngyì,
Póyáng Wáng Huī garrisoned in Pògāng to the east.
Jùn followed the Prince, overseeing the secretariat.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
when the State of Póyáng was established,
Jùn was appointed Gentleman,
and followed the Prince to garrison in Jīngkǒu.
When the Prince moved to Yǐngzhōu,
Jùn concurrently served as Administrator of the Capital Affairs.
Gāozǔ was fond of rhapsodies and poems,
and at that time, those who presented literary works at the Southern Gate were numerous.
Their ornate and beautiful pieces were noteworthy,
and some were praised and promoted.
In the sixth year,
Jùn imitated Yáng Xióng's "Official Admonitions" and presented them.
Gāozǔ praised him,
and bestowed silk upon him.
He was appointed Supernumerary Palace Attendant,
and served directly in the Wéndé Academy of Scholars,
transcribing twenty volumes each of the Shǐjì and Hànshū.
He also received an imperial order to compose new stele inscriptions with Lù Chuí,
the details of which are too numerous to include.
Yǔ Yúlíng
, was the younger brother of Sànqí Chángshì Qiánlóu
. At seven, he could speak on abstruse philosophy
. When he grew up,

Jiǎn zhī fù (簡之賦) and
Zhōu Shēngyì (周升逸)'s arguments

Literature has not fallen,
there must be extraordinary talents,
and one who leads them,
if not my brother,

Every time I wish to discuss it,
there is no one to talk with,
I miss my Zǐjiàn (子建),
to deliberate and discuss together.
Discriminating between the clear and turbid,
making them like the Jīng (涇) and Wèi (渭) rivers;
discussing them like the monthly appraisals,
similar to
those of Rǔnán (汝南).
Once the red and black are decided,
and the yellow is distinguished,
it will make those who harbor rats feel ashamed,
and the unqualified feel disgraced.
It will be like Yuán Shào (袁紹),
fearing to meet Zǐjiāng (子將);
like those
who stole cattle,
remotely ashamed of Wáng Liè (王烈).
Longing for you but unable to see you,
how can my distress be?
During the Tàiqīng (太清) era,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) invaded and captured the capital.
When Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
he appointed Jiānwú (肩吾) as Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書).
At that time, the various regional governors in the upstream areas
all held their prefectures to resist Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) issued a forged imperial edict, sending Jiānwú (肩吾) to Jiāngzhōu (江州),
to persuade Dāngyáng Gōng Dàxīn (當陽公大心).
Dàxīn (大心) soon surrendered the entire prefecture to the rebels.
Jiānwú (肩吾) then fled into the territory of Jiànchāng (建昌).
After a long time,
he finally managed to reach Jiānglíng (江陵),
and died shortly thereafter.
His collected works circulated in the world.
Liú Zhāo (劉昭), courtesy name Xuānqīng (宣卿),
was a native of Gāotáng (高唐), Píngyuán (平原).
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Jìn (晉) Tàiwèi (太尉) Shí (寔).
His grandfather, Bólóng (伯龍),
was known for his filial piety during his father's mourning period.
Sòng Wǔdì (宋武帝) decreed that the Heir Apparent and all the princes should go to offer condolences.
His highest office was Shǎofù Qīng (少府卿).
His father, Biāo (彪),
was Qí (齊) Zhēnglǔ Jìn'ān Wáng (征虜晉安王)'s jìshì (記室).
Zhāo (昭) was bright and alert in his youth,
and at seven, he understood the principles of Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊).
When he grew up,
he diligently studied and was skilled at writing.
His maternal cousin, Jiāng Yān (江淹), had praised him early on.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
he began his career as Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請),
and was successively promoted to Zhēngběi Xíng Cānjūn (征北行參軍)
and Shàngshū Cāngbù Láng (尚書倉部郎),
soon thereafter appointed Wúxī Lìng (無錫令).
He successively served as Xuānhuì Yùzhāng Wáng (宣惠豫章王) and Zhōngjūn Línchuān Wáng (中軍臨川王)'s jìshì (記室).
Initially,
Zhāo (昭)'s paternal uncle, Róng (肜), compiled various Jin Histories, annotating Gān Bǎo (干寶)'s Jìn Jì (晉紀) into forty volumes.
Later, Zhāo (昭) himself compiled "Hòuhàn Tóngyì" (後漢同異) to annotate Fàn Yè (范曄)'s work,
which was widely praised for its extensive thoroughness.
He was promoted to Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎),
and then went out to serve as Shàn Lìng (剡令),
where he died in office.
His collected annotations to "Hòuhàn" (後漢) were one hundred eighty volumes,
"Yòutóng Zhuàn" (幼童傳) ten volumes,
and his collected writings ten volumes.
His son, Tāo (縚),
courtesy name Yánmíng (言明),
was also fond of learning
and thoroughly understood the Sānlǐ (三禮).
During the Dàtóng (大同) era,
he served as Shàngshū Cíbù Láng (尚書祠部郎),
but soon resigned his post
and did not serve again.
Tāo (縚)'s younger brother, Huǎn (緩),
courtesy name Hándù (含度),
was famous in his youth.
He successively held office as Ānxī Xiāngdōng Wáng (安西湘東王)'s jìshì (記室).
At that time, the western court extensively gathered literary talents,
and Huǎn (緩) was at the forefront.
He was appointed Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎),
and soon promoted to Zhènnán Xiāngdōng Wáng (鎮南湘東王)'s Zhōnglùshì (中錄事),
then followed the prince to Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
where he died.
Hé Xùn (何遜), courtesy name Zhòngyán (仲言),
was a native of Tán (郯), Dōnghǎi (東海).
His great-grandfather, Chéngtiān (承天),
was Sòng (宋) Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
His grandfather, Yì (翼),
was Yuánwàiláng (員外郎).
His father, Xún (詢),
was Qí (齊) Tàiwèi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (太尉中兵參軍).
Xùn (遜) could compose poetry at eight,
and at twenty, he was recommended as Xiùcái (秀才) by the prefecture.
Fàn Yún (范雲) of Nánxiāng (南鄉) saw his policy proposals
and praised them greatly,
thus forming a friendship that transcended age.
From then on, every piece of writing or poem he produced,
Fàn Yún (范雲) would invariably admire,
saying to his intimates:
"Recently, when observing men of letters,
their substance often exceeds that of scholars,
but their ornateness harms custom;
those who can encompass both clarity and turbidity,
and balance ancient and modern,
are seen in Hé Shēng (何生)."
Shěn Yuē (沈約) also loved his writings,
and once said to Xùn (遜):
"Every time I read your poems,
I read them three times a day,
and still cannot stop."
Such was the praise he received from famous scholars.
During the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
he began his career as Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請),
and was promoted to Zhōngwèi Jiàn'ān Wáng (中衞建安王)'s Shuǐcáo Xíng Cānjūn (水曹行參軍),
concurrently serving as jìshì (記室).
The prince loved men of letters
and spent his days with them in feasts and entertainments.
When the prince was transferred to Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
Xùn (遜) still managed the secretariat.
He returned to serve as Ānxī Ānchéng Wáng (安西安成王)'s Cānjūnshì (參軍事),
concurrently Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng (尚書水部郎),
and resigned due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Rénwēi Lúlíng Wáng (仁威廬陵王)'s jìshì (記室),
and again followed the prince to Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
where he died shortly thereafter.
Wáng Sēngrú (王僧孺) of Dōnghǎi (東海) compiled his works into eight volumes.
Initially,
Xùn (遜)'s writings and Liú Xiàochuò (劉孝綽)'s were both highly esteemed by the world,
and the world referred to them as
"Hé Liú" (何劉).
Shìzǔ (世祖) wrote an essay discussing them, saying:
"Among those who wrote many poems and were capable, there was Shěn Yuē (沈約);
among those who wrote few but were capable, there were Xiè Tiǎo (謝朓) and Hé Xùn (何遜)."
At that time, there was Yú Qiān (虞騫) from Kuàijī (會稽),
skilled at composing five-character-line poetry,
whose fame was equal to Xùn (遜)'s.
His highest office was Wángguó Shìláng (王國侍郎).
Later, there were also Kǒng Wēngguī (孔翁歸) from Kuàijī (會稽) and Jiāng Bì (江避) from Jìyáng (濟陽),
both serving as Nánpíng Wáng (南平王)'s Dàsīmǎ Fǔ (大司馬府)'s jìshì (記室).
Wēngguī (翁歸) was also skilled at composing poetry.
Bì (避) was learned and insightful,
and furthermore annotated the "Lúnyǔ" (論語) and "Xiàojīng" (孝經).
Both men had collected works.
Zhōng Róng (鍾嶸), courtesy name Zhòngwěi (仲偉),
was a native of Chángshè (長社), Yǐngchuān (潁川).
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Jìn (晉) Shìzhōng Yǎ (侍中雅).
His father, Dāo (蹈),
was Qí (齊) Zhōngjūn Cānjūn (中軍參軍).
At that time, there was a skillful diviner, Zhāng Yǒudào (張有道), who said to Xiàoxù (孝緒):
"I see your reclusive traces, but your heart is difficult to discern.
Unless we examine it with tortoise shells and milfoil,
there's no way to verify it."
When he arranged the hexagrams,
after manipulating five changing lines,
he said:
"This will be Xián (咸), 'Influence/Wooing.'
It is the method of responsive interaction,
not a sign of auspicious retreat."
Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"How do you know that the later line won't become 'the ninth in the uppermost place'?"
Indeed, it formed the Dùn (遯) hexagram, 'Retreat.'
Yǒudào (有道) sighed and said:
"This is what is meant by 'A fat retreat, nothing that would not be advantageous.'
The image truly corresponds to virtue,
with both heart and traces aligned."
Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"Although I obtained the Dùn (遯) hexagram,
and the 'ninth in the uppermost place' line is not activated,
the path to ascension [to immortality]
means I should now highly decline and take leave, like Xǔ Shēng (許生)."
Thereupon, he composed the Gāoyǐn Chuán (高隱傳, 'Biographies of Lofty Recluses'),
starting from Yán (炎) and Huáng (黃),
and ending at the close of Tiānjiān (天監),
divided into three categories after careful deliberation,
totaling several *juàn* (卷).
He also wrote an essay which stated:
"The essence of the ultimate Way
lies in non-action (*wúwéi*);
the traces of the Sage
lie in alleviating evils.
Evils are alleviated through traces,
but the use of traces deviates from the essence;
since the essence is non-action,
action is not the ultimate of the Way.
However, if traces are not manifested,
then the world cannot be pacified;
if the essence is not thoroughly investigated,
then the Way is truly lost.
Qiū (丘) and Dàn (旦) sought to preserve their traces,
and thus should have temporarily obscured their essence;
Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊) only clarified their essence,
and likewise should have deeply suppressed their traces.
Since traces can be suppressed,
this is why those few masters had something in excess;
since the essence was obscured,
Níqiū (尼丘) was therefore insufficient.
Those who do not grasp the One
lack that clear wisdom;
those who embody the Two
alone possess discerning insight.
[一０] However, the Sage, having reached the extreme of enlightenment,
instead initiated his traces;
the Worthy, not yet having attained the supreme position,
further spoke of his essence.
This is truly because traces are needed to save the world,
and none but a Sage can do it;
the essence truly clarifies principle,
and can be illuminated by the Worthy.
If one can embody this essence and traces,
and comprehend that suppression and elevation,
then the intentions of Kǒng (孔) and Zhuāng (莊)
would be more than half understood."
Nánpíng Yuánxiāng Wáng (南平元襄王) heard of his reputation,
and sent him a letter inviting him,
but he did not go.
Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"It's not that my ambition scorns wealth and status,
but rather my nature fears the imperial court.
If I could be harnessed,
how would I be different from a swift steed?"
Originally,
at the end of Jiànwǔ (建武),
the east gate of Qīngxī Gōng (青溪宮) collapsed inexplicably,
[一一] and a great wind uprooted the willow trees outside the east gate of the Eastern Palace.
Someone asked Xiàoxù (孝緒) about this,
and Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"Qīngxī (青溪) is the old imperial residence.
Qí (齊) corresponds to the element Wood;
the east is the position of Wood.
Now that the east gate has collapsed by itself,
Wood must be declining."
The consort of Póyáng Zhōngliè Wáng (鄱陽忠烈王)
was Xiàoxù's (孝緒) elder sister.
The king once ordered his carriage,
intending to visit him,
but Xiàoxù (孝緒) dug through the wall and fled,
ultimately refusing to see him.
His nephews would send gifts annually,
but he accepted none of them.
When people questioned him about it,
he replied:
"It was not my original wish,
therefore I do not accept it."
The stone statue he worshipped
had been damaged before,
and he wished to repair it.
One night, it was suddenly restored,
and everyone found it extraordinary.
In Dàtóng (大同) second year,
he died,
at the age of fifty-eight.
His disciples composed an elegy for his virtues and conduct,
posthumously naming him Wénzhēn Chǔshì (文貞處士).
His works, such as the Qī Lù (七錄) and others, comprising 250 *juàn* (卷),
circulated in the world.
Táo Hóngjǐng (陶弘景), courtesy name Tōngmíng (通明),
was a native of Mòlíng (秣陵) in Dānyáng (丹陽).
Initially,
his mother dreamt of a green dragon emerging from her bosom,
and also saw two celestial beings holding incense burners arriving at her place.
Afterwards, she became pregnant,
and subsequently gave birth to Hóngjǐng (弘景).
As a child, he had extraordinary conduct.
At the age of ten,
he obtained Gě Hóng's (葛洪) Shénxiān Chuán (神仙傳, 'Biographies of Immortals'),
which he studied day and night,
and thus developed the aspiration for nourishing life.
He said to people:
"Looking up at the azure clouds
and seeing the white sun,
I don't feel it's far."
When he grew up,
he was seven *chǐ* (尺) and four *cùn* (寸) tall,
with a brilliant and elegant divine demeanor,
bright eyes and sparse eyebrows,
a slender physique and long ears.
He read over ten thousand *juàn* (卷) of books.
He was skilled in playing the *qín* (琴)
and adept at cursive and clerical scripts.
Before he reached twenty,
Qí Gāodì (齊高帝) became chancellor,
and appointed him as tutor to the various princes,
bestowing upon him the title Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請).
Although he was in a noble household,
he kept to himself and did not engage with external matters,
solely dedicating himself to reading.
Many matters of court protocol and historical precedents
were decided by him.
In Yǒngmíng (永明) tenth year,
he submitted a memorial resigning from his emolument,
and the emperor granted it,
bestowing upon him a bundle of silk.
When he departed,
dukes and ministers bid him farewell at the Zhēnglǔ Tíng (征虜亭),
with splendid tents and provisions,
and carriages and horses filling the roads.
Everyone said that since Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊),
there had been no such event.
Both court and commoners honored him.
Thereupon, he settled in Qūqǔ Shān (句曲山) in Jùróng (句容).
He said:
"Below this mountain is the Eighth Cave Palace,
named Jīntán Huáyáng Zhī Tiān (金壇華陽之天), 'Heaven of Jintan Huayang,'
with a circumference of 150 *lǐ* (里).
In ancient times during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the three Máojūn (茅君) of Xiányáng (咸陽) attained the Dao,
and came to preside over this mountain,
hence it is called Máoshān (茅山)."
He then established a hermitage on the mountain
and styled himself Huáyáng Yǐnjū (華陽隱居, 'Recluse of Huayang').
He first received talismans, diagrams, scriptures, and methods from Sūn Yóuyuè (孫遊岳) of Dōngyáng (東陽).
He traveled throughout famous mountains,
searching for elixirs of immortality.
Whenever he passed through a ravine or valley,
he would surely sit or lie there,
reciting poetry and lingering,
unable to stop.
At that time, Shěn Yuē (沈約) was the Administrator of Dōngyáng Jùn (東陽郡),
and, respecting his lofty aspirations and integrity,
repeatedly sent letters inviting him,
but he did not come.
Hóngjǐng (弘景) was a man who was
adaptable and cautious,
his presence and reclusion perfectly aligned;
his mind was like a clear mirror,
grasping things as soon as they appeared,
his words never superfluous or contradictory,
and he always became aware of things.
In the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
Qí Yídū Wáng Kēng (齊宜都王鏗) was killed by Míngdì (明帝).
That night,
Hóngjǐng (弘景) dreamt that Kēng (鏗) bid him farewell.
He then inquired about matters in the netherworld,
and Kēng (鏗) spoke extensively of various secrets and marvels.
Thus, he composed the Mèng Jì (夢記, 'Record of Dreams').
In the early Yuánwáng (永元) era,
he built a three-story tower.
Hóngjǐng (弘景) resided on the top floor,
his disciples in the middle,
and guests on the bottom floor,
thus completely isolating himself from others.
Only one family servant was allowed to attend him.
He particularly loved the sound of the wind in the pines,
and whenever he heard its rustling,
he would be filled with joy.
Sometimes he would wander alone among springs and rocks,
and those who saw him thought he was an immortal.
His nature delighted in writing,
he esteemed the unusual and strange,
he cherished every moment,
and as he grew old, he became even more diligent.
He was particularly adept at Yin-Yang and the Five Phases,
wind-direction analysis and star-counting,
mountains, rivers, and geography,
local produce,
medical arts, and materia medica.
He compiled "Dìdài Niánlì" (Chronicle of Imperial Reigns).
He also once constructed an armillary sphere,
saying,
"This is needed for cultivating the Dao,
not just for court historians."
When the righteous army pacified Jiànkāng,
and he heard discussions of abdicating the throne,
Hóngjǐng cited prognostic charts and oracles,
where in several places, the character
"Liáng"
was formed.
He ordered his disciples to present these.
Gāozǔ had already associated with him early on,
and after ascending the throne,
his favor and courtesy towards Hóngjǐng became even more profound.
Letters and inquiries never ceased,
and officials' carriages were constantly seen arriving.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (507 CE),
he moved to the eastern stream of Jījīn.
He was skilled in the methods of *bìgǔ* (abstention from grains) and *dǎoyǐn* (breathing exercises),
and though over eighty years old, he had the appearance of a strong man.
He deeply admired Zhāng Liáng's character,
saying,
"No ancient worthy can compare."
He once dreamed that the Buddha bestowed upon him a Bodhi prediction,
naming him Shènglì Púsà.
Thereupon, he went to the Ashoka Pagoda in Mào County and made a vow,
receiving the Five Great Precepts.
Later, Tàizōng visited Nánxú Prefecture,
admired his pure conduct,
summoned him to the inner hall,
talked with him for several days, and then he departed.
Tàizōng greatly respected and admired him.
In the early Dàtōng period (527 CE),
he was ordered to present two swords to Gāozǔ.
One was named Shànshèng,
and the other Wēishèng,
〔一二〕both were fine treasures.
In the second year of Dàtóng (536 CE),
he died,
aged eighty-five.
〔一三〕His complexion remained unchanged,
and his limbs were pliable as before.
An imperial edict posthumously appointed him Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
and granted him the posthumous title Zhēnbái Xiānshēng.
Furthermore, a *shèrén* was sent to supervise his funeral.
Hóngjǐng had left instructions for a simple burial,
and his disciples followed them.
Zhūgě Qú, courtesy name Yòuwén,
was a native of Yángdū, Lángyé,
whose family had resided in Jīngkǒu for generations.
Qú served the recluse Guān Kāngzhī in his youth,
and extensively studied the classics and histories.
He then took the recluse Zāng Róngxù as his teacher.
Róngxù, who authored the "Jìnshū",
credited Qú with contributing to its revelations and clarifications,
comparing him to Hú Suì.
In the early Jiànwǔ reign of Qí (494 CE),
Jiāng Sì, acting official of Nánxú Prefecture, recommended Qú to Míngdì, saying:
"Qú is content in poverty and adheres to the Dao,
delights in rites and cultivates poetry.
He has never presented his calling card to local officials
or waited in attendance at government offices.
Given his detached and reclusive nature,
he can promote purity and refine customs.
I request that he be appointed to the position of Yìcáo Cóngshì."
The emperor granted this,
but Qú declined and did not accept.
Xiè Tiǎo of Chén Commandery, then administrator of Dōnghǎi Prefecture, issued an instruction:
"In the past, Zhǎngsūn Dōngzǔ
demonstrated the integrity of Lóngqiū;
〔一四〕Wénjǔ Běizī
was highly praised for his moral conduct.
This served to inspire the greedy and strengthen the weak,
and to uphold exemplary models.
The hermit Zhūgě Qú
is imbued with such lofty character,
following in the footsteps of previous worthies.
Does he conceal a pearl beneath coarse cloth,
or hide jade awaiting its price?
Or is he a solitary, pure recluse
who serves no princes or kings?
I hear that in serving his parents, he endures the hardship of eating beans,
and in providing for them, he has little provision of wild vegetables.
How can I alone enjoy immense wealth
and forget this small share of grain?
He may be sent one hundred *hú* of grain."
During the Tiānjiān era,
Prefect Xiāo Chēn, Inspector Ānchéng Wáng Xiù, and Pōyáng Wáng Huī all treated him with exceptional courtesy.
When Qú mourned his mother, he became emaciated.
Huī repeatedly visited to inquire about him.
After the mourning period ended,
he was recommended as a *xiùcái*,
but did not accept.
Qú was diligent in teaching and guiding,
and students came to him daily.
His residence was small and humble,
unable to accommodate them,
so Prefect Zhāng Yǒu built him a lecture hall.
Qú conducted himself with purity and uprightness,
and his wife and children never saw a change in his expression, whether of joy or anger.
Morning and evening, he was assiduous,
lecturing and reciting without cessation,
and people increasingly revered him for this.
In the seventh year of Tiānjiān (508 CE),
Gāozǔ issued an edict inquiring about him to Prefect Wáng Fèn.
Fèn immediately responded with the full truth.
Before he could be summoned for employment,
he died at home that year.
Qú's twenty volumes of writings
were collected and recorded by his disciple Liú Jiǎo.
〔一五〕
Shěn Yǐ, courtesy name Chǔmò,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His father, Tǎnzhī,
was the Director of the Department of State Affairs during the Qí dynasty.
Yǐ was pure and quiet in his youth, with outstanding conduct,
and he admired the character of Huáng Shúdù and Xú Rúzi.
He did not study books for the sake of mere textual analysis,
nor did his writings favor superficial embellishment.
He often stayed alone in a room,
and people rarely saw his face.
Yǐ's paternal uncle, Bó,
was prominent and influential in the Qí era.
Whenever Bó returned to Wúxīng,
guests crowded his gate,
but Yǐ never went to his door.
When Bó visited him,
Yǐ would not step beyond his threshold for greeting or farewell.
Bó sighed, saying:
"Now I know that being noble is not better than being humble."
Soon after, he was summoned to be the Left Chamberlain of Nánjùn Wáng,
but he did not accept.
Yǐ's personal conduct was very refined;
he was filial to his mother and friendly to his brothers,
and was praised and admired by his community.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (485 CE),
he was summoned to be *Zhùzuò Láng*;
in the second year of Jiànwǔ (495 CE),
he was summoned to be *Tàizǐ Shèrén*;
he did not accept either.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán (500 CE),
he was again summoned to be *Tōngzhí Láng*,
which he also did not accept.
Yǐ had never managed his family estate,
and during the chaos and warfare at the end of Qí,
he and his family ate only once a day.
If anyone offered him fine grain or meat,
he would close his door and refuse.
He only supported himself by gathering firewood and foraging,
and remained perfectly content, never changing his joyful disposition.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (507 CE),
a large-scale northern expedition was launched,
and adult males were conscripted.
Liǔ Yùn, the Prefect of Wúxīng, drafted Yǐ for service.
Lù Rèn, the *Biéjià* of Yáng Prefecture, sent a letter rebuking him.
Yùn was greatly ashamed,
treated Yǐ with generous courtesy, and sent him home.
He died at home that year.
He authored dozens of articles.
Liú Huìfěi, courtesy name Wénxuān,
〔一六〕was a native of Péngchéng.
In his youth, he was widely learned
and skilled in writing.
He began his career as the Judicial Staff Officer for Ānchéng Wáng.
He once returned to the capital,
passing through Xúnyáng on his way.
He visited Kuāngshān,
and called upon the recluse Zhāng Xiàoxiù.
〔一七〕They found great joy in each other's company,
and he resolved to stay there for the rest of his life.
Consequently, he did not re-enter officialdom
and resided at Dōnglín Temple.
He also constructed a garden north of the mountain,
named Lígoù Yuán,
and people at the time called him Lígoù Xiānshēng.
He was transferred to be the Jìshì Cānjūn for the Tàiwèi.
He was sent out to be the Sīmǎ of the Guànjūn and the Grand Administrator of Dōngguǎn.
While in the commandery, he was known for his "purity and harmony" (Qīnghé).
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng,
and concurrently served as the Sīmǎ of the Zuǒwèi.
He was then transferred to be the Zīyì Cānjūn of the Zhèn Xī.
When Qí Wǔdì died,
Míngdì assumed the role of Prime Minister.
He eliminated those who differed from him,
and Jìzhí was unable to pander to him.
Míngdì became somewhat wary of him,
and so sent him out to be the Chángshǐ of the Fǔguó and the Grand Administrator of Běihǎi.
Being a senior assistant in a frontier post
was rarely undertaken by those of noble birth.
Someone advised Jìzhí to call upon the Emperor to express his gratitude.
When Míngdì saw him,
he immediately retained him,
appointing him as Pìaoqí Zīyì Cānjūn,
and concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
He was then transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Jiàn'ān.
His administration emphasized purity and tranquility,
which benefited the common people.
Upon his return, he served as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
then was promoted to Yóujī Jiāngjūn, concurrently Tíngwèi.
When the Liáng dynasty was established,
he was promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng.
He often stated that "once one's official career reaches the rank of two thousand *dàn*,
one's initial wish is fulfilled,
there is no need to busy oneself with human affairs."
Thereupon, he resigned due to illness and returned to his hometown.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū at home.
Gāozǔ said,
"The Liáng dynasty has come to rule the world,
yet I do not see this man."
In the tenth year,
he died at home,
at the age of seventy-five.
Jìzhí had always been exceptionally pure and ascetic.
He had lived in seclusion for over ten years.
When he died,
his family had nothing but bare walls.
His descendants had nothing with which to shroud and inter him.
Those who heard of it were all saddened by his aspirations.
Xiāo Shìsù
was a native of Lánlíng.
His grandfather, Sīhuà,
was a Sòng Zhēng Xī Yítóng Sānsī.
His father, Huìmíng,
was the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
Both had great reputations.
Shìsù became an orphan and poor at an early age,
and was taken in and cared for by his uncle, Huìxiū.
He began his career as a Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn for the Qí Sītú,
then was promoted to Zhùzuò Zuǒláng,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng.
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
he served as Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
When the Liáng dynasty was established,
Gāozǔ brought him in as the Zhōngwèi Pìaoqí Jìshì Cānjūn.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he served as the Yǒu for Línchuán Wáng,
then again as Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,
and Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng.
When he was first appointed,
Gāozǔ bestowed eighty thousand coins upon him.
Shìsù dispersed it all among his relatives and friends in a single day.
He was then promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ,
and Zhìzhōng of Nán Xúzhōu.
He had a quiet and retiring nature,
few desires,
loved learning,
and was skilled in "pure conversation" (qīngyán).
Fame and gain were not spoken of by him,
and joy and anger did not show on his countenance.
Whether in society or in office,
he always acted according to his feelings and was straightforward,
never boasting or being arrogant.
He was naturally simple and unadorned,
and gentlemen all respected him for this.
When he was in Jīngkǒu,
he already had the intention of settling there for good,
and so built a house on Mount Shè.
He was then summoned to be Zhōngshū Shìláng,
but he declined the appointment.
He then returned to his mountain dwelling,
living in solitude and avoiding official duties.
No one but his relatives was allowed to reach his fence gate.
His wife,
the daughter of Tàiwèi Wáng Jiǎn,
had lived separately from him for a long time,
and so he had no children.
In the eighth year,
he died.
His relatives and old friends traced his actions and conduct,
and posthumously named him Zhēnwén Xiānshēng.
The historian says: Gù Xiànzhī and Táo Jìzhí
were those who prolonged their lives in retirement;
as for Xiāo Shìsù, his desire for officialdom was even less.
Compared to those who clung to their stipends and indulged in favor,
lingering in the human world,
there was a distinct difference.
Collated notes
Biographies, Chapter 47: Good Officials: Yǔ Bì, Shěn Yǔ, Fàn Shùzēng, Qiū Zhòngfú, Sūn Qiān, Fú Jǐ, Hé Yuǎn.
Emperor Xuān of Han once believed that
"for government to be peaceful and lawsuits settled,
it depends on good officials of the two thousand *dàn* rank!"
Former historians also said:
