"The Grand Administrator of today
is the feudal lord of ancient times."
Therefore, the office of chief official
is known as "cherishing the people."
Thus, guiding virtue, regulating rites,
and transforming customs and traditions
must all come through them.
At the end of Qí, there was chaos and disorder.
Government was controlled by petty individuals.
Taxes and levies arose like clouds,
and corvée labor was limitless.
Most administrators and magistrates relied on powerful families,
each fostering greed and tyranny,
exploiting and extorting,
and distressing the common people.
The world was shaken,
and people had nowhere to turn.
Gāozǔ, while still in the fields,
understood the suffering of the people.
When the Liáng dynasty was established,
he issued a broad and lenient decree,
and the various miscellaneous levies from the chaotic times
were all abolished.
Thereupon, within the four seas,
people were finally able to rest their shoulders.
Upon ascending the throne,
he personally attended to all affairs,
listening to governance until sunset,
seeking out the ailments of the people.
He then dispatched light carriages to inspect local customs,
and set up "lungs-and-stones" (fèishí) to allow the poor to reach him,
endeavoring to show compassion and relief,
and alleviate their urgent distress.
In the first year,
he first abolished the household tax (rénzī)
and imposed a tax on adult males (jìdīng wéi bù).
He himself wore washed clothes,
and the imperial treasury had no ornate decorations.
The palace quarters used no more than silk and colorful fabrics,
no pearls, gems, brocades, or embroidery.
The imperial kitchens removed grand feasts,
serving vegetables daily,
and drinking no more than three cups of wine: thus he led the nation in frugality.
Whenever selecting chief officials,
he sought to choose the incorruptible and impartial.
All were summoned before the emperor,
who personally exhorted them on the principles of governance.
He first promoted Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng Dào Gài to be the Nèishǐ of Jiàn'ān,
and Zuǒmín Shìláng Líu Zōng to be the Grand Administrator of Jìn'ān.
Gài and others, in their official capacities,
were all noted for their integrity.
He also issued an order: if a small county had capable officials,
they would be promoted to large counties;
if a large county had capable officials,
they would be promoted to the two thousand *dàn* rank.
Thereupon, Qiū Zhòngfú, the magistrate of Shānyīn, who had outstanding administrative achievements,
was appointed Nèishǐ of Chángshā.
Hé Yuǎn, the magistrate of Wǔkāng, who was pure and impartial,
was appointed Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng.
Those who were appointed as officials with credentials
often followed suit.
As for Yǔ Bì of Xīnyě and other officials,
they enriched their administration with classical learning,
some spreading benevolence where they served,
others being remembered after they left.
They were truly good officials of later times.
Thus, this chapter on good officials is compiled.
Yǔ Bì, courtesy name Xiūyě,
was a native of Xīnyě.
His father, Shēnzī,
was the Sòng Yōngzhōu Cīshǐ.
When Bì was ten years old,
he suffered the sorrow of his father's death,
and during the mourning period, he became emaciated from grief,
which was praised by his provincial compatriots.
At twenty,
he was appointed Zhǔbù by the province,
passed the Xiùcái examination,
and successively rose to Ānxī Zhǔbù,
Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng,
and Pìaoqí Gōngcáo Shǐ.
He was widely read in various books and
had eloquent speech.
During Qí Yǒngmíng,
when peace was established with Wèi,
Bì was appointed acting Sànqí Chángshì to be an envoy.
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng,
and oversaw record-keeping in the Eastern Palace.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there was great chaos.
The Registrar, Qū Dá,
killed the county magistrate and established himself as king.
This was passed down for several generations.
When a later king had no heir,
he established his nephew, Fàn Xióng.
After Xióng died,
his son Yì succeeded him.
In the third year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of Jìn (337 CE),
Yì died.
His slave, Wén, usurped the throne and established himself.
Wén was originally a slave of Fàn Zhì, a chieftain of the Yí people in Xījuǎn county of Rìnán.
He often herded cattle in a mountain gully
when he found two snakeheads (Channa argus).
They transformed into iron,
so he used them to forge a knife.
When it was finished,
Wén faced a stone and swore, saying:
"If I can chop this stone and break it,
then I shall become king of this country."
He then raised the knife and chopped the stone.
It was as if he were cutting straw,
and Wén's heart was uniquely surprised by this.
Fàn Zhì often sent him to trade in Línyì.
He then taught the king of Línyì how to build palaces and military vehicles and weapons.
The king favored and trusted him.
Later, he slandered the king's sons,
who each fled to other countries.
When the king died without an heir,
Wén pretended to welcome a prince from a neighboring country,
put poison in his drink and killed him,
then coerced the people of the country and established himself.
He raised an army and attacked the small neighboring countries,
swallowing them all up,
and had a force of forty to fifty thousand men.
At that time, Jiāng Zhuāng, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu, sent his trusted associates Hán Jí and Xiè Zhì,
one after another, to oversee Rìnán Commandery.
Both were corrupt and cruel,
and all the countries suffered from them.
In the third year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù (347 CE),
the court sent Xiàhóu Lǎn to be the Grand Administrator.
His oppression and exploitation were even more severe.
Línyì had previously lacked fertile land
and coveted the rich land of Rìnán,
always wishing to seize it.
By this time,
taking advantage of the people's resentment,
it raised an army and attacked Rìnán,
killing Lǎn
and offering his corpse as a sacrifice to heaven.
They remained in Rìnán for three years
before returning to Línyì.
The Inspector of Jiāozhōu, Zhū Fān, later sent the Supervisor Liú Xióng to garrison Rìnán.
Wén again
slaughtered and annihilated him. He advanced and plundered Jiǔdé Commandery,
harming officials and common people.
He sent an envoy to inform Fān,
wishing to make Mount Héng, the northern border of Rìnán, the boundary.
Fān did not agree
and again sent Supervisors Táo Huǎn and Lǐ Qú to attack him.
Wén returned to Línyì,
but soon after again garrisoned Rìnán.
Five years later,
Wén died,
and his son Fó succeeded him,
still garrisoning Rìnán.
Huán Wēn, the General who Conquers the West, sent the Supervisor Téng Jùn and the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn, Guàn Suì, to lead troops from Jiāo and Guǎng provinces to attack him.
Fó fortified the city and held it firmly.
Suì ordered Jùn to deploy a large force in front,
while Suì himself led seven hundred elite soldiers
and entered by climbing over the ramparts from the rear.
Fó's troops were shocked, panicked, and fled.
Suì pursued them to Línyì,
where Fó then requested surrender.
At the beginning of Shēngpíng of Emperor Āi (357 CE),
he again became a menace, and Inspector Wēn Fàngzhī attacked and defeated him.
In the third year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān (399 CE),
Fó's grandson, Xūdá, again attacked Rìnán,
capturing the Grand Administrator, Jìng Yuán.
He then advanced and plundered Jiǔdé,
capturing the Grand Administrator, Cáo Bǐng.
Dù Yuàn, the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, sent the Protector Dèng Yì and others to defeat him.
Yuàn was then appointed Inspector.
In the third year of Yìxī (407 CE),
Xūdá again attacked Rìnán,
killing the Chief Clerk.
Yuàn sent the Maritime Patrol Supervisor Ruǎn Fěi to attack and defeat him,
slaying and capturing a great many.
In the ninth year (413 CE),
Xūdá again attacked Jiǔzhēn.
Dù Huìqī, acting as Commandery Administrator, fought him,
beheading his son, King Jiāolóng Zhēn Zhī, and his general, Fàn Jiàn, and others,
and capturing Xūdá's son Néng alive,
along with over a hundred other captives.
After Yuàn's death,
Línyì plundered Rìnán and Jiǔdé commanderies every year,
killing and pillaging many people.
〔一０〕Jiāozhōu thus became weak and depleted.
After Xūdá died,
his son Dízhēn succeeded him.
His younger brother Díkǎi's mother fled.
Dízhēn regretted being unable to accommodate his mother's brother (step-brother),
so he abandoned the country and went to Tiānzhú (India),
ceding the throne to his nephew.
The Chancellor, Zàng Lín, strongly advised against it, but he did not listen.
After his nephew was established, he killed Zàng Lín.
Zàng Lín's son then attacked and killed him,
and established Wén Dí, the half-brother of Díkǎi (same mother, different father).
Wén Dí was later killed by Dānggēnchún, a prince of Fúnán.
The high minister Fàn Zhūnóng suppressed the rebellion
and established himself as king.
After Zhūnóng died,
his son Yángmài succeeded him.
In the second year of Yǒngchū of Sòng (421 CE),
he sent envoys to offer tribute,
and Yángmài was appointed King of Línyì.
After Yángmài died,
his son Duō succeeded him.
He admired his father
and again called himself Yángmài.
〔一一〕
The customs of their country: their dwellings are elevated structures
called "yúlán."
Doors and windows all face north.
They write on tree leaves as paper.
Men and women all wrap a horizontal strip of jíbèi cloth around their waists downwards,
which is called "gānmàn,"
also known as "dōumàn."
They pierce their ears and wear small rings.
The noble wear leather sandals,
while the common walk barefoot.
This is true for Línyì, Fúnán, and all countries to their south.
Their king wears ceremonial robes,
adorned with yīngluò (necklaces),
like the ornaments of a Buddha statue.
When he goes out, he rides an elephant,
blows conch shells, beats drums,
is shaded by a jíbèi umbrella,
and uses jíbèi as banners and flags.
The country has no established penal code.
Those who commit crimes are trampled to death by elephants.
Their major clans are called Brāhman.
Marriages must take place in the eighth month.
Women propose to men first,
indicating that men are of lower status than women.
They marry within the same clan.
They have a Brāhman lead the groom to see the bride,
who takes his hand and entrusts herself to him,
and they say a chant:
"Jílì, Jílì" (auspicious, auspicious),
which is considered the completion of the ceremony.
The deceased are cremated in the wilderness,
which is called "huǒzàng" (cremation).
Widows live alone,
with disheveled hair until old age.
The king practices Nígān Dào (Jainism),
casting gold and silver human statues,
ten arm-spans in circumference.
At the beginning of Yuánjiā (424 CE),
Yángmài invaded and plundered Rìnán and Jiǔdé commanderies.
Dù Hóngwén, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu, erected his banner intending to attack him,
but stopped upon hearing that a replacement was coming.
Eight years later,
he again attacked Jiǔdé Commandery,
entering the estuary of Sìhuì.
Ruǎn Mízhī, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu, sent the company commander Xiāng Dàoshēng to lead troops to attack him.
They attacked Qūlì city but could not capture it,
so they withdrew.
Thereafter, they frequently sent envoys to offer tribute,
but their plundering did not cease.
In the twenty-third year (446 CE),
Jiāozhōu Inspector Tán Hézhī and General Zhènwǔ Zōng Quán attacked him.
Hézhī sent his Sīmǎ (Chief Clerk), Xiāo Jǐngxiàn, as the vanguard.
Yángmài, hearing of this, was afraid
and wanted to offer ten thousand catties of gold and one hundred thousand catties of silver,
and return the people he had plundered from Rìnán.
However, his high minister Sēng Dá advised him against it,
so he sent the great commander Fàn Fúlóng to garrison his northern border, Qūlì city.
Jǐngxiàn attacked the city
and captured it,
beheading Fúlóng
and capturing countless gold, silver, and miscellaneous items.
Taking advantage of the victory, he advanced directly
and immediately captured Línyì.
Yángmài and his son barely escaped with their lives.
He seized their rare treasures,
all of which were unnamed valuables.
He also melted down their gold statues,
obtaining several hundred thousand catties of gold.
Hézhī later died of illness,
seeing a "Hú god" haunting him.
During the Xiàowǔ, Xiàojiàn, and Dàmíng reigns,
〔一二〕 Fàn Shénchéng (范神成), King of Línyì (林邑), repeatedly sent his Registrar (長史) to present memorials and tribute.
In the first year of the Tàiyù reign of Emperor Míng (明帝),
he again sent envoys to present local products.
During the Yǒngmíng reign of Qí (齊),
Fàn Wénzàn (范文贊) repeatedly sent envoys to present tribute.
In the ninth year of Tiānjiān,
Wénzàn’s (文贊) son, Tiānkǎi (天凱), presented a white monkey.
An imperial edict stated:
“Fàn Tiānkǎi (范天凱), King of Línyì (林邑), residing across the sea,
has sincerely offered his loyalty and reached out to us,
travelling afar to present tribute.
This is truly commendable.
He should be granted a noble title
and bestowed with glory and favour.
He is appointed as Envoy with Credentials (持節), Overseer of all Military Affairs along the Coast (督緣海諸軍事), General Who Awe the South (威南將軍), and King of Línyì (林邑).”
In the tenth year,
and the thirteenth year,
Tiānkǎi (天凱) repeatedly sent envoys to present local products.
Shortly after, he died of illness.
His son, Bìcuìbámó (弼毳跋摩), ascended the throne
and presented memorials with tribute.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng,
King Gāoshìshèngkǎi (高式勝鎧) sent envoys to present local products.
An imperial edict appointed him as Envoy with Credentials (持節), Overseer of all Military Affairs along the Coast (督緣海諸軍事), General Who Pacify the South (綏南將軍), and King of Línyì (林邑).
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he again sent envoys to present tribute.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,
the acting King of Línyì (林邑), Gāoshìlǜluóbámó (高式律羅跋摩), sent envoys to present tribute.
An imperial edict appointed him as Envoy with Credentials (持節), Overseer of all Military Affairs along the Coast (督緣海諸軍事), General Who Pacify the South (綏南將軍), and King of Línyì (林邑).
In the sixth year,
he again sent envoys to present local products.
The kingdom of Fúnán (扶南)
is south of Rìnán Jùn (日南郡),
within a great bay west of the sea.
It is about seven thousand *lǐ* (里) from Rìnán (日南)
and over three thousand *lǐ* (里) southwest of Línyì (林邑).
Its capital is five hundred *lǐ* (里) from the sea.
There is a great river, ten *lǐ* (里) wide,
flowing northwest,
then east into the sea.
The kingdom has a circumference of over three thousand *lǐ* (里).
The land is low-lying, flat, and broad.
Its climate and customs are largely similar to Línyì (林邑).
It produces gold, silver, copper, tin, agarwood, ivory, peacocks, and five-coloured parrots.
About three thousand *lǐ* (里) to its south lies the kingdom of Dùnxùn (頓遜),
situated on a sea peninsula.
Its territory spans a thousand *lǐ* (里),
and its capital is ten *lǐ* (里) from the sea.
It has five kings,
all subordinate to Fúnán (扶南).
Dùnxùn’s (頓遜) eastern border connects to Jiāozhōu (交州),
while its western border adjoins the kingdoms outside the territories of Tiānzhú (天竺) and Ānxī (安息),
allowing for trade and exchange.
This is because
Dùnxùn (頓遜) extends into the sea for over a thousand *lǐ* (里),
and the expansive sea has no accessible shores,
so ships have never been able to pass directly through.
At its market,
traders from east and west gather,
with over ten thousand people daily.
Precious goods and treasures
are all available there.
There is also a “wine tree,”
resembling a pomegranate.
Its flower juice is collected and stored in jars,
turning into wine after several days.
Beyond Dùnxùn (頓遜),
on a large island in the great sea,
is the kingdom of Píqiān (毗騫),
eight thousand *lǐ* (里) from Fúnán (扶南).
It is said that its king is twelve *chǐ* (丈二) tall,
with a neck three *chǐ* (三尺) long.
〔一三〕He has been immortal since ancient times,
and his age is unknown.
The king is divine and sacred.
He knows the good and evil deeds of his people and all future events.
The king knows everything,
so no one dares to deceive him.
In the south, he is called the "Long-necked King."
According to their customs,
they have houses and clothes,
and eat polished rice.
Their language
differs slightly from Fúnán (扶南).
There is a mountain that produces gold.
Gold appears naturally on the rocks,
without any limits.
According to their law, criminals are punished
by having their flesh eaten in front of the king.
The country does not receive merchants.
If anyone comes, they are also killed and eaten.
Therefore, merchants dare not approach.
The king always resides in a multi-storied building,
does not eat meat,
and does not worship spirits or gods.
His descendants live and die like ordinary people;
only the king is immortal.
The King of Fúnán (扶南) often sent envoys to exchange letters.
He always presented the King of Fúnán (扶南) with fifty pure gold eating utensils.
Some were shaped like round plates,
others like pottery bowls,
called *duōluó* (多羅),
holding five *shēng* (升),
and still others like smaller bowls,
holding one *shēng* (升).
The king could also write in Tiānzhú (天竺) script.
His writings, about three thousand words,
explained his past lives,
resembling Buddhist scriptures,
and discussed good deeds.
It is also said that Fúnán’s (扶南) eastern border is the great expansive sea.
In the sea, there is a large island.
On the island are various Bó (薄) kingdoms.
East of these kingdoms are the Wǔzhōu (五洲) islands.
Travelling further east across the expansive sea for over a thousand *lǐ* (里),
one reaches the Great Natural Island.
On it, there are trees that grow in fire.
People near the island peel their bark,
spin it into cloth,
making small towels a few *chǐ* (尺) long.
They are indistinguishable from burnt hemp, but slightly greenish-black in colour.
If they become slightly dirty,
they are thrown into fire,
and emerge clean again.
Sometimes they are used as lamp wicks,
and never seem to burn out.
The customs of Fúnán (扶南) originally involved nudity,
tattooed bodies, and unbound hair,
without prescribed clothing.
They had a woman as their ruler,
named Liǔyè (柳葉).
She was young and strong,
resembling a man.
To its south was a border kingdom.
〔一四〕A person named Húntián (混填), who worshipped spirits and gods,
dreamt that a deity bestowed a bow upon him.
He boarded a merchant ship and went out to sea.
Húntián (混填) rose early and went to the temple.
He found a bow under the sacred tree,
and immediately, following his dream, boarded a ship and sailed into the sea,
eventually entering the outer territories of Fúnán (扶南).
When Liǔyè (柳葉) and her people saw the ship arrive,
they wanted to seize it.
Húntián (混填) immediately drew his bow and shot at their ships,
piercing through one side.
The arrow hit a retainer.
Liǔyè (柳葉) was greatly frightened,
and led her people to surrender to Húntián (混填).
Húntián (混填) then taught Liǔyè (柳葉) to wear cloth through her head,
so her body would no longer be exposed.
He then governed her kingdom,
took Liǔyè (柳葉) as his wife,
and their children were made kings over seven cities.
Later, King Hùnpánkùang (混盤況) used deception and force to sow discord among the various cities,
making them suspicious of each other.
He then raised an army, attacked, and unified them.
He then sent his descendants to divide and govern the cities,
who were called "Minor Kings."
Pán Kuàng (盤況) died at over ninety years old.
His middle son, Pán Pán (盤盤), was enthroned,
and the affairs of the state were entrusted to his great general, Fàn Màn (范蔓).
Pán Pán (盤盤) died three years after his enthronement.
The people of the state collectively elevated Màn (蔓) to be king.
Màn (蔓) was brave and strong, possessing strategies and tactics.
He again used military might to attack neighboring states,
all of which submitted to him.
He styled himself the Great King of Fúnán (扶南).
He then built large ships,
traversed the expansive sea,
and attacked over ten states including Qū Dōukūn (屈都昆), Jiǔ Zhì (九稚), and Diǎn Sūn (典孫),
opening up territory five to six thousand *lǐ* (里).
Next, when he was about to attack the state of Jīnlín (金隣),
Màn (蔓) fell ill.
He sent his crown prince, Jīn Shēng (金生), to act on his behalf.
Màn's (蔓) sister's son, Zhān (旃),
who was at that time a general of two thousand men,
usurped the throne from Màn (蔓) and established himself.
He sent someone to deceive Jīn Shēng (金生) and kill him.
When Màn (蔓) died,
he had an infant son named Cháng (長),
who was living among the common people.
When he reached twenty years of age,
he gathered strong men from the state and ambushed and killed Zhān (旃).
Zhān's (旃) great general, Fàn Xún (范尋), then killed Cháng (長) and established himself.
He further improved the internal administration of the state,
built towers and pavilions for enjoyment,
and received guests three or four times in the morning and afternoon.
The common people presented gifts of charred sugarcane, turtles, and birds.
The state law had no prisons.
Those who committed crimes
first fasted for three days.
Then, an axe was heated to extreme redness,
and the accused was made to hold it and walk seven steps.
Alternatively, a gold ring and a chicken egg were thrown into boiling water,
and the accused was made to retrieve them.
If they were innocent,
their hands would be scorched and烂 (làn) (ruined),
but if they were guilty, their hands would not be harmed.
Also, crocodiles were kept in the city moat,
and fierce beasts were caged outside the city gates.
Those who were guilty
were fed to these fierce beasts and crocodiles.
If the animals did not eat them, they were considered innocent,
and were released after three days.
Large crocodiles were over two *zhàng* (丈) long,
shaped like *tuó* (鼉) (alligators).
They had four feet,
a snout six or seven *chǐ* (尺) long,
and teeth on both sides,
sharp as knives and swords.
They usually ate fish,
but also devoured deer and people if encountered.
They were found south of Cāngwú (蒼梧) and in foreign countries.
During the Wú (吳) dynasty,
Zhōngláng (中郎) Kāng Tài (康泰) and Xuānhuà Cóngshì (宣化從事) Zhū Yīng (朱應) were sent as envoys to Xún's (尋) state.
The people of the state were still naked,
except for women who wore 'pierced-head' garments.
Tài (泰) and Yīng (應) said to them:
"The state is truly excellent,
but the people's exposure is strange."
Xún (尋) then ordered the men of his state to wear *héngfú* (橫幅).
*Héngfú* (橫幅)
is now called *gānmàn* (干漫).
Wealthy families made them from brocade,
while the poor used cloth.
During the Tàikāng (太康) era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝),
Xún (尋) first sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the first year of the Shēngpíng (升平) era of Emperor Mù (穆帝),
King Zhú Zhāntán (竺旃檀) presented a memorial offering tamed elephants.
An imperial edict stated:
"This item incurs no small labor and expense,
detain it and do not send it."
Later, King Jiāochénrú (憍陳如),
originally a Brāhmaṇa from Tiānzhú (天竺),
had a divine voice tell him
"You should be king of Fúnán (扶南)."
Jiāochénrú (憍陳如) was delighted in his heart.
He traveled south to Pán Pán (盤盤).
When the people of Fúnán (扶南) heard of this,
the whole state rejoiced and supported him,
welcoming and enthroning him.
He again reformed the system
and adopted the laws of Tiānzhú (天竺).
When Jiāochénrú (憍陳如) died,
the subsequent king, Chí Lí Bámó (持梨跋摩),
presented a memorial offering local products during the reign of Emperor Wén of Sòng (宋文帝).
During the Yǒngmíng (永明) era of Qí (齊),
King Shéyé Bámó (闍邪跋摩) sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (天監),
Bámó (跋摩) again sent envoys to deliver a coral Buddha statue
and offer local products.
An imperial edict stated:
"Fúnán (扶南) King Jiāochénrú Shéyé Bámó (憍陳如闍邪跋摩),
residing across the sea,
has for generations presided over the southern lands.
His sincerity is widely evident,
offering precious tribute through multiple translations.
He should be rewarded and accepted,
and granted an honorable title.
He is appointed General Guarding the South and King of Fúnán (安南將軍、扶南王)."
Today, the people of his state are all ugly and dark,
with curly hair.
They do not dig wells where they live;
dozens of households share one pond for drawing water.
Their custom is to worship heavenly deities.
Heavenly deities are represented by copper statues,
those with two faces have four arms,
those with four faces have eight arms.
Each hand holds something,
perhaps a child,
or a bird or beast,
or the sun and moon.
Their king rides an elephant when going out or entering,
and his consorts and attendants do likewise.
When the king sits, he half-squats with one knee raised,
letting his left knee hang to the ground.
White felt is spread before him,
and a gold basin and incense burner are placed upon it.
According to their state customs,
during mourning, beards and hair are shaved off.
There are four types of burial for the dead: water burial means casting them into the river,
fire burial means burning them to ashes,
earth burial means interring them,
and bird burial means abandoning them in the wilderness.
Their nature is greedy and stingy,
without propriety or righteousness.
Men and women are free to follow their desires in relationships.
In the tenth year,
and thirteenth year,
Bámó (跋摩) repeatedly sent envoys to offer tribute.
In that year he died,
and his illegitimate son, Liú Bámó (留跋摩), killed his legitimate younger brother and established himself.
In the sixteenth year,
he sent the envoy Zhú Dāng Bǎolǎo (竺當抱老) to present a memorial and offer tribute.
In the eighteenth year,
he again sent envoys to deliver an auspicious sandalwood image from Tiānzhú (天竺) and bodhi tree leaves,
along with fire-pearls, turmeric, and storax incense.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (普通),
the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng (中大通),
and the first year of Dàtóng (大同),
envoys were repeatedly sent to offer local products.
In the fifth year,
envoys were again sent to offer live rhinoceroses.
It was also said that their state possessed a Buddha's hair,
twelve *chǐ* (尺) long.
An imperial edict ordered the *shāmén* (沙門) Shì Yúnbǎo (釋雲寶) to accompany the envoys to retrieve it.
Previously,
in the eighth month of the third year,
Gāozǔ (高祖) rebuilt the stupa of King Āyù (阿育王),
from beneath the old stupa were taken *shèlì* (舍利) and Buddha's nails and hair.
The hair was blue-black in color.
When the monks extended it with their hands,
it would lengthen or shorten according to their hands.
When released, it would coil back into the shape of a snail shell.
According to the Saṃgha Sūtra, it is stated:
"The Buddha's hair is blue and fine,
like the fibers of a lotus root stem."
The Buddha Samādhi Sūtra states:
"When I was in the palace, I washed my head,
and measured my hair with a ruler;
it was twelve *chǐ* (尺) long.
When released, it spiraled to the right,
forming a snail pattern."
This is consistent with what Gāozǔ (高祖) obtained.
King Āyù (阿育王) was the Iron Wheel King,
who ruled Jambudvīpa (閻浮提),
the entire world.
After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
in one day and one night,
he commanded ghosts and spirits to build eighty-four thousand stupas.
This was one of them.
During the Wú (吳) dynasty, a nun resided there,
maintaining a small monastery.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) later destroyed it,
and the stupa also perished.
After Wú (吳) was pacified,
various Daoists rebuilt it at the old site.
When Emperor Zhōng of Jìn (晉中宗) first crossed the Yangtze River,
it was further repaired and adorned.
During the Xián'ān (咸安) era of Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文),
the *shāmén* (沙門) Master Ān Fǎshī Chéng (安法師程) was commissioned to build a small stupa,
but he died before it was completed.
His disciple Sēng Xiǎn (僧顯) continued and completed its construction.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán (太元) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武), a golden finial and dew-receiving basin were added.
The King of Hénán,
his ancestors originated from the Xiānbēi Mùróng clan.
Originally,
Mùróng Yìluògān had two sons.
The eldest illegitimate son was named Tǔyùhún,
and the legitimate son was named Huī.
When Luògān died,
Huī inherited the position.
Tǔyùhún avoided him and moved west.
Huī pursued him to keep him,
but the cattle and horses all ran west,
refusing to return.
Consequently, they journeyed westward up Lǒng,
crossed Fúhǎn,
went out southwest of Liángzhōu,
and settled at Chìshuǐ.
Their land was south of Zhāngyè,
west of Lǒngxī,
and south of the Hé (Yellow River),
hence it was taken as their designation.
Its territory extended east to Diéchuān,
〔三一〕 bordered Yútián to the west,
touched Gāochāng to the north,
and connected to Qínlǐng in the northeast,
spanning over a thousand *lǐ* (Chinese miles).
It was anciently the land of Liúshā.
There was a scarcity of grass and trees,
and little water.
There was ice and snow in all four seasons,
with particularly heavy rain and hail only in the sixth and seventh months.
When it was clear, wind blew sand and gravel,
often obscuring the light.
The land produced wheat but no other grains.
There was Qīnghǎi, several hundred *lǐ* square.
If mares were pastured near it,
they would invariably conceive foals.
The locals called these "dragon offspring,"
hence their country had many good horses.
They had houses,
interspersed with *bǎizǐzhàng* (tents made of felt),
which were *qiónglú* (yurts).
They wore robes with small sleeves,
trousers with narrow openings,
and tall, long-skirted hats.
Women wore their hair braided.
Later, Tǔyùhún’s grandson, Yèyán,
was quite literate.
He claimed that his great-grandfather Yìluògān was first enfeoffed as Duke of Chānglí,
and "I am indeed the son of the Duke’s grandson."
According to ritual, the father’s personal name was used as the state’s clan name,
so they took the surname Tǔyùhún,
which also became the state’s name.
By the time of his last grandson, Āchái,
they first received official titles from the Central Plain.
His nephew Mùyán,
at the end of Sòng Yuánjiā era, again styled himself King of Hénán.
Mùyán died,
and his cousin Shíyín succeeded him.
He then used written documents,
built cities,
and constructed palaces.
His lesser kings also built residences.
There was Buddhism in the country.
Shíyín died,
and his son Dùyìhóu succeeded him.
Yìhóu died,
and his son Xiūliú succeeded in his place.
During Qí Yǒngmíng era,

Dài (Xiūliú) was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Xīqín, Hé, and Shā three prefectures, General Who Guards the West, Protector-Colonel of the Qiāng, and Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two prefectures.
When Liáng arose,
Dài was promoted to General Who Conquers the West.
Dài died,
and his son Fúliánchóu inherited the title.
〔三二〕 In the thirteenth year of Tiānjiān,
he sent envoys to present two gold-mounted agate goblets.
He also memorialized to establish a nine-story Buddhist temple in Yìzhōu,
which was granted by imperial edict.
In the fifteenth year,
he again sent envoys to present a red dancing dragon colt and local products.
His envoys sometimes arrived two or three times a year,
or once every two years.
Their land bordered Yìzhōu,
and trade was constant.
The people, attracted by its profits,
often went there,
teaching them writing,
and acting as interpreters for them.
They gradually became more cunning and intelligent.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
they again presented local products.
Chóu died,
and his son Hēluózhēn succeeded him.
In the third year of Dàtōng,
he was appointed by imperial edict as General Who Pacifies the West, Protector-Colonel of the Qiāng, and Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two prefectures.
Zhēn died,
and his son Fófǔ inherited the title.
His crown prince also sent envoys to present a white dragon colt to the Crown Prince.
In the country of Gāochāng,
the Kǎn clan was in power.
Later, it was attacked and conquered by Jǔqú Màopú’s brother Wúhuì, the King of Héxī.
Their king, Kǎn Shuǎng, fled to Ruìruì.
Wúhuì occupied it and claimed kingship,
but his rule perished after one generation.
The people of the country then established the Qū clan as king,
named Jiā.

Yuán Wèi granted him the titles of General of Chariots and Cavalry, Minister of Works, Area Commander of all military affairs in Qínzhōu, Inspector of Qínzhōu, and Founding Duke of Jīnchéng Commandery.
He died after twenty-four years in office,
and was posthumously titled King Zhāowǔ.
His son Zǐjiān,

held the titles of Envoy with Imperial Credentials, General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry, Regular Mounted Attendant, Area Commander of all military affairs in Guāzhōu, Inspector of Guāzhōu, Founding Duke of Héxī Commandery,
〔三三〕 and Gāochāng King with Concurrent Authority of the Three Excellencies, and succeeded to the throne.
His country was formerly the land of Chēshī.
It bordered Hénán to the south,
connected to Dūnhuáng to the east,
adjoined Gūicí to the west,
and bordered Chìlè to the north.
It established forty-six garrisons,
including Jiāohé, Tiándì, Gāoníng, Línchuān, Héngjié, Liǔpó, Wūlín, Xīnxīng, Yóuníng, Shǐchāng, Dǔjìn, Báilì, etc.
〔三四〕 These were all their garrison names.
The officials included Four-Garrison Generals and various other generals,
Chief Clerk,
Aide-de-camp,
Palace Attendant Cadet,
Middle Army Cadet,
Conveyance Secretary,
Conveyance Clerk,
Counselor,
Commandant,
and Chief Scribe.
The language of the people of the country was largely similar to that of the Central Plain.
They had the Five Classics, historical records of successive dynasties, and collected works of various philosophers.
Their facial features resembled those of Gāolí.
They braided their hair and let it hang down their backs,
wearing long-bodied, small-sleeved robes and wide-crotched trousers.
Women braided their hair but did not let it hang down,
wearing brocade sashes, necklaces, rings, and bracelets.
Marriage involved six rites.
Their land was high and dry.
They built city walls of earth,
constructed houses with wood,
and covered them with earth.
The climate, hot and cold, was similar to Yìzhōu.
They cultivated all nine grains,
and people mostly ate fish, mutton, and beef.
They produced good horses, grape wine, and rock salt.
There were many trees and plants.
The fruit of a certain plant was like cotton pods,
with threads inside like fine hemp,
called *báidiézǐ*.
The people of the country often collected it to weave into cloth.
The cloth was very soft and white,
and used in trade.
There were "court crows"
that gathered every morning in front of the king’s palace,
forming ranks.
They were not afraid of people and dispersed only after sunrise.
During the Dàtóng era,
Zǐjiān sent envoys to present a singing salt pillow, grapes, good horses, felt carpets, and other items.
The country of Huá
was a branch of Chēshī.
In the first year of Hàn Yǒngjiàn,
the Eight Huá people assisted Bān Yǒng in attacking the northern barbarians and rendered meritorious service.
Yǒng memorialized for the Eight Huá to be appointed Marquis of the Rear Department Who Befriends Hàn.
From Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
communication with the Central Plain ceased.
Not until the fifteenth year of Tiānjiān,
did their king Yàndàiyīlì first send envoys to present local products.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
they again sent envoys to present a yellow lion, white sable furs, Persian brocade, and other items.
In the seventh year,
they again presented a memorial and tribute.
That day,
the Sītú (司徒) once wished to send a letter
to express a desire to mend his ways and make a fresh start.
Lǐ Lóngrén (李龍仁) had already been dispatched,
and was on the verge of setting out,
when it was heard that Fáng (房) was already far away.
So, the dispatch was halted.
It is unknown
whether Zūndào's (遵道) words here are true or false;
but since I have heard something,
I cannot but tell you everything.
As for the principles of good and bad fortune,
I imagine you will contemplate them yourself.
Jǐng (景) sent a reply saying: I have heard that for one to establish oneself and make a name,
it is a matter of righteousness;
what one holds most dear in one's person
is life itself.
If a matter aligns with righteousness,
then a loyal officer will not begrudge his body;
if punishments
are unjust,
then a gentleman will indeed value his life.
In the past, Wēizǐ (微子) went mad and departed from Yīn (殷),
and Chén Píng (陳平) harbored wisdom and turned his back on Chǔ (楚)—
there was good reason for this.
I am but a commoner from the countryside,
originally lacking in artistic skill.
Initially, I met Tiānzhù (天柱),
and was undeservedly granted a place in the counsels of the tent;
later, I encountered Yǒngxī (永熙),
and was entrusted with the responsibility of weapons and warfare.
Coming
out to serve the country,
I have spanned two cycles of twelve years,
facing danger and treading difficulty,
how could I avoid wind and frost?
Thus, I personally wore official robes,
and enjoyed imperial food,
wealth and nobility in my time,
honor throughout my
life.
Why would I suddenly raise flags and banners,
grasp drums and staffs,
and confront you facing north?
Why indeed?
It is truly out of fear of peril and demise,
lest I invite calamity and misfortune.
To sacrifice one's body
without righteousness
would mean both body and name are destroyed.
Why is this?
In the late part of last year,
Zūnwáng (尊王) fell ill;
the spirits did not bless the good,
and prayers offered no cure.
This led to favored individuals usurping
power and authority,
and eunuchs indulging in deceit and manipulation.
Superiors and subordinates suspected each other,
and trusted allies became disloyal.
My wife and children were at home,
besieged without cause.
As for Duàn Kāng's (段康) plot,
I knew not the
reason.
Lú Qián (廬潛) entered the army,
I was unsure why.
Cautious and careful,
I constantly felt trepidation.
With such a face,
how could I not doubt myself?
When the army returned to Chángshè (長社),
I hoped
to present my case,
but the letter had not yet reached,
when axes and battle-axes were already at hand.
Since our flags were facing each other,
and the distance was not far,
〔一０〕I sent urgent letters repeatedly,
also expressing my humble feelings;
but the commanders
relied on their might,
〔一一〕and disregarded me completely,
wielding halberds and pushing spearheads,
solely intent on slaughter.
They built a dam and flooded the area,
leaving only three planks.
Looking at each other,
our lives hung by a
thread.
Unable to bear death,
we fought outside the city.
Even beasts hate death,
and humans love life.
To surrender territory and be detained by Qín (秦) was not something we did willingly.
However, Zūnwáng (尊王) in the past
had given me much,
and we stood shoulder to shoulder to assist the imperial house.
Although our situations differed,
and there were slight variations in warmth and cold,
the Chéngxiàng (丞相) and Sītú (司徒) were merely like geese flying in formation.
Fortune, emolument, and official honor
are inherently bestowed by
Heaven.
To receive them after effort
〔一二〕is not a matter of contention.
To wish to swallow charcoal
—how absurd that is!
Moreover,
to steal another's property
is still called theft,
but when emolument leaves the public office,
it is taken by mutual consent.
Now, although the power of Wèi (魏) is declining,
the Mandate of Heaven has not changed.
To seek grace at a private residence
is hardly worth mentioning.
You kindly showed
“one cannot secure Hángǔ (函谷) Pass in the east,
and be controlled by others.”
This is like instructing me to be like the virtuous Jì Zhòng (祭仲) and praising the Jì (季) family.
A country without a master,
I have never
heard of this in the rites.
Acting unlawfully,
how can one take instruction?
I humbly believe that to share wealth to support the young,
is a matter that leads to a good end;
to give up one's home to save orphans,
who would call that a minor quarrel?
You further said that my
“forces are insufficient to strengthen myself,
and are as perilous as stacked eggs.”
However, Zhòu (紂) had hundreds of millions of people,
yet he was ultimately overthrown by ten worthy ministers.
Jié (桀) was victorious a hundred times,
but eventually
had no successor.
〔一三〕The battle of Yǐngchuān (潁川) is indeed a lesson from Yīn (殷).
Importance lies with people,
not with the tripod's virtue.
If one can be loyal and trustworthy,
though weak, one will surely become strong.
Deep sorrow gives rise to
sages;
what hardship is there in being in danger?
Furthermore, now Liáng Dàoyōngxī (梁道邕熙)
recruits with propriety,
clothing us in tiger patterns,
〔一四〕and binding us with good official positions.
They are about to enclose the Five Sacred Mountains
and pool the
Four Seas,
to sweep away evil and save the common people.
In the east, they control Ōuyuè (甌越);
in the west, they connect with Qiān (汧) and Lǒng (隴).
The troops of Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚) are fierce and strong,
with thousands of armored soldiers;
the infantry of Wú (吳) and cavalry of Jì (冀)
command
a hundred thousand archers.
Moreover, the righteous volunteers under my command are like a forest,
rising up with righteousness and taking power,
not by prior arrangement.
When a great wind blows,
dry branches will surely break;
when frost briefly falls,
autumn leaves
will naturally wither.
If this is considered weak,
who can be called strong?
You also falsely accuse me of duplicity,
and suspect me of serving two states.
Weighing human sentiments,
how could it come to this?
In the past, Chén Píng (陳平) abandoned Chǔ (楚),
and returning to Hàn (漢) became a king;
Bǎilǐ Xī (百里奚) left
Yú (虞),
and entering Qín (秦) became a hegemon.
Indeed, clarity or confusion depends on the ruler,
and acceptance or rejection depends on the times.
Acting with deference to rites,
Heaven will protect.
The letter claims that your soldiers and horses are fresh and strong,
and will launch an attack on a chosen day,
boasting of your strategic advantage,
and setting a date for complete annihilation.
I humbly believe that cold winds and white dew
belong to the same season.
When autumn winds
stir up dust,
how different are the horses' heads?
You only know the fierce contention of the north,
but are unaware of the alliance from the west and south.
If you wish to pursue your will on the road ahead,
you do not realize the pits and traps in
Its side.
It is as if saying to abandon danger and return to the true mandate,
and to turn misfortune into escape from the net.
They scoff at my foolishness and delusion,
and these also laugh at your obscurity and ignorance.
Now,
I have led two states,
raising banners for a northern expedition.
Bears and tigers rise together,
〔一五〕to recover the Central Plains.
Jīng, Xiāng, Guǎng, and Yǐng already belong to Guān Yòu.
Xiàngchéng and Xuánhù also submit to the Southern
Court.
It is taken by our own effort;
why need a gracious grant?
However, circumstances are not constant,
and there are myriad paths to reason.
For your sake,
it would be best to cede territory for a dual peace,
with a tripartite
standoff.
〔一六〕Yān, Wèi, Jìn, and Zhào are sufficient for mutual support and emolument.
Qí, Cáo, Sòng, and Lǔ entirely return to Dàliáng.
This allows me to contribute my strength to the Southern Court,
strengthening friendly relations in the north,
with bolts of
silk exchanged,
and war chariots motionless.
I would establish achievements for the present age,
and you would complete the heritage of your ancestors.
Each would secure their borders,
personally enjoying the seasons.
The common people would be well-governed and peaceful,
and the four
classes would live in security.
How could this compare to driving farmers from their fields,
and resisting a formidable enemy on three fronts,
avoiding weapons at the front and rear,
and facing spearheads in the heartland?
Even if Tài Gōng
were the general,
he could not survive.
If this is left to men of high intelligence,
how can success be achieved?
Then, reconsidering your letter, it states
that my wife and children are all held by Sī Kòu.
To use this as a threat,
perhaps it can make me turn back.
This must be based on a narrow suspicion,
not understanding the greater principle.
Why so?
In the past, Wáng Líng sided with Hàn,
but his mother remained and did not return.
Tài Shàng was imprisoned by Chǔ,
but he calmly asked for soup.
How much more so with one's wife and children?
Can they be of concern?
If you think their execution
is beneficial,
you cannot be stopped.
If killing them causes no harm,
it is merely a slaughter again.
My family's burden rests with you,
what concern is it of mine?
And what Zūn Dào conveyed
was largely not erroneous;
but being in chains,
I fear it may not have been fully expressed.
Therefore, I reiterate my words,
and further elaborate on the details.
What I hope for is a good plan,
and for you to
kindly reply in due course.
However, in the past, with the leader of the alliance,
our relationship was like a zither and a lute.
Slanderers came between us,
turning us into enemies.
Plucking the strings and drawing arrows,
I cannot but feel sorrow.
Tearing silk to return
this letter,
who knows what I can express?
In the twelfth month,
Jǐng led his army to besiege Qiáochéng but could not take it.
He retreated and attacked Chéngfù,
capturing it.
He also dispatched his Xíngtái Zuǒ Chéng, Wáng Wěi, and Zuǒ Mín Lángzhōng, Wáng Zé, to the court to present a strategy,
requesting that all the sons and younger brothers of Yuán be established as the Lord of Wèi,
to be assisted in a northern expedition.
This was granted.
An edict was issued, appointing Crown Prince Shèrén Yuán Zhēn as Xiányáng Wáng.
Once he crossed the Jiāng,
he would be permitted to assume the illegitimate throne,
and be supplied with an imperial carriage and escort.
Qí Wénxiāng also sent Mùróng Shàozōng to pursue Jǐng.
Jǐng retreated into Wōyáng.
He still had several thousand horses,
tens of thousands of armored soldiers,
and over ten thousand chariots.
They confronted each other north of Wō.
Jǐng's army ran out of food.
The soldiers were all northerners,
unwilling to cross south.
His generals, Bào Xiǎn and others, each led their divisions to surrender to Shàozōng.
Jǐng's army disintegrated.
He then, with a few trusted cavalry, crossed the Huái River from Xiáshí.
Gradually gathering scattered soldiers,
he obtained eight hundred horse and foot soldiers,
and fled to Shòuchūn.
The governor of the province, Wéi Àn, took him in.
Jǐng petitioned for demotion,
but a generous edict denied it,
still appointing him as Yùzhōu Mù,
his original official position remaining unchanged.
Once Jǐng occupied Shòuchūn,
he harbored thoughts of rebellion.
He recruited all the residents of the surrounding cities
as soldiers,
and arbitrarily suspended market tax and land rent.
All the daughters of the common people were distributed to his generals and soldiers.
He also petitioned for ten thousand bolts of brocade
for army cloaks.
Lǐngjūn Zhū Yì argued
that the brocade from the imperial treasury was only for awarding to those near and far,
and could not be used for military uniforms in border cities.
He requested that blue cloth be sent instead.
Jǐng received the cloth
and used it all for cloaks and shirts,
thus favoring the color blue.
He also stated that the weapons provided by the court
were mostly not refined.
He petitioned for blacksmiths from Dōngyě,
wishing to produce more.
An imperial order granted them all.
After Jǐng's defeat at Wōyáng,
he made many demands.
The imperial court was tolerant and generous,
never refusing.
Earlier,
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng commanded various armies to besiege Péngchéng.
His army was defeated and he was lost to Wèi.
By this time,
he sent an envoy back to relate Wèi's request to renew former friendly relations.
In the second month of the second year,
Gāozǔ again allied with Wèi.
Jǐng, hearing this, was alarmed,
and urgently submitted a firm remonstrance,
but Gāozǔ did not heed him.
Thereafter, his memorials and petitions became arrogant,
and his words disrespectful.
Póyáng Wáng Fàn, stationed at Héféi,
and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Yārén both repeatedly memorialized that Jǐng harbored rebellious intentions.
Lǐngjūn Zhū Yì said:
“Hóu Jǐng has only a few hundred rebellious renegades.
What can they do?”
He suppressed these reports and did not submit them,
and instead increased rewards,
thus making Jǐng's treacherous plot even more resolute.
He also learned that Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé resented the imperial court
and secretly ordered a liaison,
to which Zhèngdé agreed to initiate from within.
In the eighth month,
Jǐng finally raised troops in rebellion,
attacking Mǎtóu and Mùzhà,
capturing Tàishǒu Liú Shénmào and Shùzhǔ Cáo Qiú, and others.
Thereupon, an edict appointed the governor of all provinces, Póyáng Wáng Fàn, as Nándào Dūdū,
〔一七〕Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ Fēngshān Hóu Zhèngbiǎo as Běidào Dūdū,
Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Liǔ Zhònglǐ as Xīdào Dūdū,
and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì Péi Zhīgāo as Dōngdào Dūdū,
to jointly attack Jǐng.
They crossed from Lìyáng.
Also, Kōufǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī, Dānyáng Yǐn, Shàolíng Wáng Lún was ordered to hold the jié,
and oversee all the armies.
The garrison was there,
and fearing that your servant would restrict them,
they fled back without cause;
they also informed your servant that they intended to rebel.
Your Majesty did not rebuke them for disobeying orders and abandoning their posts,
but instead accepted their slanderous insinuations.
To treat your servant thus,
where can I find peace?
This is the eighth fault.
Although your servant's talent falls short of the ancients,
I have indeed experienced many things.
In governing the people and leading the multitude,
from youth to old age,
since I was young, I have been active,
often without a single unexecuted plan.
But when I committed myself to the
Dao,
I exhausted my loyal counsel,
yet every time I presented a memorial,
it was suppressed.
Zhū Cǎo arbitrarily controlled the military,
Zhōu Shízhēn was in overall charge of arms,
Lù Yàn and Xú Lín superintended
grain and silk.
All of them explicitly sought bribes;
without payment, nothing would proceed.
[二四] The truth of matters beyond the border
was decided in the secretariat of the Shèrényuàn;
the appointment of generals and the dispatching of armies
required memorials to the designated
authorities.
Your servant had no bribes to offer,
and thus was suppressed and obstructed.
This is the ninth fault.
The Prince of Póyáng garrisoned Héféi,
bordering your servant.
I respected him as a member of the imperial lineage,
always treating him with deference;
yet the heir-prince was cowardly and weak,
merely feigning preparedness and defense.
When your servant had an
envoy,
he would certainly attack and shoot at them,
sometimes publicly declaring your servant to be a rebel,
or accusing your servant of minor faults.
To attract and secure loyalty requires propriety;
how can a loyal and valiant person endure this?
This is the
tenth fault.
The remaining matters
cannot be fully enumerated.
Caught between advancement and retreat, I was in a dire straits,
and frequently submitted memorials.
My words were direct and my language strong,
which displeased the Dragon's Scales,
and thus a stern imperial edict was issued,
and I was immediately
to be attacked.
Shùnhuá was truly filial,
yet he still fled from his vicious father's rod;
Zhào Dùn was loyal and virtuous,
yet he did not punish the regicide.
What kinship or crime do I have,
that I should sit and await
annihilation?
Hán Xìn was heroic and exceptional,
he defeated Xiàng Yǔ and established the Hàn dynasty,
but in the end was cooked by a woman,
only then regretting Kuǎ Tōng's words.
Each time your servant reads historical accounts,
my heart often laughs at this.
How can I follow their overturned carriage,
and gratify Your Majesty's sycophantic officials?
Therefore, I have raised the army of Jìnyáng,
to cross the Chángjiāng amidst chaos,
wishing to ascend the scarlet steps,
tread upon the
patterned stone,
verbally present what is right and wrong,
point out what is good and bad,
execute the wicked officials by Your Majesty's side,
and cleanse the corrupt governance of the imperial court.
Then I shall return to guard my fief,
to preserve my loyalty and integrity;
this is your servant's utmost wish.
On the first day of the third month,
the people within the city, deeming Jǐng to have broken his oath,
raised beacons and beat drums, shouting.
Thereupon, Yáng Yārén, Liǔ Jìnglǐ, and the heir of Póyáng, Sì, advanced to the north of Dōngfǔ City.
Before their palisades were even erected,
they were attacked by Sòng Zǐxiān, one of Jǐng's generals,
and utterly defeated.
Several thousand drowned in the Huái River.
The rebels sent their severed heads to the palace gates.
Jǐng again sent Yú Zǐyuè,
requesting peace once more.
Emperor Wǔ sent the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Shěn Jùn to Jǐng's location.
Jǐng had no intention of leaving,
and Jùn firmly admonished him.
Jǐng was enraged,
and immediately released the water from in front of the stone gate,
attacking the city by a hundred routes,
day and night without ceasing.
The city then fell.
Thereupon, all imperial regalia, clothing, and playthings, as well as the concubines of the rear palace, were plundered.
Princes, marquises, and court officials were rounded up and sent to Yǒngfú Province,
and the guards of the two palaces were removed.
Wáng Wěi was made to guard Wǔdé Hall,
Yú Zǐyuè was stationed at Tàijí East Hall.
A forged imperial edict proclaimed a general amnesty throughout the realm,
and Jǐng declared himself Grand Commander, Controller of All Domestic and Foreign Military Affairs, and Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat,
retaining his titles of Attendant Censor, Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Grand Chancellor, and Prince.
Initially,
the piled corpses in the city could not be buried in time,
and there were those already dead but unburied,
or about to die but not yet expired.
Jǐng gathered them all and burned them,
the stench was perceptible for over ten *lǐ*.
The Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Bāo Zhèng, was critically ill;
the rebels dragged him out and burned him.
He writhed in the flames
for a long time before expiring.
Thereupon, all supporting armies dispersed.
Jǐng issued a forged edict saying:
"Recently,
traitorous officials usurped authority,
almost endangering the state.
Thanks to the Chancellor's brilliant rise,
assisting my person,
the regional commanders, governors, and prefects may each return to their original posts."
Xiāo Zhèngdé was demoted to Attendant Censor and Grand Marshal,
and all officials were restored to their ranks.
Jǐng sent Dǒng Shàoxiān to lead troops to attack Guǎnglíng.
The Inspector of Nányǎn Province, the heir of Nánkāng, Huìlǐ, surrendered the city to him.
Jǐng appointed Shàoxiān as Inspector of Nányǎn Province.
Initially,
the Inspector of Běiyǎn Province, the Marquis of Dìngxiāng, Zhī, and the Marquis of Xiāngtán, Tuì,
along with the former Inspector of Tóng Province, Guō Fèng, had jointly raised an army
to provide aid.
By this point,
Fèng plotted to join Jǐng with Huái'yīn.
Zhī and the others were unable to restrain him,
and all fled to Wèi.
Jǐng appointed Xiāo Nòngzhāng as Inspector of Běiyǎn Province.
The provincial people raised troops to resist him.
Jǐng sent the Palace Guard Commander Qiū Zǐyīng and the Palace Guard General Yáng Hǎi to lead troops to reinforce.
Hǎi killed Zǐyīng
and led his army to surrender to Wèi.
Wèi then occupied Huái'yīn.
Jǐng again sent the Commissioner Yú Zǐyuè and Zhāng Dàhēi to lead troops into Wú.
The Administrator of Wújùn, Yuán Jūnzhèng, welcomed their surrender.
After Zǐyuè and the others arrived,
they plundered Wú,
greatly extorting provisions,
forcing and abducting women and children,
and cruelly oppressing the populace.
There was no one in Wú who did not resent and hate them.
Thereupon, they each erected city walls and palisades to defend themselves.
In this month,
Jǐng moved his garrison to Xīzhōu,
and sent Commissioner Rèn Yuē as the Southern Circuit Administrator,
garrisoning Gūshú.
In the fifth month,
Gāozǔ passed away in the Wéndé Palace.
Previously,
after Táichéng had fallen,
Jǐng first sent Wáng Wěi and Chén Qìng to pay respects to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ said:
“Where is Jǐng now?
You may summon him.”
At that time, Gāozǔ was seated in the Wéndé Palace.
Jǐng then entered the court,
with five hundred armored soldiers as his personal guard,
and ascended the hall wearing a sword.
After bowing,
Gāozǔ asked:
“You have been in military service for a long time;
surely you are not too weary?”
Jǐng remained silent.
He then asked again:
“From which province are you,
that you dare to come here?”
Jǐng again could not answer,
and his attendants answered for him.
Upon leaving,
he said to Xiānggōng Wáng Sēngguì:
“I have often stood in the saddle facing the enemy,
with arrows and blades crossing,
yet my spirits were calm and unhurried,
without any fear.
Today, upon seeing Xiāo Gōng,
I was intimidated;
is this not the inviolable might of Heaven?
I must not see him again.”
Although Gāozǔ’s external power had been diminished,
his spirit remained indignant.
At times, when matters were reported to him,
he would frequently reject them.
Jǐng deeply respected and feared him,
and also did not dare to press him.
Jǐng sent soldiers to stand guard inside the palace chambers.
Gāozǔ asked Zhìjújiān Zhōu Shízhēn:
“Who are these people?”
He replied:
“The Chancellor.”
Gāozǔ then wrongly said:
“What Chancellor?”
He replied:
“It is Chancellor Hóu.”
Gāozǔ angrily said:
“His name is Jǐng,
what do you mean Chancellor!”
Thereafter,
for every request made,
many were not to his liking.
Even his imperial meals were curtailed,
and he consequently grieved and fell ill, and passed away.
Jǐng then secretly withheld the news of his death,
and provisionally interred him in the Zhāoyáng Palace.
Outside, none of the civil or military officials knew of it.
After more than twenty days,
the imperial coffin was moved to the Tàijí Front Hall,
and the Crown Prince was welcomed to ascend the imperial throne.
Thereupon, he issued a false edict pardoning people from the north who had been enslaved,
hoping to gain their service.
He also sent Yítóng Lái Liàng to lead troops to attack Xuānchéng.
Xuānchéng Nèishǐ Yáng Huá lured Liàng and beheaded him.
Jǐng again sent his general Lǐ Xiánmíng to punish Huá,
but Huá surrendered the commandery.
Jǐng sent Yítóng Sòng Zǐxiān and others to lead their forces eastward to Qiántáng.
Xīnchéng Shùzhǔ Dài Sēngyì held the county and resisted them.
[二五]
This month,
Jǐng sent Zhōngjūn Hóu Zǐjiàn into Wú’s army,
to arrest Yú Zǐyuè and Zhāng Dàhēi and return them to the capital for execution.
At that time, Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ Línchénggōng Dàlián held the province,
and Wúxīng Tàishǒu Zhāng Shèng held the commandery.
From Nánlíng upwards,
everyone was holding their ground.
The area where Jǐng’s commands were effective
was only west of Wújùn
and north of Nánlíng.
In the sixth month,
Jǐng appointed Yítóng Guō Yuánjiàn as Shàngshū Púyè, Běidào Xíngtái, and Commander of all Jiangbei military affairs,
stationed in Xīnqín.
Local people Lù Jí, Dài Wénjǔ, and others raised an army of over ten thousand men,
killed Jǐng’s Tàishǒu Sū Dányú,
and proclaimed former Huáinán Tàishǒu Wénchénghóu Níng as their leader
to resist Jǐng.
Sòng Zǐxiān heard of this and attacked them.
Jí and the others abandoned the city and fled.
Jǐng then divided the two counties of Hǎiyán and Xūpǔ in Wújùn to form Wǔyuán Commandery.
At this point,
Jǐng killed Xiāo Zhèngdé in the Yǒngfú Province.
He enfeoffed Yuán Luó as Xīqín Wáng,
and Yuán Jǐnglóng as Chénliú Wáng.
[二六] More than ten of the Yuán clan’s sons and younger brothers were enfeoffed as kings.
He appointed Liǔ Jìnglǐ as Shǐchíjié, Dàdūdū,
subordinate to the Grand Chancellor,
to participate in military affairs.
Jǐng sent his Zhōngjūn Hóu Zǐjiàn, Jiānxíngtái Liú Shénmào, and others to lead an army on an eastern campaign,
which conquered Wúxīng.
They captured Tàishǒu Zhāng Shèng and his son and sent them to the capital,
where Jǐng had them both killed.
Jǐng appointed Sòng Zǐxiān as Sītú,
Rèn Yuē as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Ěrzhū Jìbó, Chìluó Zǐtōng, Péng Jùn, Dǒng Shàoxiān, Zhāng Huàrén, Yú Qìng, Lǔ Bóhé, Hēxī Jīn, Shǐ Ānhé, Shí Línghù, Liú Guīyì,
all as Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
This month,
Póyáng Sìwáng Fàn led troops to Zàkǒu.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Xúnyángwáng Dàxīn intercepted him and moved westward.
Jǐng moved his camp to Gūshú.
Fàn’s generals Péi Zhītì and Xiàhóu Wēishēng surrendered to Jǐng with their forces.
In the eleventh month,
Sòng Zǐxiān attacked Qiántáng.
Dài Sēngyì surrendered.
Jǐng established Qiántáng as Línjiāng Commandery,
and Fùyáng as Fùchūn Commandery.
He appointed Wáng Wěi and Yuán Luó both as Yítóng Sānsī.
In the twelfth month,
Sòng Zǐxiān, Zhào Bóchāo, and Liú Shénmào advanced to attack Kuàijī.
Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ Línchénggōng Dàlián abandoned the city and fled.
Liú Shénmào was sent to pursue and capture him.
Jǐng appointed Péi Zhītì as Shǐchíjié, Píngxī Jiāngjūn, Hézhōu Cìshǐ,
and Xiàhóu Wēishēng as Shǐchíjié, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
This month,
an envoy from Báijì arrived.
Seeing the city and its surroundings in ruins,
he wailed outside the Duānmén gate.
Passersby who saw this could not help but shed tears.
Jǐng was greatly enraged when he heard this,
and sent him to be confined in Xiǎozhuāngyán Temple,
not allowing him to enter or exit.
In the first month of Dàbǎo First Year,
Jǐng issued a false edict to promote himself, granting forty palace guards,
and providing feathered banners and drums for his front and rear entourages,
and establishing Left and Right Chángshǐ and four Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Former Jiāngdū Lìng Zǔ Hào raised an army in Guǎnglíng,
beheaded Jǐng’s Cìshǐ Dǒng Shàoxiān,
and proclaimed former Tàizǐ Shèrén Xiāo Miǎn as Cìshǐ.
He also allied with the Wèi people for support,
and issued proclamations far and wide,
intending to campaign against Jǐng.
Jǐng was greatly alarmed when he heard this,
and immediately led Hóu Zǐjiàn and others out of Jīngkǒu,
gathering forces by land and water.
Hào fortified the city and defended it.
Jǐng attacked the city
and captured it.
Jǐng had Hào torn apart by chariots as a public display,
and all, young and old, in the city were beheaded.
He appointed Hóu Zǐjiàn as Supervisor of Nányǎnzhōu affairs.
This month,
Jǐng summoned Sòng Zǐxiān back to Jīngkǒu.
In the fourth month,
Jǐng appointed Yuán Sīqián as Dōngdào Xíngtái,
stationed in Qiántáng.
He appointed Hóu Zǐjiàn as Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wénchénghóu Níng raised an army in Wúxī Xiāng,
and within ten days,
his forces reached ten thousand.
He led them westward.
Jǐng’s Xiānggōng Mèng Zhèn and Hóu Zǐróng attacked and defeated them,
beheaded Níng,
and sent his head to Jǐng.
In the seventh month,
Jǐng established Zòujùn as Xīyǎnzhōu,
and Yángpíngjùn as Běiyǎnzhōu.
Rèn Yuē and Lú Huīlüè attacked Jìnxī Commandery
and killed Póyáng Shìzǐ Sì.
Jǐng appointed Wáng Wěi as Zhōngshū Jiān.
Rèn Yuē advanced and raided Jiāngzhōu.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Xúnyángwáng Dàxīn surrendered to him.
Shìzǔ, upon hearing that Jiāngzhōu had fallen,
sent Wèijūn Jiāngjūn Xú Wénshèng to lead his forces down to Wǔchāng
to resist Yuē.
Jǐng again issued a false edict to promote himself to Xiàngguó,
enfeoffed the twenty commanderies including Tàishān as Hànwáng,
and granted him the privilege of not needing to rush when entering court,
of being addressed without his personal name during salutations,
and of wearing a sword and shoes when ascending the hall,
following the precedent of Xiāo Hé.
Jǐng appointed Liǔ Jìnglǐ as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
Jiāng Xúnyì as Xiàngguó Zuǒchángshǐ,
Xú Hóng as Zuǒsīmǎ,
Lù Yuē as Yòuchángshǐ,
and Shěn Zhòng as Yòusīmǎ.
This month,
Jǐng led his fleet up to Wǎnkǒu.
In the tenth month,
robbers killed Wǔlín Hóu Zī at Guǎngmòmén.
Zī often entered and exited Tàizōng’s bedchamber,
which Jǐng’s faction resented,
and so they harmed him.
